lessons.title: Week 1 — Costing, pricing, records, and mobile-money controls
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 1 — Gharama, bei, rekodi, na M-Pesa
lessons.briefing:
A trade enterprise fails when price covers materials but not labour, rent, electricity, transport, defects, and tool replacement. Build a job-cost sheet: direct material, direct labour hours, overhead allocation, contingency, then margin. Cash received is not profit. Record deposits and balances against a numbered job card.

Mobile-money security: separate business and personal till where possible, never share PIN/OTP, verify prompts on the handset, and reconcile the platform statement to the sales book. A screenshot is not final proof if the handset did not receive the transaction. Refunds follow a controlled process.

Customer records contain personal data. Collect only what fulfilment requires, protect it, and set a retention period. Kenya DPA applies to a tailor’s WhatsApp list too.

lessons.title: Week 6 — Investment, compounding, diversification, and fraud checks
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 6 — Uwekezaji na hatari
lessons.briefing:
Saving protects near-term needs; investing accepts risk for longer-term growth. Order matters: control high-cost debt, build an emergency reserve, insure catastrophic risks, then invest money that is not needed next month. Match the instrument to the goal and horizon. Working-capital cash should not be locked in a volatile five-year asset.

Compounding means returns earn returns. Future value (simple annual example) = principal × (1 + rate)^years. KES 100,000 at 10% for three years becomes about KES 133,100 before tax/fees. Real return is approximately nominal return minus inflation: 10% return with 7% inflation grows purchasing power by only about 3% before costs. Fees reduce compounding every year.

Instruments have different risk/liquidity: regulated bank/SACCO deposits, Treasury bills/bonds, licensed money-market or unit trusts, listed shares, property, business reinvestment, and pensions. Do not describe any as guaranteed unless the lawful issuer guarantees it. Diversification spreads issuer, asset, sector, and timing risk; owning five companies in one collapsing industry is not full diversification. Investment in your own workshop can have high return but concentrates livelihood and capital in one place.

Due diligence: verify the provider and salesperson with the relevant Kenyan regulator (such as CMA, CBK, SASRA, RBA, or IRA depending on the product), read the prospectus/terms, know custody and withdrawal rules, understand return source, and keep statements. Scam signs: guaranteed unusually high monthly return, recruitment commissions, urgency, secrecy, personal mobile-money number, no audited information, and inability to explain the underlying asset. If you cannot explain how it earns money, do not invest. This curriculum is education, not personalised financial advice.
lessons.briefingSw: Akiba ni kwa muda mfupi; investment ina risk na muda. Emergency fund kwanza. Compound: principal × (1+rate)^years. Real return ni return minus inflation. Diversify. Hakikisha regulator (CMA/CBK/SASRA/RBA/IRA). Guaranteed high monthly return ni red flag.

lessons.title: Week 5 — Loans: true cost, affordability, collateral, and debt traps
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 5 — Mikopo na gharama yake
lessons.briefing:
Borrow for a productive purpose with a repayment source—not because an app says “limit available”. Define the asset or working-capital gap, amount, timing, expected extra cash, and fallback. Compare SACCO, bank, asset finance, supplier credit, government programme, digital lender, and equity. The lowest instalment is not automatically cheapest; a longer term can produce a larger total cost.

Read: principal, annual interest method, effective annual rate/APR where supplied, flat versus reducing balance, fees, insurance, taxes, grace period, instalment dates, late penalties, early-settlement charge, variable-rate clause, collateral, guarantor liability, and default process. Flat 12% on the original principal every year costs more than 12% on a reducing balance. Ask for the amortisation schedule and total amount payable in shillings.

Example (simplified): borrow KES 120,000 for 12 months at 12% flat plus KES 3,000 fee. Interest = 120,000 × 12% = 14,400; total = 137,400; average instalment = 11,450. A reducing-balance offer at the same stated 12% produces less interest if there are no extra fees. Compare cash received after deducted fees as well as total paid.

Affordability: debt-service coverage ratio (DSCR) = cash available for debt service ÷ required debt payments. A DSCR of 1.0 leaves no cushion; many businesses target above 1.2–1.5 depending on risk. Stress-test a 20% sales drop, delayed customer, exchange-rate increase, or machine downtime. Never borrow short-term expensive money to finance a long-term asset without a credible refinancing plan. Keep a debt register and pay on time to protect credit history.
lessons.briefingSw: Kopa kwa matumizi yanayozalisha cash. Linganisha principal, flat/reducing, APR, fees, insurance, penalty, collateral na total payable. Flat 12% si sawa na reducing 12%. DSCR = cash ya kulipa deni / instalment. Stress-test mauzo yakishuka.

lessons.title: Week 3 — Business model, operations, people, and customer systems
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 3 — Business model na usimamizi
lessons.briefing:
A business model explains who the customer is, what problem you solve, why they choose you, how you deliver, and how money remains after costs. “I repair cars” is too broad. “Same-day cooling-system diagnosis for matatu operators, with written pressure-test results” is a defined offer. Validate demand by interviewing customers, observing current alternatives, and testing a small paid service—not by asking friends whether they like the logo.

Operations turn promises into repeatable work. Map enquiry → inspection → quotation → deposit → job card → quality test → balance → handover → aftercare. Set capacity: productive hours, bay or machine availability, and lead time. Work in progress that sits waiting for parts ties up cash. Use reorder levels for fast-moving stock, approve suppliers by quality and delivery, and count inventory regularly. Separate customer parts from business stock and label every job.

People management requires job descriptions, safe induction, fair schedules, task supervision, feedback, and records. Do not call every worker an “independent contractor” to avoid lawful obligations. Separate duties where possible: the person receiving cash should not alone alter invoices and reconcile the till. Owner withdrawals are drawings, not wages hidden inside material cost.

Customer management: quote scope, exclusions, time, price, warranty, and approval for additional work. Complaints become data. Track on-time delivery, rework, gross margin, stock loss, repeat customers, and safety incidents. A weekly 20-minute review of those numbers is management; shouting at apprentices after a late job is not.

lessons.title: Sanitation Ladder & Faecal-Oral Disease Routes
lessons.titleSw: Ngazi ya Usafi na Njia za Magonjwa ya Kinyesi-Mdomo
lessons.briefing: In post-crisis communities the collapse of sewage infrastructure is one of the fastest triggers of epidemic disease. Before we build any toilet we must understand *why* sanitation saves lives — the faecal-oral transmission chain — and *how* to select the right technology from the WHO sanitation ladder for our specific context (soil type, water table, population density, water scarcity).
lessons.outline: The F-diagram (six pathways from faeces to mouth); WHO/JMP sanitation service ladder (open defecation to safely managed); R0 for cholera/typhoid/hepatitis A; pit latrine siting rules (15 m from wells, 30 m from streams); estimating daily faecal load (150-400 g wet weight/person/day); handwashing critical control points (after defecation, before food prep).

exercises.prompt: A cholera epidemic has an estimated R0 = 4 in a camp without latrines. A WASH team installs pit latrines with slabs and handwashing stations, blocking an estimated 65% of transmission pathways. What is the new approximate R_eff?
exercises.explanation:
R_eff = R0 x (1 - p_block) = 4 x (1 - 0.65) = 4 x 0.35 = 1.4. Outbreaks barely sustain when R_eff is just above 1, so further measures are still needed.

Why the other options are wrong: This would result from blocking only 35% of pathways. 0.6 would require blocking 85% of pathways. R_eff = R0 only if no intervention is made.

options.text: R_eff = 2.6
R_eff = 0.6
R_eff = 4.0
R_eff = 1.4

exercises.prompt: The minimum horizontal distance between a pit latrine and a hand-dug well is ___ metres, and the pit base must sit at least ___ metres above the seasonal high water table.
exercises.explanation: 15 m lateral separation reduces pathogen migration in most soil types. 2 m unsaturated zone allows sufficient natural attenuation of faecal coliforms before reaching the water table.

exercises.prompt: Match each F-diagram pathway to its correct example vector.
exercises.explanation: The F-diagram identifies six pathways. Breaking any one reduces disease burden; handwashing with soap (Fingers pathway) is the most cost-effective single intervention.

right.text: Unwashed hands transferring pathogens to food
Houseflies carrying faecal matter to open cooking pots
Vegetables irrigated with raw effluent
Drinking water contaminated at the source

exercises.prompt: A 300-person camp wants to site a pit latrine. The nearest borehole is 20 m away upslope. The seasonal high water table is 1.8 m below ground. Which siting problem is critical?
exercises.explanation:
The pit base must be 2 m or more above the seasonal high water table. At 1.8 m depth the margin is insufficient. A raised-platform latrine or UDDT is needed.

Why the other options are wrong: The minimum separation from a borehole is 15 m, not 30 m. 20 m is adequate. The 30 m rule applies to perennial streams. The latrine is downslope (borehole is upslope). Downslope siting is correct. The water table depth is the real problem. The water table at 1.8 m violates the 2 m minimum unsaturated zone rule.

options.text: The borehole is too close — 20 m is less than the 30 m minimum
Water table is too shallow — pit base will be below the 2 m safety margin
The latrine is upslope of the borehole — groundwater will be contaminated
No problem — this site meets all siting rules

exercises.prompt: A community of 400 people produces approximately ___ kg of wet faeces per day and ___ litres of urine per day.
exercises.explanation: Using mean values: 400 x 250 g = 100,000 g = 100 kg faeces; 400 x 1.5 L = 600 L urine. Urine contains about 80% of excreted nitrogen, making diversion for agricultural reuse highly valuable.

lessons.title: Urine-Diversion Dry Toilets (UDDTs)
lessons.titleSw: Vyoo vya Mgawaniko wa Mkojo (UDDT)
lessons.briefing: The urine-diversion dry toilet (UDDT) is the most resource-efficient sanitation technology for water-scarce off-grid communities. By separating urine from faeces at source, it eliminates odour, desiccates pathogens, and produces two safe agricultural inputs — liquid fertiliser and dry humus — without any water for flushing.
lessons.outline: Why separation matters (pathogen matrix and nutrient value); UDDT vault geometry and desiccation chamber sizing; cover material selection (ash, sawdust, dry soil); urine collection and storage — pH kill curve for pathogens; emptying protocols and safe use of dry humus; construction sequence — block or brick vault with fibreglass divider pedestal.

exercises.prompt: A family uses a UDDT and adds dry wood ash after every faecal deposit. What is the primary mechanism by which ash prevents pathogen survival?
exercises.explanation:
Wood ash pH is typically 10-12. A layer of ash around faecal matter raises local pH above 9, which is lethal to bacterial pathogens within hours and inactivates the most resistant helminth eggs within weeks.

Why the other options are wrong: Ash does absorb some moisture but its primary mechanism is alkalinity, not desiccation. Dry soil or sawdust are better pure-desiccant materials. Ash does not release chlorine. It works through alkalinity (high pH). Ash is not a nutrient for beneficial competitive bacteria. Its action is chemical — high pH.

options.text: Ash raises the pH above 9, creating conditions lethal to most faecal pathogens including Ascaris eggs
Ash absorbs all moisture, causing rapid physical dessication
Ash releases chlorine gas which disinfects the chamber
Ash is a nutrient that feeds beneficial bacteria which outcompete pathogens

exercises.prompt: A standard UDDT vault measures 0.8 m x 0.8 m x 1.0 m, giving a volume of ___ litres. One vault serves a 5-person family for approximately ___ months of filling before switching to the second vault.
exercises.explanation: Volume = 0.8 x 0.8 x 1.0 = 0.64 m3 = 640 L. At a generation rate of about 1 L/person/day of faeces + cover material, a 5-person family fills the vault in roughly 6 months, after which the second vault is used while the first desiccates for 6 more months.

exercises.prompt: Match each urine/faeces property to the correct percentage share.
exercises.explanation: These ratios explain why urine diversion recovers most of the fertiliser value while keeping the small faeces fraction manageable and dry.

left.text: Share of nitrogen excreted in urine
Share of toilet waste volume that is urine
Share of phosphorus excreted in urine
Share of potassium excreted in urine

exercises.prompt: Urine collected from a healthy household with no UTI cases should be stored for a minimum of how long before direct application to food crops?
exercises.explanation:
WHO guidelines recommend at least 1 month storage (during which pH rises to 8-9, inactivating most pathogens) and dilution 1:5 before applying to edible crops as an additional safety margin.

Why the other options are wrong: While urine from healthy individuals is nearly sterile, WHO still recommends 1 month storage before crop application to ensure pathogen inactivation and as a precautionary principle. 6 months is required only when diarrhoeal or UTI cases are present in the household. For a healthy household, 1 month is sufficient. 2 years is not required. At 1 month, pH-driven inactivation makes urine safe for most crops.

options.text: It can be applied immediately — urine is sterile
6 months — the same as for faecal humus
1 month, then dilute 1:5 with water before applying
2 years — urine is too dangerous without long storage

exercises.prompt: A family of 6 produces approximately ___ litres of urine per year. If maize requires 120 kg N/ha and urine contains 6 g N/L, this family's annual urine fertilises approximately ___ hectares of maize.
exercises.explanation: Urine volume = 6 x 1.5 L x 365 = 3,285 L per year. N available = 3,285 L x 6 g/L = 19,710 g = 19.7 kg N. Area fertilised = 19.7 kg / 120 kg/ha = 0.164 ha, approximately 0.16 ha.

lessons.title: Biogas Digesters from Organic Waste
lessons.titleSw: Vichombo vya Biogas kutoka Taka za Kikaboni
lessons.briefing: Anaerobic digestion converts organic waste — animal manure, food scraps, human excreta — into biogas (60-70% methane) for cooking and lighting, plus digestate, a liquid fertiliser superior to raw manure. A household fixed-dome digester replaces charcoal consumption, reduces deforestation, and permanently processes disease-carrying waste.
lessons.outline: Anaerobic digestion biochemistry (hydrolysis, acidogenesis, methanogenesis); fixed-dome vs floating-drum digester designs; digester sizing from daily feedstock; HRT and temperature effects; biogas quality, pressure, and appliance compatibility; digestate composition and safe agricultural use; troubleshooting (no gas, acidification, foam).

exercises.prompt: A biodigester has pH 6.1 after 3 weeks of operation with heavy kitchen scraps (mostly fat and protein). What is the most likely cause and fix?
exercises.explanation:
High-fat, high-protein kitchen scraps rapidly produce volatile fatty acids that overwhelm the slower methanogens, dropping pH below the viable range for methanogenesis. Stopping feed allows methanogens to catch up; lime water carefully neutralises pH.

Why the other options are wrong: Adding more feedstock when already acidified will worsen the VFA overload. The methanogenic Archaea need time to process existing acids. High temperature would accelerate digestion, not cause acidification. Acidification is from substrate overload. Methanogens are strict anaerobes. Introducing oxygen kills them and destroys the anaerobic process entirely.

options.text: Too little methane — add more feedstock to stimulate gas production
VFA overload acidifying the digester — stop feeding and add small doses of lime water
Temperature is too high — cool the digester
The digester needs oxygen — open the inlet to aerate

exercises.prompt: A family of 5 has 3 cattle producing 15 kg manure/day each. Diluted 1:1 with water at 25 degrees C with HRT of 35 days, the required digester volume (before the 25% safety factor) is ___ m3. With the safety factor, specify a ___ m3 digester.
exercises.explanation: Total manure = 3 x 15 = 45 kg/day. Diluted 1:1 = 90 L/day = 0.09 m3/day. Volume = 0.09 x 35 = 3.15 m3. Hmm — re-check: 2 cattle x 15 kg = 30 kg/day, diluted = 60 L = 0.06 m3/day, x 35 = 2.1 m3, x 1.25 = 2.625, specify 2.5 m3 (round down). If 3 cattle: 45 kg, 90 L, 0.09 m3/day x 35 = 3.15 m3, x 1.25 = 3.94, specify 4 m3. The worked example uses 2 cattle.

exercises.prompt: Match each anaerobic digestion stage to what it produces.
exercises.explanation: The three-stage cascade is sequential. If any stage is blocked (e.g., methanogens inhibited by low pH), the preceding products accumulate and further suppress the system.

right.text: Sugars and amino acids from complex polymers
Volatile fatty acids, hydrogen and CO2
Methane and carbon dioxide (biogas)

exercises.prompt: Why is a fixed-dome (Deenbandhu) digester preferred over a floating-drum (KVIC) design for off-grid East Africa?
exercises.explanation:
The fixed-dome uses locally available materials, has no rusting steel parts, and has a lifespan of 20+ years. The floating drum corrodes and must be repainted every few years — a significant maintenance burden in remote areas.

Why the other options are wrong: Biogas composition depends on feedstock and microbial conditions, not digester geometry. Both designs produce similar gas quality. Fixed-dome digesters are usually mesophilic (20-37 C). They do not self-heat to thermophilic range (50-65 C) without an external heat source. Fixed-dome pressure is variable (it rises as gas accumulates and slurry is pushed to the expansion chamber). Constant pressure is the advantage of the floating-drum design.

options.text: Produces higher methane percentage than floating-drum designs
Operates at thermophilic temperatures without external heating
Delivers constant gas pressure through a mechanical regulator
Built entirely from local brick and cement with no moving parts; lifespan exceeds 20 years and requires no steel maintenance

exercises.prompt: Biogas is approximately ___% methane and ___% carbon dioxide by volume. Its calorific value is approximately ___ kWh per cubic metre.
exercises.explanation: Typical biogas is 55-70% CH4 (commonly quoted as 60%) and 30-45% CO2. At 65% CH4 the calorific value is approximately 6 kWh/m3, compared to 10 kWh/m3 for pure methane. H2S at 0.1-1% contributes to corrosion of metal appliances if not scrubbed.

lessons.title: Composting Latrines & Vermicomposting
lessons.titleSw: Vyoo vya Mbolea na Ufugaji wa Minyoo
lessons.briefing: Composting latrines use aerobic thermophilic decomposition inside the vault to produce safe humus in 3-12 months. When earthworms (Eisenia fetida) are added — vermicomposting — the process accelerates 4-fold and produces vermicast, one of the highest-quality soil amendments available. Both approaches close the nutrient loop while destroying pathogens through heat and biological competition.
lessons.outline: Aerobic vs anaerobic decomposition and pathogen kill by heat; composting latrine (Clivus Multrum) vault design and airflow; C:N balance for thermophilic composting; Eisenia fetida biology and temperature limits; vermicomposting latrine design — worm bin integration; vermicast quality, application rates, and market value; combined UDDT + vermicompost system.

exercises.prompt: A composting latrine operator wants to achieve WHO Category A pathogen reduction (safe for food crops). What thermophilic condition must the pile sustain?
exercises.explanation:
WHO guidelines for composting require 55 °C for a minimum of 3 days with at least one turning to expose all material to thermophilic conditions. This achieves Category A, suitable for direct application to food crops.

Why the other options are wrong: While 70 °C would kill pathogens, composting piles rarely reach this temperature uniformly. WHO requires sustained 55 °C over 3 days with turning to ensure all material is treated. 35 °C is insufficient for thermal kill of Ascaris eggs. 55 °C is the minimum required for the thermophilic kill mechanism. A well-managed thermophilic composting latrine achieves Category A in 3 days of sustained 55 °C. The 2-year period is a conservative rule of thumb for cold piles, not a universal requirement.

options.text: 70 °C for 1 hour — a short burst of extreme heat is sufficient
Any temperature above 35 °C for 30 days achieves pathogen kill
55 °C for at least 3 days with turning to ensure uniform heat penetration
Composting latrines never reach pathogen-safe levels — always co-compost for 2 years

exercises.prompt: Eisenia fetida worms consume up to their body weight per day and cannot survive temperatures above ___ °C. A family of 5 generating 1.25 kg faeces per day needs at least ___ kg of worms in the vermicompost vault.
exercises.explanation: E. fetida dies above 35 °C. Processing rate is 0.5 kg waste per kg worms per day. To process 1.25 kg/day: 1.25 / 0.5 = 2.5 kg worms needed. At about 2,000 worms per kg this is approximately 5,000 individual worms.

exercises.prompt: Match each carbon material to its approximate C:N ratio.
exercises.explanation: The target C:N for thermophilic composting is 25-30:1. Blending nitrogen-rich faeces (8:1) with high-carbon materials restores the balance. Wood chips require the smallest volume per scoop due to their very high C:N ratio.

exercises.prompt: Why must vermicast from a cold vermicomposting latrine be stored for 6 months before applying to food crops?
exercises.explanation:
Ascaris eggs are the most thermally resistant pathogen. Cold vermicomposting does not reach 55 °C, so thermal kill is absent. 6 months of storage at ambient temperature allows enough time for natural die-off through desiccation and biological antagonism.

Why the other options are wrong: E. fetida in vermicast is not a human pathogen. The concern is faecal pathogens, particularly Ascaris eggs, not worms. Vermicast is not chemically toxic. The storage requirement is purely for pathogen inactivation. Vermicast nutrients (especially ammoniacal N) are highly plant-available from day one. The storage requirement is for pathogen safety, not nutrient availability.

options.text: The worms in the vermicast will contaminate crops if applied immediately
Vermicast is chemically toxic when fresh and must be neutralised by time
Worms do not generate sufficient heat to kill Ascaris eggs, so extended storage time is needed for biological and desiccation inactivation
Nutrients in fresh vermicast are not yet plant-available

exercises.prompt: Vermicast contains approximately ___% available nitrogen and ___% phosphorus by dry weight, compared to conventional compost at 0.75% N and 0.4% P. In Kenya, vermicast sells for approximately ___ KES per kilogram.
exercises.explanation: Vermicast typical analysis: 1.5-2.5% N (use 2.0% midpoint), 0.8-1.2% P (use 1.0%). Conventional compost runs 0.5-1.0% N, 0.3-0.5% P — roughly half as concentrated. Vermicast commands KES 30-80/kg on the Kenyan organic market vs KES 5-10/kg for conventional compost, making vermicomposting latrines both hygienic and economically attractive.

lessons.title: Constructed Wetlands & Greywater Treatment
lessons.titleSw: Mabwawa ya Ujenzi na Matibabu ya Maji Kijivu
lessons.briefing: Greywater (kitchen and laundry wastewater) represents 60-75% of a household's wastewater and is far easier to treat than blackwater. Constructed wetlands — engineered shallow gravel beds planted with Phragmites or Canna — provide passive, low-energy treatment of greywater and secondary effluent, producing water safe for irrigation while building soil carbon and habitat.
lessons.outline: Greywater composition and typical contaminants; simple treatment train (screening, settling, wetland); HSSF wetland design; vertical flow wetland for higher-rate treatment; plant selection (Phragmites, Canna, Typha); sizing calculations (hydraulic loading rate, BOD5 removal); overflow management and mosquito control; photo capture — field wetland assessment.

exercises.prompt: A household HSSF wetland has influent BOD5 of 180 mg/L, flow = 0.4 m3/day, area = 12 m2, and areal rate constant k = 0.15 m/day. What is the approximate effluent BOD5?
exercises.explanation:
Ce/Ci = exp(-0.15 x 12 / 0.4) = exp(-4.5) = 0.011. Ce = 180 x 0.011 = 1.98 mg/L, approximately 1.8-2.0 mg/L. This meets WHO effluent standards for restricted irrigation.

Why the other options are wrong: 18 mg/L would require exp(-k*A/Q) = 0.1, meaning k*A/Q = 2.3. With these values k*A/Q = 4.5, giving much better than 18 mg/L removal. 50% removal would occur if Ce/Ci = 0.5. Constructed wetlands at these design parameters achieve far greater than 50% BOD5 removal. The first-order model gives approximately 2 mg/L, not 0.1 mg/L. Complete sterilisation does not occur in a biological treatment wetland.

options.text: About 18 mg/L — adequate for tree irrigation only
About 90 mg/L — only 50% removal
About 0.1 mg/L — complete sterilisation
About 1.8 mg/L — excellent treatment

exercises.prompt: A household of 8 people generates 50 L greywater per person per day. At a hydraulic loading rate of 25 L/m2/day, the required HSSF wetland area is ___ m2. A rectangular bed 4 m wide would be ___ m long.
exercises.explanation: Total flow = 8 x 50 = 400 L/day. Area = 400 / 25 = 16 m2. Length = 16 m2 / 4 m width = 4 m long. The bed would be 4 m x 4 m x 0.6 m gravel depth — a compact footprint achievable on a standard homestead plot.

exercises.prompt: Match each wetland plant species to its primary characteristic.
exercises.explanation: Plant selection matches species strengths to functional roles. Phragmites is the workhorse for treatment; Canna and Typha add value through harvestable products; Vetiver stabilises embankments.

right.text: Robust common reed — best for primary HSSF treatment at high BOD5
Flowering plant with edible rhizome and good phosphorus uptake
Cattail/bulrush — fast-growing, leaves harvested for basket weaving
Drought-tolerant edge plant for erosion control around wetland beds

exercises.prompt: Why does a horizontal subsurface flow (HSSF) wetland pose a lower mosquito breeding risk than a surface-flow pond?
exercises.explanation:
In HSSF design, water level is maintained 50-100 mm below the gravel surface. Mosquitoes require standing water on an accessible surface to lay eggs. The dry gravel surface prevents breeding.

Why the other options are wrong: Wetland plants do not produce insecticide compounds. The mosquito control comes from the physical design (subsurface flow), not chemical repellence. Mosquito larvae are aquatic and need standing water — they cannot survive in unsaturated gravel regardless of pore size. The key is keeping water below the surface. HSSF wetlands are biological treatment systems. Adding chlorine would kill the beneficial microbes that provide treatment. No disinfectant is used.

options.text: The plants in the wetland release insecticide-like compounds that repel mosquitoes
Gravel is too coarse for mosquito larvae to survive in
HSSF wetlands are treated with chlorine which kills larvae
Water flows entirely below the gravel surface — the top of the bed stays dry so mosquitoes cannot lay eggs

exercises.prompt: Walk to a greywater discharge point near your household or community (kitchen drain, laundry area, or roadside). Photograph the area and assess it against the five criteria in the rubric below. Submit your best-quality photo with a written assessment.
exercises.explanation: Unmanaged greywater creates mosquito habitat, nutrient runoff to water bodies, and slipping hazards. This exercise builds the habit of seeing greywater as a resource to capture rather than a waste to dump.

rubric.criterion: Photo clearly shows the greywater discharge point or drain outlet
Written assessment identifies at least two contaminants or hazards present
Learner recommends appropriate treatment option (grease trap, wetland, or soakaway) with reason
Photo quality — clear, in focus, good natural light
Assessment includes estimated daily volume generated at this point

lessons.title: Final circuits, cables, and conduit
lessons.titleSw: Circuits, kebo, na conduit
lessons.briefing:
Final circuits are designed: load, length, grouping, insulation, and protective device. A 2.5 mm² radial or ring for sockets is common in examples you will meet — but you follow the drawing and calculation, not a rumour. Cooker and shower circuits are dedicated for a reason.

Ring final circuits need both legs continuous; a break turns them into two overloaded radials. Test continuity of ring (r1, rn, r2) as taught. Never spur a spur if the method forbids it.

PVC conduit: cut square, deburr so insulation is not stripped, bend with a spring, and do not overfill. Draw wires with lubricant approved for PVC, not cooking oil. Leave draw wires in spare ways. Box entries must not have sharp edges.

Label circuits in the CU. The next electrician’s life depends on your marker pen.
lessons.briefingSw: Fuata drawing. Ring lazima iwe complete. Conduit kata sawa, deburr, usijaze kupita kiasi. Andika majina ya circuits kwenye CU.

exercises.explanation: That is why ring tests exist.

options.text: Safer

exercises.explanation: Design, not tradition alone.

exercises.explanation: Unlabelled boards cause wrong isolation.

options.text: Decoration

The painter

exercises.explanation: Ring finals are tested for continuity of both legs.

exercises.hint: Protective device must protect the cable.
exercises.explanation: Undersized conductors on big MCBs are fire starters.

options.text: Leave it — it has worked two weeks

lessons.title: Earthing, bonding, and protective devices
lessons.titleSw: Earthing, bonding, na vifaa vya ulinzi
lessons.briefing:
The earth conductor exists so that a live-to-metal fault makes a large current (or an RCD imbalance) and the protective device disconnects. It is not a spare neutral. Combining earth and neutral incorrectly (wrong use of PEN, missing links, bootleg earths) is how cases stay live.

Kenya installations you meet may be TN-S, TN-C-S, or TT at the origin — follow the existing earthing arrangement and the spec; do not invent a mix. Main bonding of pipes and extra bonding in bathrooms follow the drawing and regulations you are taught.

MCBs (or fuses) protect against overcurrent. RCDs protect against earth leakage / shock in many final circuits. An MCB will not always trip on a high-resistance earth fault that still can kill. That is why testing and correct device selection matter.

Never “borrow” an earth from a neighbouring circuit’s sheath unless the design says so. Never disconnect earths to stop a nuisance trip without finding the fault.
lessons.briefingSw: Earth ni njia ya fault, si neutral. MCB hulinda overcurrent; RCD hulinda uvujaji. Usichanganye earth na neutral. Usikate earth ili “kutuliza” trip.

exercises.prompt: The earth wire exists primarily to:
exercises.explanation: Earthing lets the MCB/fuse/RCD clear a fault instead of leaving metalwork live.

options.text: Carry current in normal use like the live
Provide a low-impedance path so protective devices disconnect on a fault
Make the cable look thicker
Power the doorbell only

exercises.prompt: An RCD is mainly intended to detect:
exercises.explanation: RCD ≠ MCB. They complement each other.

options.text: Overload on a cooker only
Imbalance between live and neutral (earth leakage)
Whether the bulb is LED
Wi-Fi strength

exercises.prompt: Using the water pipe as the only earth without a proper electrode/arrangement is:
exercises.explanation: Bonding is not a substitute for a designed earth.

options.text: Always excellent
Dangerous and non-compliant in modern practice
Required by all cookers
A type of MCB

exercises.prompt: Nuisance RCD trips should be solved by:
exercises.explanation: Defeating protection is how shocks happen later.

options.text: Removing the earth
Insulation and leakage investigation, not defeating protection
Fitting a bigger fuse in the RCD
Wetting the CU

exercises.prompt: A device that trips when live and neutral currents differ is an ___.
exercises.hint: Residual Current Device. RCCB is also used.
exercises.explanation: RCD/RCCB detects imbalance. Store that abbreviation.

exercises.prompt: A metal kettle case tingles. The socket earth pin is not connected. What is correct?
exercises.hint: Class I metal appliances need a working earth.
exercises.explanation: A missing earth on Class I gear is a serious defect. Isolate, tag, repair.

options.text: Tell the user to wear rubber shoes and continue
Take the kettle out of service and restore the earth at socket and flex
Swap live and neutral only
Paint the kettle

lessons.title: Safe isolation and proving dead
lessons.titleSw: Isolation salama na kuthibitisha kifo cha current
lessons.briefing:
Treat every circuit as live until you prove it dead. The sequence taught in competent installation practice is: identify, isolate, lock/tag, test your tester on a known live source (or proving unit), test the circuit conductors, then test the tester again. A dead lamp on a tester with a flat battery has killed people.

The consumer unit is not a junk drawer. Stand on dry footing, use insulated tools, and do not lean on earth pipes. Remove loads, then isolate. Single-pole isolation of a circuit that still has a borrowed neutral is a trap — understand the wiring before you trust a switch.

Permits and college lock-out boards exist because “I thought it was off” is not a defence. If you cannot lock, you must still control the device and put a warning. Never use the installation’s own socket as the only proof that your tester works while you are already inside the CU.

First aid: you do not become the second casualty. Isolate, then help. That order is part of the unit.
lessons.briefingSw: Chukulia waya kuwa hai. Isolate, funga, jaribu tester, jaribu circuit, jaribu tester tena. Usitumie tester na betri mbovu. Elewa neutral. Usijaribu kuokoa mtu kabla ya kuzima umeme.

exercises.prompt: What is the first action before opening a consumer unit for work?
exercises.explanation: Proving dead prevents electrocution. Never use the circuit itself as the only proof that the tester works.

options.text: Tighten every screw you see
Isolate the supply and prove dead with a proving unit / known live source
Stand in water for better earth
Remove the earth first

exercises.prompt: Why test the tester before and after proving a circuit dead?
exercises.explanation: The proving unit (or known live) confirms the instrument still works.

options.text: To waste time

NITA requires three testers

lessons.title: Week 6 — Maintenance and breakdown: diagnose, isolate, restore
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 6 — Matengenezo na breakdown
lessons.briefing:
After install and test, CDACC expects maintenance and breakdown competence. Planned maintenance: inspect, tighten (to torque, not “until it squeals”), clean, test RCDs at recommended intervals, IR sample, thermal scan if you have it, and record. A consumer unit full of dust and insects is a maintenance fail waiting to become a fire.

Breakdown: take a symptom (no lights ring 2, RCD trip, burning smell). Isolate and prove dead. Then diagnose — lost neutral, overloaded circuit, failed lamp, moisture in an outside fitting, nuisance RCD from a leaking kettle. Replacing every MCB “to be sure” is not diagnosis. Use the test instruments from the testing week.

Root cause: if an RCD trips, find the leaking appliance or damp fitting; do not bridge the RCD. If a motor trips on overload, check mechanical lock and current, not only the starter coil. Restore: refit covers, re-test the affected circuit, and write the job card. Temporary tails hanging out of a CU are not a completed breakdown job.

Competence includes knowing the limit of your authorised work. Service heads and company meters are not yours to open. Escalate.
lessons.briefingSw: Matengenezo: kaza, safisha, jaribu RCD, andika. Breakdown: isolate, gundua sababu, usibadilishe kila MCB. Usiruke RCD. Job card. Usifungue meter ya kampuni.

lessons.title: Week 5 — Plan the installation: survey, load, and drawings
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 5 — Panga ufungaji: survey, mzigo, na michoro
lessons.briefing:
CDACC electrical cores begin with planning, not with a coil of twin-and-earth. Conduct a site survey: construction type, routes, existing supply capacity, and hazards (wet, flammable, overhead lines). Take measurements. Write a survey note the supervisor can use. “It looked fine” is not a survey.

Load estimation: list luminaires, sockets (diversified as taught), cookers, motors, and future spare. Size cables and protective devices to IEE/IEC practice as in your college tables — current-carrying capacity, voltage drop, and fault protection must all pass. An MCB bigger than the cable is a fire design. Record system sizes and share them.

Drawings: obtain the design, produce a working drawing and a materials list (cables, accessories, glands, trunking). Logistics: access, storage, permits to work, isolation of the existing supply, and a team with named roles. Raising a permit is an element of the unit, not bureaucracy you skip.

This week’s artefact: a one-page load schedule for a two-bedroom staff house plus a materials list and a simple lighting/power layout. That is how  the installation unit is evidenced before you chase conduits.
lessons.briefingSw: Survey wa site, hatari, na vipimo. Kadiria mzigo. Ukubwa wa kebo na MCB kwa IEE — voltage drop na fault. Mchoro wa kazi, orodha ya vifaa, permit. Usianze conduit bila mpango.

exercises.prompt: A 32 A MCB protecting 1.5 mm² lighting cable is wrong because:
exercises.explanation: Planning includes matching protection to CCC of the cable.

options.text: MCBs must always be 6 A
The device will not protect the conductor — fire risk
Lighting cannot use MCBs
IEE requires aluminium only

exercises.explanation: Long small cables fail voltage drop even if CCC looks fine in a short run.

lessons.title: Inspection and testing basics
lessons.titleSw: Ukaguzi na majaribio
lessons.briefing:
Dead tests before live tests. Continuity of protective conductors (including bonding), insulation resistance (typically 500 V IR tester on many LV circuits — follow the instrument and standard you were taught), and polarity: live to the switch, not the other way round.

A failed IR (low megohms) means moisture, damaged insulation, or connected equipment. Disconnect lamps and sensitive electronics as instructed before IR tests. Do not IR-test a circuit with a surge-protected socket still in, then blame the student meter.

When the instructor allows live testing: earth-fault loop and RCD trip times are measured with the correct instrument. Record results on the schedule. A test not written down did not happen for assessment.

Never energise an installation that failed dead tests. Paperwork is part of competence.
lessons.briefingSw: Majaribio ya dead kwanza: continuity, insulation, polarity. Kisha live tests kwa ruhusa. Andika matokeo. Usitie umeme kama dead tests zimeshindwa.

exercises.prompt: Insulation resistance tests are usually done:
exercises.explanation: IR on a live circuit is wrong practice.

options.text: After you hand the keys over, never before
As a dead test before energising
Only on the kettle
With a wet finger

exercises.prompt: Polarity on a lighting circuit means:
exercises.explanation: A switch in the neutral leaves the lampholder live when “off”.

options.text: Earth is optional

The lamp cap is painted

exercises.prompt: Low IR might be caused by:
exercises.hint: Paths to earth that should not exist.
exercises.explanation: Investigate; do not just raise the MCB.

options.text: Perfect dry cables
Damp, damaged insulation, or connected electronic loads
Correct bonding only
Too many labels

exercises.prompt: Test results belong:
exercises.explanation: Failed results still get recorded, then defects repaired.

options.text: In your head
On the installation schedule / certificate as taught
On WhatsApp status
Only if they pass

exercises.prompt: Confirming that the switch is in the live conductor is a ___ test.
exercises.hint: Live vs neutral the right way.
exercises.explanation: Polarity failures leave fittings live when switched off.

exercises.prompt: IR reads 0.02 MΩ on a new lighting radial. Trainee wants to connect the supply because the lamps work on a test lead. You should:

exercises.explanation: 0.02 MΩ is a serious insulation failure.

options.text: Energise — lamps working is enough

Fit a larger MCB

lessons.title: AC Fundamentals — Single-Phase vs 3-Phase & Power Factor
lessons.titleSw: Misingi ya Umeme wa AC — Awamu Moja, Awamu Tatu na Power Factor
lessons.briefing: Direct current (DC) powers localized battery banks and electronics, but alternating current (AC) dominates power distribution because transformers can step AC voltages up to transmission levels with minimal copper conductor losses. In off-grid mini-grids, an electrical technician must master single-phase (230V) and three-phase (400V) line-to-line relationships, the power triangle (kW, kVA, kVAR), and reactive power compensation. Operating inductive motors with poor power factor overheats generators, trips breakers, and wastes up to 40% of precious generated capacity.
lessons.outline: Sinusoidal alternating waveforms (frequency, period, RMS voltage Vrms = Vpeak / sqrt(2)); single-phase 230V systems vs 3-phase 400V star (wye) and delta configurations; the line-to-line vs line-to-neutral relationship (V_LL = sqrt(3) * V_LN); neutral conductor currents and phase balancing; the AC power triangle: Real Power (P in kW), Reactive Power (Q in kVAR), Apparent Power (S in kVA); Power Factor (cos phi); inductive vs capacitive loads; calculating power factor correction capacitor banks to restore 0.70 PF up to 0.95 PF.

exercises.prompt: A 3-phase star (wye) mini-grid distribution line in Kenya delivers 230 V from each phase conductor to the neutral wire. What is the line-to-line voltage measured between Phase 1 and Phase 2?
exercises.explanation:
In a 3-phase star system, line-to-line voltage is √3 times the line-to-neutral voltage: V_LL = 230 × 1.732 ≈ 398.4 V (standardized as 400 V).

Why the other options are wrong: Phase voltages are 120° apart in time, not in phase; simple arithmetic addition is incorrect. Vector addition yields √3 × V_LN. 230 V is the line-to-neutral voltage, not line-to-line. 325 V is the peak voltage of a 230 V RMS wave, not the 3-phase line-to-line relationship.

options.text: Approximately 400 V (230 V × √3)

exercises.prompt: In a sinusoidal 230 V RMS AC electrical system, the peak voltage reached during each oscillation crest is approximately ___ Volts. If an inductive motor draws 10 kW at a power factor of 0.80, the apparent power load imposed on the generator is ___ kVA.
exercises.explanation: V_peak = V_RMS × √2 = 230 × 1.414 ≈ 325.2 V. Apparent power S = P / PF = 10 kW / 0.80 = 12.5 kVA. The generator must supply 12.5 kVA of winding and magnetic capacity to deliver 10 kW of shaft work.

exercises.prompt: Match each AC electrical power parameter to its unit and physical meaning.
exercises.explanation: P does physical work (kW); Q sustains magnetizing flux (kVAR); S is the total vector volt-amperes (kVA); PF indicates system efficiency.

right.text: Kilowatts (kW) — actual mechanical work, heating, and light
kVAR — magnetic field energy oscillating between motor and source
kVA — vector sum total load capacity required from generators
Dimensionless ratio of real power divided by apparent power (kW / kVA)

exercises.prompt: Why does connecting a capacitor bank across the terminal box of a heavy induction motor improve the performance of an off-grid diesel generator?
exercises.explanation:
Induction motors require reactive power (kVAR) to magnetize their stators. Sourcing this reactive current locally from parallel capacitors eliminates the need to transmit kVAR from the generator, reducing total line current, line voltage drops, and generator rotor heating.

Why the other options are wrong: Induction motors operate strictly on alternating current; capacitors do not rectify to DC. Engine RPM is controlled by the mechanical governor (governing frequency at 50 Hz). Capacitors have no effect on AC frequency.

options.text: Capacitors convert AC current into pure DC power inside the motor
Capacitors increase the engine RPM of the diesel generator
Capacitors step up the frequency from 50 Hz to 60 Hz
Capacitors supply local leading reactive current directly to the motor's magnetic field, reducing lagging kVAR drawn through the cables and lowering generator winding heat

exercises.prompt: In a balanced 3-phase 4-wire star distribution mini-grid with identical 10 A resistive loads on each of the three phases, the current flowing back through the neutral wire is ___ Amperes.
exercises.explanation: Because the three phase currents are equal in amplitude and separated by exactly 120 degrees, their instantaneous vector sum cancels out completely: I_N = I_1 + I_2 + I_3 = 0 A.

lessons.title: Alternators, Generators & Automatic Voltage Regulators
lessons.titleSw: Jenereta za Umeme, Alternator na Vidhibiti vya Voltage (AVR)
lessons.briefing: Whether driven by a diesel engine, biomass gasifier, or hydro turbine, the synchronous alternator is the beating heart of an autonomous AC electrical grid. Converting mechanical shaft rotation into stable 230V/400V 50Hz electricity requires understanding rotor-stator electromagnetic induction, brushless exciter architectures, and closed-loop Automatic Voltage Regulators (AVR). When heavy inductive loads switch on, generator voltage plunges without immediate excitation response. This lesson covers synchronous speed physics, residual magnetism flash procedures, AVR tuning, and diode bridge diagnosis.
lessons.outline: Synchronous speed formula N = (120 * f) / P; 2-pole (3000 RPM) vs 4-pole (1500 RPM) alternators; revolving field vs revolving armature architectures; brushless exciter system (pilot exciter, rotating 3-phase rectifier diode bridge, main rotor field); loss of residual magnetism and 12V battery "field flashing" protocol; Automatic Voltage Regulator (AVR) feedback loop, sensing transformers, and stability/voltage trimpot tuning; generator derating factors (ambient temperature, altitude > 1000m); troubleshooting low voltage, hunting oscillations, and diode failures.

exercises.prompt: A stationary 4-pole synchronous diesel generator is being commissioned in Kenya to power a 50 Hz micro-grid. What exact rotational speed in RPM must the engine mechanical governor maintain?
exercises.explanation:
N = (120 × f) / P = (120 × 50) / 4 = 6000 / 4 = 1,500 RPM. A 4-pole alternator must spin at exactly 1,500 RPM to produce 50 Hz AC.

Why the other options are wrong: 3,000 RPM corresponds to a 2-pole generator (typical of small portable petrol sets), not a 4-pole unit. 1,800 RPM is the standard speed for 60 Hz grids (e.g., North America), not 50 Hz. 1,000 RPM corresponds to a 6-pole machine.

exercises.prompt: When an idle generator fails to generate voltage due to loss of residual magnetism in the exciter iron, the recovery technique of connecting a 12V DC battery briefly to the F+ and F- field terminals is called field ___.
exercises.explanation: Field flashing injects a DC current pulse from an external battery to re-align magnetic domains in the exciter stator core, restoring residual flux.

exercises.prompt: Match each alternator subsystem to its functional engineering duty.
exercises.explanation: AVR controls voltage; diodes provide brushless DC on the shaft; UFRO protects windings during overloads; governor maintains 50 Hz shaft speed.

right.text: Senses stator AC output and dynamically controls DC exciter current
Rectifies spinning AC exciter armature output into DC for main rotor
Slashes generator voltage if engine RPM bogs down below 47 Hz
Throttles fuel injection to maintain steady 1500 RPM / 50 Hz frequency

exercises.prompt: A generator operator notices that the generator voltage and diesel engine tone are pulsing up and down cyclically every 1–2 seconds ('hunting') even with a steady electrical load. Which AVR trimpot adjustment fixes this issue?
exercises.explanation:
Hunting indicates loop instability in the AVR's voltage feedback loop. Increasing the STABILITY dampening prevents over-correction and stabilizes the output voltage.

Why the other options are wrong: Increasing voltage does not fix loop instability and will over-voltage connected appliances. Disconnecting ground is extremely dangerous and does not address AVR hunting. Hunting is a control tuning phenomenon, not an insulation breakdown.

options.text: Turn the VOLT trimpot to maximum
Disconnect the neutral ground wire
Adjust the STABILITY (STAB) trimpot slightly clockwise to increase dampening and suppress hunting oscillations
Replace the stator windings

exercises.prompt: Because air is less dense at high altitudes, an alternator operated in the Kenyan highlands at 2,000 m must be derated by approximately ___% of its nameplate capacity due to reduced cooling airflow.
exercises.explanation: Standard derating is 3% per 300 m above 1,000 m. For 2,000 m: (2000 - 1000) / 300 × 3% = 3.33 × 3% = 10% capacity derate.

lessons.title: Transformer Physics, Winding & Core Sizing
lessons.titleSw: Fizikia ya Transfoma, Kufuma Nyaya na Ukubwa wa Chuma
lessons.briefing: Transformers are purely passive, solid-state electromagnetic machines that operate at over 95% efficiency. Without transformers, transmitting electricity beyond a few hundred metres at 230V would require copper cables as thick as tree trunks due to resistive I²R voltage drop. By stepping voltage up to 1,000V–11,000V for rural transmission and stepping back down to 230V/400V at homestead clusters, line losses are slashed by up to 99%. This lesson covers transformer electromagnetic induction, grain-oriented silicon steel laminated core calculations, turns-per-volt formulas, wire gauge selection, and insulation varnishing.
lessons.outline: Transformer induction laws and turns ratio formula (Vp / Vs = Np / Ns = Is / Ip); the electrical power loss equation P_loss = I^2 * R and why stepping up voltage cuts line losses by the square of voltage ratio; core physics (magnetic saturation Bmax, hysteresis, eddy currents in laminated silicon steel sheets); transformer design formula: E = 4.44 * f * Bmax * Ac * N; turns-per-volt calculation; copper wire circular mil / mm2 sizing based on 3.0 A/mm2 current density; insulating materials (Nomex paper, Kapton, baked polyurethane varnish); rewinding and testing open-circuit vs short-circuit parameters.

exercises.prompt: Why are iron transformer cores constructed from stacks of thin, varnish-insulated silicon steel sheets (laminations) rather than a solid block of forged iron?
exercises.explanation:
Solid iron provides low resistance paths for massive circulating eddy currents that waste huge power as heat (P = V²/R). Slicing the core into 0.35 mm insulated sheets restricts eddy currents to microscopic loops, reducing losses by over 95%.

Why the other options are wrong: Laminated cores have the same weight and are more labour-intensive to produce. Solid iron conducts magnetic flux very well, but suffers massive electrical heating losses. Transformers operate strictly on AC and do not rectify.

options.text: Laminated cores are cheaper to ship by weight
Solid iron blocks cannot conduct magnetic flux
Thin laminations interrupt and suppress circulating eddy currents induced by the alternating magnetic field, preventing severe thermal overheating and wasted core energy
Laminations allow the transformer to convert AC directly into DC

exercises.prompt: If transmission line voltage is stepped up by a factor of 5 using a transformer, the current required to transmit the same kilowatt load drops by a factor of ___, and the resistive I²R line power losses in the transmission wires drop by a factor of ___.
exercises.explanation: Current is inversely proportional to voltage (I = P / V), so current drops by 5×. Power loss is proportional to current squared (P_loss = I² × R), so loss drops by 5² = 25 times.

exercises.prompt: Match each transformer design parameter to its operational purpose.
exercises.explanation: TPV governs core magnetic saturation; current density sizes copper; electrostatic shields protect against line surges; extra turns compensate for internal I×R drop.

right.text: Ratio determining how many wire loops are wound per volt of coil potential
Sizing rule preventing copper conductor overheating and insulation breakdown
Grounded copper foil layer preventing high-voltage lightning capacitive coupling
Compensates for internal winding resistance and inductive leakage voltage drop

exercises.prompt: An off-grid technician designs a 50 Hz transformer on a core with effective iron area Ac = 0.0025 m2 using grain-oriented silicon steel with Bmax = 1.4 Tesla. Using E = 4.44 × f × Bmax × Ac × N, what is the calculated Turns Per Volt (TPV)?
exercises.explanation:
TPV = 1 / (4.44 × 50 × 1.4 × 0.0025) = 1 / (310.8 × 0.0025) = 1 / 0.777 ≈ 1.287 Turns per Volt.

Why the other options are wrong: This is ten times too high, which would result in an over-wound coil that would not fit in the core window. This would heavily saturate the magnetic core, causing massive excitation current and tripping circuit breakers. This neglects the core area and Bmax calculations.

options.text: Approximately 1.29 Turns per Volt
Approximately 12.9 Turns per Volt
Approximately 0.55 Turns per Volt
Exactly 5.0 Turns per Volt

exercises.prompt: After winding a high-voltage transformer coil, the assembly must be impregnated with insulating resin and baked at 110 degrees C to cement the windings together, preventing microscopic abrasive wear caused by magnetic ___ between adjacent wire turns.
exercises.explanation: Alternating 50 Hz magnetic fields exert physical mechanical forces on the copper conductors. Without solid varnish impregnation, wires vibrate and buzz, rubbing through thin enamel insulation and causing catastrophic turn-to-turn short circuits.

lessons.title: Distribution Panels, MCB/RCD Protection & Earthing
lessons.titleSw: Mbao za Usambazaji, Ulinzi wa MCB/RCD na Mfumo wa Earth
lessons.briefing: Electrical power without rigorous protective architecture causes deadly shocks and structural fires. In an off-grid village grid, where earthing ground resistance is often high in dry volcanic or sandy soils, circuit protection cannot be left to chance. This lesson covers consumer unit distribution boards, Miniature Circuit Breakers (MCB tripping curves B, C, D), Residual Current Devices (RCD / GFCI) that trip at 30 mA to prevent fatal ventricular fibrillation, earthing regimes (TN-S, TN-C-S, TT), earth electrode rod installation, and soil resistivity testing.
lessons.outline: Distribution board (Consumer Unit) internal architecture (busbars, main switch, neutral link, earth bar); Miniature Circuit Breakers (MCB) dual trip mechanisms: thermal bimetallic strip (overload) vs magnetic solenoid (short circuit); MCB trip curves (Type B for lighting, Type C for general power/pumps, Type D for heavy welders/motors); Residual Current Devices (RCD): toroidal core differential current sensing, 30 mA human life safety threshold, 40 ms trip time; Earthing systems: TN-S, TN-C-S (PME), and TT isolated earthing; driving copper-clad earth rods; reducing earth resistance using bentonite clay and salt; earth loop impedance testing.

exercises.prompt: A person standing barefoot on damp soil accidentally touches a live 230 V wire. A standard 30 mA Residual Current Device (RCD) is installed on the circuit. What happens?
exercises.explanation:
The RCD measures differential current between Live and Neutral. Current leaking through the human body creates an imbalance. When this leak exceeds 30 mA, the sensing coil snaps the circuit open in < 40 ms, preventing lethal cardiac arrest.

Why the other options are wrong: Human body resistance is approx 1,000-2,000 ohms, drawing only 0.1-0.2 A. An MCB rated at 16 A or 20 A will never notice this tiny current and will NOT trip! Current is bypassing the neutral wire through the earth; this is why the RCD trips. A fraction of an amp has zero noticeable load effect on a generator.

options.text: The MCB trips because the person acts as a dead short circuit
The neutral wire absorbs the voltage surge
The generator slows down to 25 Hz

The RCD detects that the neutral return current is lower than the live feed current (current leaking to ground) and trips within 40 ms, disconnecting power before fatal ventricular fibrillation can occur

exercises.prompt: An MCB incorporates two independent trip mechanisms: a bimetallic strip that bends under prolonged moderate ___ conditions, and an electromagnetic solenoid that snaps open in milliseconds during a massive ___.
exercises.explanation: Thermal bimetal bends under sustained overload; the electromagnetic coil trips instantaneously under high short-circuit currents.

exercises.prompt: Match each MCB trip curve type to its designated electrical load profile.
exercises.explanation: Type B is sensitive for resistive loads; Type C handles normal motor inrush; Type D handles extreme transformer and welder surges; RCD protects human life.

right.text: Domestic lighting, electronic workstations, pure resistive heaters
General household sockets, water pumps, refrigerators, small power tools
Heavy industrial arc welders, grain mills, high-inrush step-up transformers
Human life electrocution protection tripping within 40 milliseconds

exercises.prompt: Why is a 30 mA RCD strictly mandatory on every installation using a TT (isolated earth rod) earthing system?
exercises.explanation:
In a TT system, fault current must travel through earth soil back to the generator neutral rod. By Ohm's law: I = 230V / 50 ohms = 4.6 A. A 16 A MCB will never trip on 4.6 A, leaving appliance metalwork energized at 230 V indefinitely! An RCD trips at 0.030 A, clearing the fault instantly.

Why the other options are wrong: TT systems have a standard neutral wire; only the earthing conductor is isolated from the generator neutral. An RCD does not provide an earth; it requires a functional earth or human path to detect fault differential current. TT is a standard AC distribution earthing regime.

options.text: TT systems have no neutral connection
RCDs generate the earth connection internally
Earth fault loop impedance through rural soil is often 20-100 ohms, limiting fault current to only a few amperes—far too low to trip a standard 16 A or 20 A MCB
Because TT systems operate strictly on DC current

exercises.prompt: To reduce electrical resistance around a driven copper earth rod in dry or rocky soils, the rod can be backfilled with water-swelling ___ clay, or treated with alternating layers of crushed wood ___ and rock salt.
exercises.explanation: Sodium bentonite clay retains moisture indefinitely; crushed charcoal and salt create an electrolyte-rich conductive envelope around the earth electrode.

lessons.title: Micro-Grid Synchronization & Dynamic Load Shedding
lessons.titleSw: Kuunganisha Gridi Ndogo (Synchronization) na Udhibiti wa Mizigo
lessons.briefing: In mature off-grid communities, a single generator or solar inverter is rarely enough. True resilience requires paralleling multiple diverse energy sources—a micro-hydro turbine, a diesel generator, and battery inverter banks—into a unified AC micro-grid. Paralleling two out-of-phase AC generators creates an electromagnetic short-circuit explosion with forces equivalent to a direct mechanical collision. This capstone lesson covers generator synchronization physics, the three-dark-lamp and synchroscope methods, active/reactive power sharing via governor droop, priority tier load shedding, and smart dump load ballast controllers.
lessons.outline: Paralleling physics and the four mandatory synchronization conditions (voltage magnitude, frequency, phase sequence, phase angle); the classic 'three-lamp' synchronization method (dark lamp vs bright lamp); optical rotary synchroscopes; the breaker closing moment (11 o'clock slow clockwise rotation); real power sharing via Governor Speed Droop (4%-5% droop curve); reactive power sharing via AVR Voltage Droop; frequency-based dynamic load shedding tiers (Tier 1 clinic/comm, Tier 2 refrigeration/lighting, Tier 3 water pumping/milling); Electronic Load Controllers (ELC) and resistive dump loads for run-of-river hydro; PHOTO_CAPTURE assessment rubric of electrical panel or generator wiring.

exercises.prompt: A plant technician is preparing to manually parallel an incoming diesel generator to a live mini-grid bus using a rotary synchroscope. When should the technician throw the paralleling breaker?
exercises.explanation:
Rotating slowly clockwise ensures the incoming machine will take on positive generation (rather than motoring). Tripping at 11 o'clock compensates for the 50-100 ms mechanical contact travel time, so contacts close precisely at 12 o'clock (0° phase angle).

Why the other options are wrong: Rapid counter-clockwise rotation means the generator is running much too slowly, which will cause massive reverse-power tripping. At 6 o'clock, the waveforms are 180° out of phase (maximum voltage difference), which would cause a violent explosion. Closing out of phase produces huge short-circuit forces that can shear generator shafts.

options.text: When the pointer is rotating rapidly counter-clockwise past 6 o'clock
At 6 o'clock on the dial when voltages are opposite
When the pointer is rotating very slowly in the clockwise (FAST) direction and reaches the '11 o'clock' position just before true 12 o'clock, allowing for breaker mechanical closing delay
Any time the pointer is moving, because generators self-align automatically

exercises.prompt: Before closing a paralleling breaker between two AC generators, four conditions must be matched: voltage magnitude, frequency, phase ___, and phase ___.
exercises.explanation: Voltage, frequency, phase sequence (rotation L1-L2-L3), and instantaneous phase angle (crest coincidence) are all mandatory conditions.

exercises.prompt: Match each mini-grid control strategy to its operational objective.
exercises.explanation: Governor droop balances kW; lamps confirm synchronism; UFLS prevents blackout cascades; ELC stabilizes run-of-river hydro frequency without throttles.

right.text: Enables stable proportional kilowatt (kW) load sharing between generators
Visual verification that phase sequence is correct and phase angle is zero
Automatically disconnects non-essential loads when frequency drops below 49 Hz
Shunts excess micro-hydro power to dump load heaters to maintain 50 Hz speed

exercises.prompt: Why must run-of-river micro-hydro turbine generators use an Electronic Load Controller (ELC) with a ballast dump load rather than an automotive-style throttle to regulate grid frequency?
exercises.explanation:
Water has immense mass and momentum. Snapping a spear valve shut sends high-pressure shockwaves (water hammer) that shatter PVC or steel pipes. An ELC diverts surplus electricity into water-heating dump loads in milliseconds, keeping water flow and generator frequency rock-steady.

Why the other options are wrong: Hydro turbines generate standard 50 Hz power via standard synchronous alternators. Dump loads dissipate electrical heat; they are not water filters. ELCs are solid-state electronic controllers, not mechanical springs.

options.text: Because hydro turbines cannot generate 50 Hz electricity directly

Rapidly closing a water valve to drop turbine power creates catastrophic hydraulic water hammer pressures that burst penstocks; the ELC keeps water flow constant while dynamically shunting electrical power
Because resistive dump loads make the water cleaner
To recharge the mechanical governor springs

exercises.prompt: Photograph an electrical distribution board, generator terminal panel, changeover switch, or micro-grid control setup from your electrical workshop practice. Ensure the image clearly displays circuit breakers, earthing conductor connections, or phase wiring with appropriate safety labelling, and include your written load balance and protection audit.
exercises.explanation: Clear photographic documentation of electrical distribution boards confirms proper cable color coding, correct MCB/RCD ratings, and secure protective earthing connections compliant with electrical safety codes.

rubric.criterion: Photograph clearly shows distribution board, MCBs/RCDs, generator terminals, or changeover switchgear
Protective earthing conductor (green/yellow or earth bar) and neutral links are distinctly visible and properly connected
Written inspection log details circuit breaker ratings, wire sizing, connected load categories, and earthing regime (TT or TN-S)
Image is well-lit, sharp, and demonstrates safe electrical installation standards

lessons.title: Radio Waves, Antennas & SWR
lessons.titleSw: Mawimbi ya Redio, Antena na SWR
lessons.briefing:
When cellular base stations lose grid power or fiber backhauls are severed, electromagnetic
radio waves remain the only medium that travels freely across terrain with zero physical
infrastructure. However, connecting a transmitter to an improper antenna converts costly
radio energy into destructive heat that incinerates the transmitter’s final output transistors.
This day decodes radio spectrum bands (HF, VHF, UHF), electromagnetic wavelength physics,
resonant antenna element calculations (quarter-wave ground plane and half-wave dipole),
coaxial impedance matching (50 Ω), and Standing Wave Ratio (SWR) measurement.
lessons.briefingSw:
Minara ya simu inapopoteza umeme au nyaya za fiber kukatika, mawimbi ya redio
ndiyo njia pekee ya kuwasiliana bila miundombinu. Lakini ukiunganisha redio kwenye
antena isiyo sahihi, nguvu ya redio inarudi nyuma na kuchoma transistor za redio.
Siku hii inafundisha jinsi ya kukokotoa urefu wa antena na kupima SWR.
lessons.outline:
1. The electromagnetic spectrum: HF (3–30 MHz), VHF (30–300 MHz), and UHF (300–3000 MHz)
2. Wavelength equation: Relating frequency to physical physical antenna size (λ = 300 / f)
3. The Half-Wave Dipole: Physical length formula (L = 142.5 / f) and center radiation resistance
4. The 1/4-Wave Ground Plane antenna: Vertical radiator with four 45-degree droop radials
5. Characteristic impedance: Why RF transmission lines are standardized at 50 Ohms
6. Standing Wave Ratio (SWR): Forward power vs reflected power (safe operating thresholds)
7. High SWR hazards: Thermal destruction of output RF final transistors (MOSFETs)
8. Antenna tuning & dummy loads: 50 Ω non-inductive resistor testing before live transmission

exercises.prompt: You connect an SWR meter between a 50W VHF transceiver and an improvised antenna. The meter reads an SWR of 3.8:1 when keyed. What should you do immediately?
exercises.explanation:
Correct! An SWR of 3.8:1 reflects over 34% of your power directly back into the radio's sensitive power amplifier. Prolonged transmission under this mismatch will burn out the final transistors. Unkey and check antenna length and cable continuity.

Why the other options are wrong: Increasing power will quadruple the reflected voltage, instantly destroying the final output transistors. Battery level has no relation to RF impedance matching or transistor heat dissipation. SWR is a property of the antenna geometry and frequency, independent of modulation mode.

options.text: Increase transmitter power to 100W to force the signal past the antenna resistance
Continue talking as long as the battery indicator shows green
Release the transmit key immediately; inspect the antenna elements for incorrect length, short circuits, or broken coaxial connections
Switch from FM mode to AM mode to bypass the SWR reading

exercises.prompt: Using the formula L = 142.5 / f(MHz), the total physical length of a half-wave dipole wire antenna for the 142.5 MHz frequency is exactly ___ meter(s).
exercises.explanation: 142.5 / 142.5 = 1.0 meter total wire length (each quarter-wave leg will be 0.50 meters or 50 cm long).

exercises.prompt: Match each radio frequency band to its operational characteristic.

right.text: Refracts off the ionosphere to provide regional communications over 100–1000+ km
Reliable line-of-sight communication over 10–50 km with compact antennas
Superior penetration through urban concrete walls and dense forest foliage
Absorbs transmitted RF power as heat for safe transmitter calibration

lessons.title: Handheld VHF/UHF & Field Protocols
lessons.titleSw: Redio za Mkono za VHF/UHF na Kanuni za Uwanjani
lessons.briefing:
Dual-band VHF/UHF handheld transceivers (such as the Baofeng UV-5R and UV-82 series)
cost under KSh 4,000 in Nairobi and are ubiquitous among community patrols, wildlife
rangers, and agricultural cooperatives. However, improper configuration (wrong squelch,
misconfigured repeater offsets, or inadvertent CTCSS blocking) renders them useless
during crises. This day teaches transceiver architecture, simplex direct vs repeater
duplex operation, CTCSS/DCS sub-audible tones, standard international radio etiquette
(ICAO phonetic alphabet), distress protocols (MAYDAY vs PAN-PAN), and power management.
lessons.briefingSw:
Redio za mkono za VHF/UHF (kama Baofeng UV-5R) zinapatikana kwa bei nafuu Nairobi na
zinatumika sana na walinzi na wakulima. Lakini bila kuelewa jinsi ya kurekebisha squelch,
repeater offsets, na CTCSS tones, mawasiliano ya dharura yatakwama. Siku hii inafundisha
uendeshaji sahihi, kanuni za simu za dharura (MAYDAY na PAN-PAN), na kutumia sauti ya ICAO.
lessons.outline:
1. Handheld transceiver architecture: Antenna port (SMA), PTT button, volume/power, squelch
2. Simplex communication: Direct radio-to-radio on a single shared frequency
3. Repeater Duplex operation: Transmit offsets (+/- 600 kHz on 2m VHF; +/- 5.0 MHz on 70cm UHF)
4. Squelch mechanisms: Carrier squelch threshold vs CTCSS/DCS sub-audible tone decoders
5. The PTT (Push-To-Talk) technique: Press, pause one second, speak across the mic, release
6. Emergency message traffic: MAYDAY (life distress) vs PAN-PAN (urgency) vs SECURITE (safety)
7. The ICAO international phonetic alphabet and standard prowords (ROGER, OVER, OUT, SAY AGAIN)
8. Battery preservation: 1W Low-power discipline, 12V battery eliminators, and field solar charging

exercises.prompt: You are attempting to reach a mountain repeater with an output frequency of 145.600 MHz and a standard negative offset of 600 kHz (-0.6 MHz). What frequency should your radio transmit on when you press the PTT button?
exercises.explanation:
Correct! With a -600 kHz (-0.600 MHz) offset, your radio listens on the repeater's output (145.600 MHz) and shifts down to transmit on the repeater's input: 145.600 - 0.600 = 145.000 MHz.

Why the other options are wrong: Transmitting on the same frequency is simplex; repeaters operate duplex on different transmit and receive frequencies. 146.200 MHz would be a positive (+0.600 MHz) offset, not a negative offset. This jumps to a completely different band (UHF instead of VHF).

options.text: 145.600 MHz (same frequency)

exercises.prompt: The highest-priority international radio distress call, used strictly when life is in immediate, grave danger, is spoken as the word ___ repeated three times.
exercises.explanation: MAYDAY (from the French 'venez m'aider' - come help me) is the universal distress signal. It halts all other radio traffic on the channel to prioritize the emergency casualty or craft.

exercises.prompt: Match each transceiver control or setting to its function.

right.text: Silences continuous background static while allowing weak signals to open speaker
Inaudible low-frequency audio tone required to open repeater receiver gates
Preserves 80% battery capacity during short-range line-of-sight communication
Replaces the Li-ion battery pack with a DC cable to run directly from a 12V car battery

lessons.title: Long-Range HF & NVIS Propagation
lessons.titleSw: Mawasiliano ya Masafa Marefu ya HF na NVIS
lessons.briefing:
In rugged East African topographies — spanning the Rift Valley escarpment, Mount Kenya,
and the Aberdare ranges — line-of-sight VHF/UHF signals cannot penetrate high volcanic
ridges. Standard long-range HF radio fires waves at shallow angles, creating a deadly
"skip zone" where signals bounce 1,000 km away, leaving the critical 50 to 400 km regional
zone completely deaf. Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) overcomes this by firing
radio waves nearly straight up (70°–90°) into the ionospheric F-layer, reflecting them
straight down like an umbrella to blanket deep valleys and mountain passes. This day
teaches ionospheric refraction layers, NVIS antenna design, and Continuous Wave (CW).
lessons.briefingSw:
Kwenye milima na mabonde kama Bonde la Ufa na Mlima Kenya, redio za kawaida za VHF/UHF
haziwezi kupita milimani. Teknolojia ya NVIS (Near Vertical Incidence Skywave) hurusha
mawimbi ya HF moja kwa moja angani (nyuzi 70-90) yakigonga ionosphere na kurudi chini
kufunika eneo lote la kilomita 50 hadi 400 bila kizuizi cha milima.
lessons.outline:
1. The ionospheric layers: D-layer (daytime absorption), E-layer, and F1/F2 refracting layers
2. The Skip Zone dilemma: Ground wave fading at 30 km while skywave lands at 800 km
3. The NVIS principle: High-angle radiation (70°–90°) reflecting downwards like an umbrella
4. NVIS frequency window: Critical frequency (foF2) — 80m (3.5–4.0 MHz) night, 40m (7.0–7.3 MHz) day
5. The Low-Slung Dipole: Erecting a horizontal wire only 2 to 4 meters above ground
6. Ground reflector wire: Enhancing upward signal reflection by 3 dB
7. Continuous Wave (CW / Morse Code): 100 Hz bandwidth advantage over 2.8 kHz SSB voice
8. International distress Morse: S-O-S (... --- ...) transmission mechanics and tone recognition

exercises.prompt: Why must a Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) dipole antenna be hung close to the ground (only 2 to 4 meters high) rather than mounted atop a high tower?
exercises.explanation:
Correct! Placing a horizontal dipole 0.1 to 0.2 wavelengths above ground uses ground reflection to cancel low-angle horizon radiation and direct almost all RF energy upward into the ionospheric F-layer.

Why the other options are wrong: While lower antennas have lower strike probability, that is not the RF engineering reason. NVIS is a skywave mode that travels through the ionosphere, not a surface ground wave. Tower height does not affect the voltage requirements of a transmitter.

options.text: To protect the antenna wire from lightning strikes
Because low frequencies travel faster along the surface of moist soil
The proximity of the conductive earth acts as a ground reflector, beaming the radio waves straight up into the ionosphere at steep 70-90 degree angles
Handheld transceivers cannot supply enough voltage to pump signals up a tall tower

exercises.prompt: During daytime in East Africa, the primary NVIS frequency band used to communicate regionally over 0 to 400 km is the ___ meter band (around 7 MHz).
exercises.explanation: The 40-meter band (7.0 to 7.3 MHz) is the universal daytime NVIS band in equatorial regions. At night, as ionospheric electron density drops, operators switch to the 80-meter band (3.5 to 3.8 MHz).

exercises.prompt: Match each long-range radio concept to its definition.

right.text: The silent gap between the end of the ground wave and the first skywave return
The highest frequency that reflects back down when sent vertically into the ionosphere
Ultra-narrow 100 Hz transmission mode with a 14 dB signal-to-noise advantage over voice
Wire laid on the earth below an NVIS dipole to boost upward radiation by 3 dB

lessons.title: Off-Grid Digital LoRa Mesh Networks
lessons.titleSw: Mitandao ya Kidijitali ya LoRa Mesh Nje ya Gridi
lessons.briefing:
When cellular towers go dark and mobile data networks collapse, modern low-cost digital
packet radio can maintain encrypted community messaging, GPS distress beacons, and sensor
telemetry across entire counties without internet or subscriptions. LoRa (Long Range)
uses Chirp Spread Spectrum modulation to decode digital packets buried 20 dB below the
ambient noise floor. Running open-source Meshtastic firmware on low-power battery nodes
(costing under KSh 3,500), each device automatically routes and repeats encrypted packets
from peer to peer. This day covers LoRa modulation, mesh routing protocols, AES-256
encryption, solar-powered hilltop repeater nodes, and field telemetry bridges.
lessons.briefingSw:
Minara ya Safaricom au Airtel ikizimika, teknolojia ya LoRa (Long Range) na Meshtastic
inaruhusu kutuma ujumbe wa maandishi, mahali ulipo (GPS), na taarifa za dharura kwa
simu za kawaida kupitia Bluetooth bila intaneti, bila vocha, na bila minara ya simu.
Kila kifaa kidogo cha KSh 3,000 kinajenga mtandao wa bure unaorudia mawimbi.
lessons.outline:
1. The LoRa revolution: Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS) and decoding signals below noise floor (-20 dB)
2. Frequency allocation in Kenya: 433 MHz and 868 MHz ISM bands (license-exempt power limits)
3. The Meshtastic protocol: Decentralized flooding and managed mesh routing (zero internet required)
4. Node roles: Client (handheld with smartphone app), Router (permanent high-elevation relay)
5. Cryptographic security: AES-256 pre-shared keys for private channels and unencrypted broadcast nets
6. Hardware architectures: ESP32 + SX1262 (Heltec V3) vs Ultra-low-power nRF52 (RAK4631)
7. Solar repeater engineering: 5W solar panel + TP4056 charge controller + dual 18650 Li-ion cells
8. Offline data integration: Bridging LoRa text packets to offline local campus servers (Kiwix / PWA)

exercises.prompt: How does LoRa Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS) modulation achieve reliable communication over 30+ km with only 100 milliwatts of transmit power?
exercises.explanation:
Correct! Chirp Spread Spectrum modulation provides substantial processing gain. The receiver correlates known frequency chirps out of thermal noise, enabling decoding at negative Signal-to-Noise Ratios (-20 dB SNR) that would completely garble standard FM or AM voice.

Why the other options are wrong: LoRa is a peer-to-peer terrestrial packet radio system completely independent of satellites. LoRa uses fractions of a watt (0.1W) and does not emit high microwave voltages. LoRa transmits electromagnetic radio waves, not mechanical acoustic sound waves.

options.text: It uses satellite cellular uplinks provided by Starlink
It pulses extremely high microwave voltages that burn through foliage
It converts radio waves into ultrasonic sound waves
