exercises.explanation: Cavity/DPC hygiene is part of the craft.

options.text: Improve insulation always
Bridge the DPC and let damp rise
Replace the DPC
Square the diagonal

exercises.prompt: You should check plumb:
exercises.explanation: End-of-day surprises are expensive.

Never — the line is enough
With a tape across the road

Paint it dark
Lean the next wall the other way

lessons.title: Site safety and setting out
lessons.titleSw: Usalama wa site na setting out
lessons.briefing:
Masonry starts with a safe site: boots, gloves, goggles when cutting, and no standing under a hoist. Scaffold and trestles must be complete; a stack of blocks is not a platform. Cement burns skin — wash splashes.

Setting out: profiles, builder’s square or 3-4-5, diagonals equal for a rectangle. A wall built off a wrong line is demolished, not decorated. Check reduced levels if you have a dumpy or laser; do not assume the slab is true.

Store cement dry and blocks on a clean base. Mixing on the soil fills mortar with clay and weakens it.

The assessor will ask you to explain how you know the corner is square. “It looks square” is not an answer.
lessons.briefingSw: Vaa PPE. Usisimame chini ya hoist. Square kwa 3-4-5 au diagonals. Usichanganye chokaa kwenye udongo. Cement inawasha ngozi.

exercises.prompt: A rectangle is square in plan when:
exercises.explanation: Measure diagonals. That is craft, not theory only.

options.text: One corner looks nice
Diagonals are equal (and sides as drawn)
All blocks are wet
The mixer is loud

exercises.prompt: When cutting a concrete block you should:
exercises.explanation: Goggles and a bench. Angle grinders need extra discipline.

options.text: Hold it on your knee toward your face
Use appropriate tools, eye protection, and a stable surface
Soak it in petrol
Leave random gaps instead

exercises.prompt: Mixing mortar on bare soil is bad because:
exercises.explanation: Use a board or mixer as specified.

options.text: It is faster
Soil contaminates and weakens the mix
Cement prefers clay
It squares the building

exercises.prompt: Standing on a dry-stack of blocks to lay the next lift is:
exercises.explanation: Access equipment is part of the unit.

options.text: Efficient
Unsafe — use a proper platform
Required by CDACC
A type of profile

exercises.prompt: The 3-4-5 method is used to set a right ___.
exercises.explanation: 3-4-5 is a practical Pythagorean square.

exercises.prompt: Rain is forecast and profiles are already knocked by a wheelbarrow. You should:
exercises.explanation: A wall on a moved line is waste.

options.text: Build anyway from memory
Reset lines from datums, protect profiles, and only then lay
Double the mortar water
Remove all PPE to move faster

lessons.title: Precision Measurement & Bench Work
lessons.titleSw: Vipimo Sahihi na Kazi za Benchi
lessons.briefing: In mechanical fabrication and machine repair, visual estimation leads to loose bearings, vibrating shafts, and catastrophic equipment failure. A master mechanic works to strict tolerances using precision instruments: the vernier caliper (0.02 mm resolution), the outside micrometer (0.01 mm resolution), and optical dial indicators. This lesson covers reading vernier scales, correct zeroing, parallax avoidance, hand filing techniques, and engineer's blue surface scraping for creating true mating surfaces.
lessons.outline: Vernier caliper reading and internal/external/depth measurement; outside micrometer calibration, ratchet thimble use, and zero-error correction; dial test indicators (DTI) and runout measurement; layout tools (scriber, prick punch, engineer's square, hermaphrodite calipers); file cuts (bastard, second cut, smooth), cross-filing, and draw-filing techniques; engineer's blue surface scraping for flat bearing surfaces.

exercises.prompt: A mechanic measures an electric motor shaft with a 0.02 mm vernier caliper. The vernier zero is past the 38 mm main scale line. The 34th division on the vernier slider aligns exactly with a main scale graduation. What is the measured diameter?
exercises.explanation:
Reading = 38.00 mm + (34 × 0.02 mm) = 38.00 mm + 0.68 mm = 38.68 mm.

Why the other options are wrong: This directly adds the division count without multiplying by the 0.02 mm resolution factor. This improperly divides the 34 divisions by 2 instead of multiplying by 0.02. The zero line has only passed 38 mm, not 39 mm.

exercises.prompt: An outside micrometer has a screw spindle pitch of ___ mm per complete turn, and its thimble is divided into ___ equal graduations, yielding a measurement resolution of ___ mm.
exercises.explanation: A metric micrometer screw moves 0.5 mm per full 360-degree rotation. Dividing 0.5 mm by 50 thimble marks produces 0.01 mm per division.

exercises.prompt: Match each workshop punch and file type to its correct engineering function.
exercises.explanation: Prick punches (30°) are sharp for accurate visual placement on scribed lines. Center punches (90°) match typical drill chisel edges. Bastard files remove stock, and draw-filing smooths the surface.

right.text: Creates precise tiny locator dimple at layout line intersections
Enlarges locator dimple to seat and guide twist drill tips
Heavy metal removal when working down rough stock to near size
Moving file sideways along work to produce smooth scratch-free finish

exercises.prompt: When closing an outside micrometer onto a cylindrical workpiece, why is it critical to turn the ratchet speeder rather than rotating the main thimble?
exercises.explanation:
Gripping and turning the thimble by hand can easily exert 30-50 N of force, flexing the forged C-frame by 0.02-0.05 mm and giving inaccurate measurements or damaging the micro-threads.

Why the other options are wrong: The purpose of the ratchet stop is precision torque control, not speed. The thimble is free to turn unless the locking lever is engaged. Zero error is adjusted using the barrel spanner, not by how the thimble is turned.

options.text: The ratchet stop speeds up the measurement process by spinning freely
The main thimble is locked during measurement and cannot be turned
The ratchet slips at a calibrated torque (approx. 5-10 N), preventing frame flex and spindle deformation that cause false high or low readings
Turning the thimble reverses the zero error on the barrel

exercises.prompt: When filing soft metals like aluminium, metal particles clog the file teeth in a defect called ___. This is prevented by rubbing ___ into the file face and cleared using a ___.
exercises.explanation: Pinning occurs when soft chips weld into tooth gullets and gouge the work. Chalk fills gullets temporarily so chips cannot bond, and a brass/steel wire file card clears trapped pins.

lessons.title: Drilling, Tapping & Fasteners
lessons.titleSw: Kuchimba, Kutengeneza Nyuzi na Vifungo vya Mitambo
lessons.briefing: Drilling round, clean holes on pitch and cutting strong internal and external threads are foundational machining operations. Incorrect drill speeds overheat high-speed steel (HSS) tools, while improper tap drill sizing results in stripped threads or broken taps seized deep inside expensive castings. This lesson delivers the mathematics of spindle RPM calculation, pilot hole sequencing, 3-stage tap progressions, cutting fluids, and bolt grade torque specifications.
lessons.outline: Twist drill geometry (118° point angle, lip relief, web thinning); cutting speed formula RPM = (1000 × V) / (pi × D); pilot hole rules for drills over 10 mm; work holding safety and drill press vises; tap drill calculation formula (TDS = D - P); 3-piece tap set sequence (taper, intermediate/plug, bottoming); tap wrench technique and chip breaking (half-turn back); die stocks and external threading; metric bolt strength grades (4.8, 8.8, 10.9, 12.9) and torque tightening fundamentals.

exercises.prompt: You need to drill a 10 mm hole through a mild steel bracket using an HSS drill. Recommended cutting speed is 28 m/min. What is the calculated spindle speed in RPM?
exercises.explanation:
N = (1000 × 28) / (3.1416 × 10) = 28,000 / 31.416 ≈ 891.2 RPM.

Why the other options are wrong: This neglects the 1000 conversion factor and pi calculation. This doubles the correct speed and would quickly burn the HSS drill lips. This is half of the correct speed.

options.text: Approximately 280 RPM
Approximately 1,780 RPM
Approximately 891 RPM
Approximately 445 RPM

exercises.prompt: To tap an M10 × 1.5 standard coarse thread in steel, the required tap drill size is ___ mm. For tapping blind holes to full thread depth, the final tap used in the 3-piece progression is the ___ tap.
exercises.explanation: TDS = D - P = 10.0 - 1.5 = 8.5 mm. The bottoming tap (or plug/finisher) has lead chamfer on only 1 to 1.5 threads, enabling thread forming right to the floor of a blind hole.

exercises.prompt: Match each metric bolt grade stamping to its engineering mechanical specification.
exercises.explanation: The first digit gives tensile strength × 100 MPa; the second gives yield strength as a percentage of tensile strength. Grade 8.8 is the minimum grade used in dynamic machine frames and structural joints.

right.text: 400 MPa tensile strength, 320 MPa yield strength (mild low-stress)
800 MPa tensile strength, 640 MPa yield strength (standard high-tensile)
1000 MPa tensile strength, 900 MPa yield strength (high-stress structural)
1200 MPa tensile strength, 1080 MPa yield strength (hardened alloy cap screws)

exercises.prompt: Why must you reverse a hand tap 1/4 to 1/2 turn after every half-turn of forward cutting?
exercises.explanation:
Continuous forward rotation causes long chips to pack into the flutes. As chip pressure rises, torsional shear stresses exceed the tap's yield point, snapping the brittle hardened tap inside the workpiece.

Why the other options are wrong: Cooling is achieved through cutting fluids, not by reversing. Pitch is fixed by the tool geometry. Cutting fluid should remain in the hole to lubricate cutting action.

options.text: To cool down the cutting edge with atmospheric air
To measure the pitch with the tap flutes
To clean the cutting fluid off the threads
To snap off and clear curled metal chips from the tap flutes, preventing chips from packing tight and snapping the hardened tap

exercises.prompt: When drilling holes larger than 10 mm in mild steel, you should first drill a ___ hole sized to match the chisel ___ of the larger drill to reduce feeding thrust force by up to 50%.
exercises.explanation: The chisel edge across the central drill web does not cut cleanly; it extrudes metal. A pilot hole sized to the web width eliminates this resistance.

lessons.title: Oxy-Acetylene Cutting & SMAW Welding Fundamentals
lessons.titleSw: Kukata kwa Gesi na Misingi ya Kuchomelea Chuma (SMAW)
lessons.briefing: Metal fabrication in off-grid workshops relies heavily on thermal cutting and electric arc joining. Oxy-acetylene torches rapidly cut, pierce, and bevel thick structural steel plate without electrical power. Shielded Metal Arc Welding (SMAW / Stick) remains the most robust, wind-resistant welding process for heavy machinery, penstocks, and equipment repair. This lesson covers gas pressures, flashback arrestors, neutral flame tuning, drag lines, AWS electrode specifications (E6013 vs E7018), and weld defect inspection.
lessons.outline: Oxy-acetylene equipment setup, cylinder identification (maroon acetylene, black oxygen), and flashback arrestors; lighting and adjusting flames (carburizing, neutral at 3100°C, oxidizing); oxygen cutting torch mechanics (preheat flames, cutting lever, exothermic iron-oxygen combustion); cutting defects (drag lines, slag adherence); SMAW fundamentals (DCEN vs DCEP polarity); AWS electrode numbering breakdown (E7018, E6013); joint prep (bevel angles, root gap, tack welds); common defects (porosity, slag inclusions, lack of fusion, undercut).

exercises.prompt: Why is it strictly forbidden in workshop practice to set the acetylene regulator gauge pressure above 1.0 bar (15 PSI)?
exercises.explanation:
Acetylene is endothermic. Above 15 PSI (1.03 bar), mechanical shock, heat, or internal friction can trigger violent spontaneous dissociation (explosion) inside hoses or manifolds.

Why the other options are wrong: Standard welding hoses are pressure-tested well above 100 PSI; the danger is chemical dissociation of the gas itself. Oxygen regulators operate up to 40-100 PSI; this is purely an acetylene chemical stability threshold. Higher acetylene pressure creates a heavily carburizing flame, not oxidizing.

options.text: The hose burst rating is limited to 15 PSI
The oxygen regulator cannot overcome higher acetylene pressure
It causes the flame to turn oxidizing instantly
Free acetylene gas becomes chemically unstable above 15 PSI and can explosively decompose into carbon and hydrogen without any oxygen present

exercises.prompt: In the AWS electrode specification E7018, the number '70' indicates a minimum tensile strength of ___ thousand PSI (approx. 485 MPa), while the digit '1' indicates the electrode can be used in ___ welding positions.
exercises.explanation: The first two digits give tensile strength in ksi (70 ksi = 70,000 PSI). The third digit '1' designates all-position welding (flat, horizontal, vertical, overhead).

exercises.prompt: Match each oxy-fuel and SMAW concept to its defining technical description.
exercises.explanation: Flashback arrestors prevent catastrophic flame travel into cylinders. Neutral flames provide clean heating without carbonizing or oxidizing steel. E7018 requires dry conditions to prevent hydrogen cracking. Undercut is a classic visual defect.

right.text: Sintered metal flame barrier with non-return check valve
Equal ratio oxygen-acetylene burn producing approx. 3100 C inner cone
Low-hydrogen iron powder rod requiring dry oven storage for structural welds
Groove melted into base metal at weld toe caused by high current or long arc

exercises.prompt: You are welding structural steel trusses in a breezy off-grid location. Why is SMAW (Stick) chosen over GMAW (MIG/CO2) for this work?
exercises.explanation:
MIG welding relies on an external gas envelope (Argon/CO2) that ambient winds easily disperse, causing immediate severe porosity. SMAW produces a dense slag layer and gas cloud that withstands outdoor breeze.

Why the other options are wrong: SMAW requires substantial electrical power from an inverter or generator. MIG solid and flux-core wires are widely used in structural fabrication in indoor shop conditions. SMAW arc temperatures (3,500-4,000°C) are comparable to or higher than MIG.

options.text: SMAW requires no electrical power and runs on battery banks
MIG electrodes are too soft to weld structural steel
SMAW operates at a lower temperature than MIG
The solid flux coating produces its own heavy shielding gas and protective slag right at the arc, which cannot be blown away by wind like MIG shielding gas

exercises.prompt: When cutting heavy steel plate with an oxy-acetylene torch, the cut face should exhibit nearly vertical ___ lines. If they lag backwards more than 15 degrees, the torch travel speed was too ___.
exercises.explanation: Drag lines trace the progression of the oxygen combustion stream through the plate thickness. Fast travel leaves bottom slag behind, curving the drag lines sharply.

lessons.title: Power Transmission — Bearings, Shafts & Belt Alignment
lessons.titleSw: Usafirishaji wa Nguvu — Fani, Mihimili na Mipangilio ya Mikanda
lessons.briefing: Over 60% of rotating machinery breakdowns in mills, pumps, and generators stem from shaft misalignment, incorrect belt tension, or improper bearing installation. Pounding a rolling element bearing onto a shaft with a hammer deforms raceways instantly. This lesson covers rolling bearing classification (deep-groove ball, spherical roller, taper roller), thermal and mechanical mounting techniques, shaft keyway standards, dial indicator rim-and-face shaft alignment, and V-belt sheave deflection testing.
lessons.outline: Bearing classifications and load vectors (radial vs axial/thrust); standard bearing numbering code system (e.g., 6205, 6308); bearing fits and mounting methods (induction heaters, hot oil baths at 110°C, mechanical bearing fitting tools — never press across rolling elements); shaft keyways (parallel, woodruff, feather) and failure modes; shaft alignment principles (angular vs parallel offset); straightedge, feeler gauge, and rim-and-face dial indicator methods; V-belt drive alignment, sheave wear, and tension testing (16 mm deflection per metre of span).

exercises.prompt: A technician orders a deep-groove ball bearing stamped '6308-2RS'. What is the internal bore diameter of this bearing?
exercises.explanation:
For bearing codes 04 and higher, multiply the last two digits by 5 mm. Bore = 08 × 5 = 40 mm. (6 = deep groove, 3 = medium series, 2RS = dual rubber contact seals).

Why the other options are wrong: 08 does not mean 8 mm; 8 mm is not a standard bearing code. 30 mm bore corresponds to code 06 (06 × 5 = 30). The first two digits indicate type and series, not bore size.

options.text: 8 mm
30 mm
63 mm
40 mm

exercises.prompt: When heating a ball bearing in an oil bath or induction heater for interference mounting onto a shaft, the maximum allowable temperature is ___ degrees C, because exceeding this threshold anneals the hardened steel raceways and melts internal seals.
exercises.explanation: Bearing steels are tempered between 150°C and 200°C. Exceeding 120°C risks structural metallurgic softening, dimensional distortion, and damage to pre-lubricated seals.

exercises.prompt: Match each bearing installation and drive practice to its technical rule.
exercises.explanation: Force must never pass across the balls/rollers, as this causes brinelling indentations. V-belts drive strictly on sidewall wedging.

right.text: Apply pressing force strictly to the inner ring
Apply pressing force strictly to the outer ring
Deflect 16 mm per 1 metre of centre-to-centre pulley span
Belt must never ride on or touch the bottom floor of the pulley groove

exercises.prompt: What damage occurs if an apprentice uses a steel sledgehammer to drive a bearing onto a shaft by striking the outer race?
exercises.explanation:
Striking the outer ring to drive the inner ring forces the balls to transmit the sledgehammer shock. The hardened steel balls indent the precision raceway (true brinelling), leading to rapid fatigue spalling within hours of operation.

Why the other options are wrong: The bearing raceways are severely damaged long before a solid shaft bends. Impact does not magnetize hardened bearing steel. Radial clearance is not widened; rather, raceway geometry is destroyed by craters.

options.text: True Brinelling — the high impact forces are transmitted through the ball bearings into the raceways, denting the precision ground races and causing early noisy bearing failure
The bearing shaft will bend but the bearing remains undamaged
The outer race becomes magnetic
The clearance increases from C3 to C4

exercises.prompt: The two types of shaft misalignment measured during rim-and-face dial indicator coupling checks are ___ misalignment (offset) and ___ misalignment.
exercises.explanation: Parallel offset represents center-to-center lateral axis displacement, while angularity represents non-parallel shaft intersection. Both must be corrected with shims and lateral adjustment.

lessons.title: Micro-Hydro Turbine Fabrication & Balancing
lessons.titleSw: Kutengeneza Turbini ya Maji na Kusawazisha Mizania
lessons.briefing: Micro-hydro impulse turbines (Pelton and Turgo runners) transform falling stream water into mechanical shaft power and electricity. A well-built Pelton runner fabricated from plasma-cut or cast spoon-cups operates at over 80% hydraulic efficiency for decades. However, a high-speed runner spinning at 1,500 RPM with even 10 grams of mass imbalance generates centrifugal forces that will shatter bearing housings and snap shafts. This capstone lesson covers impulse turbine mechanics, jet velocity calculation, runner cup splitting geometry, and static two-knife-edge balancing procedures.
lessons.outline: Impulse turbine fundamentals (Pelton vs Turgo vs Crossflow); Torricelli jet velocity equation V = sqrt(2 × g × H); bucket splitter edge physics and water redirection; runner pitch circle diameter (PCD) sizing; fabricated sheet metal / cast bronze bucket attachment; nozzle needle valves and deflector plates; static balancing on parallel knife edges; dynamic vibration analysis; PHOTO_CAPTURE assessment rubric of workshop bench layout or fabricated component.

exercises.prompt: A micro-hydro site has a net head of 50 metres. Assuming a nozzle coefficient Cv of 0.98, what is the calculated water jet velocity exiting the nozzle?
exercises.explanation:
Vj = 0.98 × sqrt(2 × 9.81 × 50) = 0.98 × sqrt(981) = 0.98 × 31.32 ≈ 30.69 m/s.

Why the other options are wrong: This improperly multiplies g by 10 without taking the square root. This is roughly half of the correct jet velocity (which would match runner peripheral speed, not jet velocity). This would require a net head of over 100 metres.

options.text: Approximately 98.1 m/s
Approximately 15.3 m/s
Approximately 30.7 m/s
Approximately 45.0 m/s

exercises.prompt: To maximize hydraulic momentum transfer, a Pelton turbine runner bucket is designed with a sharp central ___ ridge that divides the water jet into two equal streams, discharging the water backwards at an angle of ___ to ___ degrees.
exercises.explanation: The splitter cuts the water jet cleanly with minimal entry turbulence. Discharging backwards at 165°-170° transfers maximum kinetic momentum to the wheel without having exiting water collide with the back of the following bucket.

exercises.prompt: Match each micro-hydro impulse turbine component to its functional engineering role.
exercises.explanation: Spear valves throttle water cleanly; deflectors prevent overspeed runaway when electrical loads trip; bucket cutouts maintain uninterrupted jet entry; knife-edge mandrels detect minute gravity imbalances.

right.text: Adjusts water jet diameter and flow rate without losing jet velocity
Rapidly diverts jet away from runner during sudden generator load dump
Prevents incoming bucket from chopping into preceding bucket's jet stream
Provides near-frictionless support for static runner wheel balancing

exercises.prompt: For optimal efficiency on an impulse Pelton runner, the peripheral speed of the runner buckets (pitch circle velocity U) should ideally be what fraction of the water jet velocity (Vj)?
exercises.explanation:
Theoretical impulse turbine efficiency peaks at U = 0.5 Vj. Due to friction losses along bucket walls and air resistance, practical optimum runner peripheral speed is 0.46 to 0.48 times the jet speed.

Why the other options are wrong: If the bucket moves at the same speed as the jet, zero force is transferred because relative velocity is zero. This is far too slow and would waste over 70% of kinetic energy in high-speed discharge water. A runner cannot spin faster than the jet driving it without external power input.

options.text: Exactly 100% (U = Vj)
Between 10% and 15%
Over 150% (U = 1.5 Vj)
Between 46% and 48% (U ≈ 0.47 Vj)

exercises.prompt: Photograph a precision bench layout, drilled/tapped workpiece, or mechanical component fabrication from your workshop practice. Ensure clear lighting showing scribing, center marks, weld seams, or bearing fits, and include your written dimensional inspection report.
exercises.explanation: Accurate documentation and visual inspection of layout lines, thread quality, and squareness verify that the fabricated component meets precision engineering standards before final assembly.

rubric.criterion: Photograph clearly shows layout lines, drilled holes, tapped threads, or fabricated machine runner
Measurement tool (vernier caliper, steel rule, or engineer's square) is visible in the frame demonstrating inspection
Written inspection notes report nominal vs actual measured dimensions and tolerance deviations
Image is sharp, well-lit, and in focus with clean edges visible

lessons.title: Iron Smelting & The Charcoal Bloomery Furnace
lessons.titleSw: Kuyeyusha Chuma na Tanuri ya Bloomery ya Mkaa
lessons.briefing: When scrap metal supplies are exhausted, a technological civilization must possess the ability to extract new elemental iron directly from raw ore. Before modern industrial blast furnaces, humanity smelted iron for 3,000 years using the Bloomery process—a direct chemical reduction furnace that produces solid sponge iron (a "bloom") without ever melting the metal into liquid iron. This lesson covers prospecting iron ores (magnetite, hematite, laterite ironstones), refractory clay furnace construction, forced-air tuyere dynamics, charcoal-to-ore chemical reduction kinetics (1,150°C to 1,250°C), fayalite slag tapping, and consolidation forging.
lessons.outline: The chemical thermodynamics of iron direct reduction (Fe2O3 + 3 CO -> 2 Fe + 3 CO2); identifying iron ores in East Africa (banded ironstone, red hematite laterite, black magnetite river sands); ore roasting and crushing; bloomery shaft furnace design (1.2 m height, 30 cm internal bore, 15° inclined ceramic tuyere); refractory furnace mud formulations (termite mound clay + quartz sand + dry straw); the 1,200°C solid-state sponge iron bloom vs liquid fayalite slag (2FeO·SiO2); furnace run sequence (preheating, charging 1:1 ore-to-charcoal ratio, continuous air blast); slag tapping protocols; extracting and heavy sledgehammer consolidation forging to squeeze out liquid glass slag.

exercises.prompt: Why does a traditional charcoal bloomery furnace produce malleable, solid wrought iron at 1,200°C rather than melting into liquid cast iron like a blast furnace?
exercises.explanation:
Blast furnaces operate at > 1,400°C where iron melts and absorbs 3-4% carbon (cast iron). The bloomery operates at 1,150-1,250°C, producing solid-state direct reduction where pure iron grains weld together without carbon absorption.

Why the other options are wrong: Charcoal is almost pure carbon (80-90% C). Furnace walls are refractory clay; metal does not soak into the walls. Iron melts easily if temperature exceeds 1,538°C regardless of air.

options.text: Because charcoal does not contain carbon
Because the furnace walls absorb all the molten metal
Because iron cannot melt in the presence of air
The bloomery operates below the melting point of pure iron (1,538°C); carbon monoxide reduces the ore in the solid state, forming a sponge of low-carbon iron that never absorbs high amounts of carbon

exercises.prompt: In a bloomery furnace, the liquid waste by-product that melts at 1,180°C and drains to the bottom, composed primarily of iron silicate, is called ___ slag.
exercises.explanation: Fayalite slag (2FeO·SiO2) is a low-melting-point iron-silicate glass that fluxes out impurities and protects the growing metallic iron bloom.

exercises.prompt: Match each iron smelting stage to its operational purpose.
exercises.explanation: Roasting cracks ore; CO reduces iron; tapping clears slag; hammering welds the solid bloom.

right.text: Drives off moisture/sulfur and fractures dense rock into porous brittle gravel
Generates carbon monoxide gas that strips oxygen atoms from iron oxide
Drains excess liquid iron-silicate out the base to prevent drowning the tuyere
Squeezes liquid glassy slag from the hot sponge bloom and welds iron pores

exercises.prompt: What is the purpose of adding chopped straw or dry animal manure to the clay and sand mix when building a refractory bloomery furnace wall?
exercises.explanation:
Clay shrinks up to 10% when fired, causing severe cracks. Sand provides non-shrinking aggregate, and organic fibers burn out to leave millions of tiny insulating voids, lowering thermal conductivity.

Why the other options are wrong: Organic fibers have zero magnetic properties. Clay does not turn into cement; it hardens via ceramic sintering. Air is supplied mechanically via the tuyere, not through porous clay walls.

options.text: To make the furnace walls conduct magnetic currents
To turn the clay into Portland cement
To attract oxygen into the combustion zone
The organic fibers burn away during initial firing, leaving microscopic insulating air voids that increase thermal efficiency while preventing catastrophic structural shrinkage cracking

exercises.prompt: The ceramic air pipe that injects high-pressure air from the bellows into the hottest combustion zone of a bloomery furnace is called a ___, and is angled downward at approximately ___ to 20 degrees.
exercises.explanation: The tuyere injects the air blast. Angling downward 15°-20° concentrates the intense 1,250°C reaction zone right above the accumulating bloom.

lessons.title: Blacksmithing — The Forge Hearth, Anvil & Tool Crafting
lessons.titleSw: Uhunzi wa Chuma — Tanuri ya Uhunzi, Fuawe na Utengenezaji Zana
lessons.briefing: The blacksmith is the mother of all crafts; without the smith, the carpenter has no saws, the stonemason has no chisels, the farmer has no plows, and the surgeon has no scalpels. Transforming raw iron or scrap leaf springs into precision tools demands mastery over incandescent thermal colors, hammer control, anvil horn physics, and the fundamental forging operations: drawing out, upsetting, punching, drifting, and hot-cutting. This lesson covers building a low-cost side-blast charcoal brake-drum forge, anvil work zones, hammer blow geometry, making tongs, and forge-welding high-carbon steel cutting edges into mild iron bodies.
lessons.outline: The brake-drum charcoal forge hearth (tuyere pipe, ash dump, centrifugal blower / hand crank); blacksmith's anvil anatomy (face, round horn, step, hardy hole, pritchel hole); anvil mounting and rebound testing (bearing ball test > 80% rebound); steel incandescent temperature color chart (faint red 600°C to yellow/white 1,200°C); hammer dynamics (cross-peen hammer, drawing out length vs spreading width); upsetting to thicken bar stock; hot punching and drifting round/square eye holes (axes, hammers); making a pair of flat-jaw blacksmith tongs from scrap rebar; the physics of forge-welding (silica sand / borax flux, liquid oxide displacement, incandescent white heat @ 1,300°C).

exercises.prompt: A blacksmith wants to forge-weld two bars of high-carbon spring steel. What thermal incandescent color must the steel reach in the forge hearth, and what visual surface indicator confirms the welding heat is reached?
exercises.explanation:
Forge-welding requires high atomic mobility right below the burning point. The steel must look 'wet' with molten liquid flux slag covering clean, incandescent white metal. Hammering at orange heat will result in immediate joint separation.

Why the other options are wrong: 800°C is far too cold; iron atoms cannot inter-diffuse or weld under hammer pressure at cherry red. Violent sparks indicate the carbon in the steel is burning away uncontrollably, destroying the metal. Black heat is brittle; hammering high-carbon steel here causes catastrophic cracking.

options.text: Dark cherry red (800°C), before any scale can form
Incandescent sweating white heat (1,250°C - 1,300°C), where the surface of the steel appears wet and greasy like melting butter, with occasional tiny white sparks
Brilliant sparking fireworks (1,400°C+)
Black heat (500°C)

exercises.prompt: When drawing out a round steel bar to reduce its diameter, the blacksmith must follow the classic progression of forging the stock into a ___ cross-section first, then an ___, and finally rolling it back into a round, to prevent internal center-burst cracking.
exercises.explanation: The 'Square-Octagon-Round' rule compresses the center of the bar uniformly. Hammering round stock directly rolls and tears the interior grain along shear planes.

exercises.prompt: Match each anvil zone to its specific forging operation.
exercises.explanation: Face provides high-energy bounce; horn bends curves; step protects chisels; hardy hole locks bottom dies.

right.text: Heavy drawing out, leveling, planishing, and high-rebound hammer work
Bending smooth continuous curves, forging rings, and forming scrolls
Chipping hot stock through with a cold chisel without dulling the tool
Sockets bottom tooling such as hot-cut chisels, swage blocks, and benders

exercises.prompt: Why is anhydrous borax or fine silica quartz sand sprinkled onto steel during the preparation for a forge-weld?
exercises.explanation:
Iron oxidizes rapidly in air, creating a barrier scale that melts only at 1,370°C. Borax/silica dissolves this scale into liquid slag at 1,100°C, cleaning the metal surfaces so hammer impacts weld pure steel grains together.

Why the other options are wrong: Borax (Na2B4O7) contains boron and sodium, not carbon. Flux has no effect on tool weight; it is squeezed out during hammering. Flux is applied hot and has no adhesive bonding strength when cold.

options.text: It acts as a flux that chemically dissolves hard iron oxide scale into a low-melting-point liquid slag, which squirts out when hammered to permit pure metal-to-metal bonding
It adds carbon to the weld joint to make it harder
It lowers the weight of the finished tool
It glues the two cold steel bars together before heating

exercises.prompt: When punching an eye hole through an axe head or hammer, the final plug of waste metal is popped out over the round ___ hole of the anvil to allow the slug to fall through cleanly.
exercises.explanation: The pritchel hole (12-16 mm round hole in the heel of the anvil) allows punches and slugs to clear the bottom of the work without striking the anvil face.

lessons.title: Heat Treatment — Annealing, Normalizing, Quenching & Tempering
lessons.titleSw: Utireshaji Vyuma — Kupunguza Ugumu, Kurekebisha, Kuzima na Kutuliza
lessons.briefing: Forging a blade or chisel is only half the battle; without proper heat treatment, a high-carbon tool is either as soft as a butter knife (bends on impact) or as brittle as glass (shatters into shrapnel on the first blow). Steel is a crystalline alloy whose crystal lattice transforms between pearlite, austenite, and martensite under thermal control. This lesson covers the iron-carbon phase diagram, grain refinement through normalizing, stress-relief annealing, rapid water/oil quenching to trap needle-like martensite, and the precise art of temper colors (straw, bronze, peacock, spring blue) to dial in edge-retention versus impact toughness.
lessons.outline: Iron-carbon metallurgy: Ferrite, Cementite (Fe3C), Pearlite, and Austenite (face-centered cubic FCC at 727°C+); the critical transformation temperatures (A1 at 727°C, A3 curve); Full Annealing (slow furnace cooling to achieve machinable softness); Normalizing (air cooling to refine coarse forged grains); Quenching physics: the rapid shear transformation of Austenite into needle-hard Martensite (65 HRC); quench media selection (brine, water, canola/motor oil); Quench cracking and warping prevention; Tempering kinetics (sacrificing excess hardness to gain toughness); Oxide Temper Color spectrum (220°C pale straw for razors, 260°C brown for axes, 290°C blue for springs and cold chisels); differential tempering.

exercises.prompt: A blacksmith forged a heavy wood-cutting axe from an automotive 5160 leaf spring. After hardening the steel to martensite, to what temper color should the cutting edge be tempered to withstand chopping hard acacia wood without chipping or bending?
exercises.explanation:
Pale straw (220°C / 62 HRC) is too brittle for chopping knots in hard timber and will chip out. Spring blue (300°C / 50 HRC) is too soft and the edge will roll over. Brown/purple at 260°C is the classic axe temper.

Why the other options are wrong: Straw heat is ideal for straight razors and surgical blades, but chips instantly under chopping shock. Spring blue is too soft for cutting edges; the edge will dull and roll over on the first log. Untempered martensite will shatter into dangerous fragments on the first heavy impact.

options.text: Pale Straw (220°C / 62 HRC)
Spring Blue (300°C / 50 HRC)
Purple to Brown (approx. 260°C / 56-58 HRC), providing the ideal balance of tough impact resistance and long-lasting edge retention
Leave it untempered at 65 HRC

exercises.prompt: When heating carbon tool steel for quench hardening, the steel fully transforms into Austenite above the critical temperature of 727°C, which is verified in the field because the steel completely loses its ___.
exercises.explanation: Austenite is non-magnetic. Touching a magnet to the red-hot tool verifies that the Curie/A1 transformation temperature has been exceeded.

exercises.prompt: Match each heat treatment process to its primary industrial objective.
exercises.explanation: Annealing softens; normalizing refines grain; quenching hardens; tempering toughens.

right.text: Produces maximum structural softness for sawing, drilling, and filing
Refines coarse crystal grains and relieves uneven forging stresses
Traps carbon in distorted BCT lattice to form glass-hard Martensite
Relieves internal quench stresses to exchange excess hardness for toughness

exercises.prompt: What catastrophic failure occurs if a blade made from high-carbon alloy spring steel (5160) is quenched directly into cold ice water instead of warm oil?
exercises.explanation:
Water cools steel at > 1,000°C/sec. High-carbon alloy steels have high hardenability; the rapid transformation to martensite creates severe localized volume expansion, tearing the brittle steel apart along internal stresses.

Why the other options are wrong: Quenching does not add carbon; carbon content is fixed. Thermal quenching does not magnetize steel. The steel will harden, but it will simultaneously crack and shatter.

options.text: The steel turns into cast iron
Catastrophic quench cracking: The cooling rate of ice water is excessively violent, creating massive thermal and volume expansion stresses that crack the blade in half with an audible 'ping'
The blade becomes permanently magnetized
The steel fails to harden at all

exercises.prompt: In differential tempering of a cold chisel, heat stored in the heavy unquenched shank flows forward into the bare ground cutting edge, and the entire tool is plunged into water when the oxide color reaches ___ blue (approx. 290°C to 300°C).
exercises.explanation: Cold chisels strike steel and stone under heavy sledgehammer blows; a spring blue temper (50-52 HRC) withstands violent impact without shattering.

lessons.title: Greensand Mold Making & Pattern Engineering
lessons.titleSw: Utengenezaji wa Ukungu wa Mchanga (Greensand) na Sampuli za Vyuma
lessons.briefing: When machinery components break in remote field stations—a water pump impeller, a V-belt pulley, a pipe flange, or a bearing housing—replacement parts cannot be ordered online. Metal casting allows a workshop to replicate complex mechanical geometries using scrap aluminium or bronze. The cornerstone of the foundry is the Greensand mold: an economical, reusable composite of silica sand, bentonite clay binder, and moisture that holds sharp dimensional details against molten metal. This lesson covers pattern draft angles, shrinkage allowances, molding flask carpentry (cope and drag), gating system hydraulics (sprues, runners, ingates), and riser placement to feed solidification shrinkage.
lessons.outline: The physical chemistry of Greensand (85-90% clean sub-angular silica sand, 8-10% sodium/calcium bentonite clay, 3-5% water); the hand-squeeze ball test for sand moisture; wooden pattern design rules: parting lines, draft taper angle (1° to 3°), and metal shrinkage allowances (1.3% for aluminium, 1.5% for bronze, 2.0% for cast iron); parting powder (talc, fine dry wood ash, graphite); molding flask anatomy (lower drag, upper cope, alignment register pins); ramming technique and venting needles; gating system engineering: pouring basin, tapered sprue, runner trap, ingates, and feeding risers (feeder heads) to eliminate internal shrinkage voids.

exercises.prompt: A foundry patternmaker is carving a wooden pattern for an aluminium V-belt pulley that must have a finished outside diameter of exactly 200.0 mm. Accounting for aluminium's 1.3% solidification shrinkage, what diameter must the wooden pattern be carved to?
exercises.explanation:
Aluminium contracts by 1.3% as it freezes from liquid to solid. The pattern must be oversized by 1.3%: 200.0 × 1.013 = 202.6 mm. When cast, the molten aluminium freezes and shrinks down to the target 200.0 mm.

Why the other options are wrong: If carved at 200 mm, the finished casting will shrink to 197.4 mm and will be undersized scrap. This is a 6.5% oversize, which would require massive machining to bring to size. This subtracts shrinkage instead of adding it, making the part double-undersized.

exercises.prompt: Greensand for foundry mold making consists of 85% to 88% silica sand, 8% to 10% bentonite clay binder, and ___ to 5% moisture. When squeezed firmly in the fist, the sand lump should snap cleanly with sharp edges, leaving the palm of the hand ___.
exercises.explanation: 3% to 5% water activates bentonite. If properly tempered, the sand feels firm and snaps cleanly like a cookie, leaving the palm dry. Wet sticky sand generates dangerous steam.

exercises.prompt: Match each sand casting component to its structural or hydraulic role.
exercises.explanation: Cope is top; drag is bottom; sprue carries molten metal in; riser feeds solidification shrinkage.

right.text: The upper/top half of the two-part molding flask
The lower/bottom half of the two-part molding flask
Vertical tapered channel where molten metal is poured from the ladle
Reservoir of molten metal that stays liquid last to feed shrinkage voids

exercises.prompt: Why must vertical wooden pattern walls feature a 1° to 3° draft taper angle?
exercises.explanation:
A pattern with 90° perpendicular walls rubs against sand throughout its entire vertical withdrawal, causing sand to crumble and collapse. A 1°-3° taper breaks contact the instant the pattern moves upward by 1 mm, leaving sharp, pristine cavity edges.

Why the other options are wrong: Draft taper has a negligible effect on weight; its purpose is clean pattern extraction. Patterns are used in dry molding flasks, not water. Solidification rate depends on section thickness and sand thermal conductivity, not draft angle.

options.text: To make the casting heavier
To prevent vacuum suction and friction from tearing and destroying the delicate packed greensand mold walls when the pattern is extracted vertically
To make the pattern float in water
To allow the molten metal to freeze faster

exercises.prompt: Before pouring molten metal into a greensand mold, a heavy iron weight must be placed on top of the cope flask to counteract the powerful ___ pressure of the dense liquid metal, which would otherwise float the cope and blow out molten metal.
exercises.explanation: Molten metal is dense (aluminium 2.4 g/cm3, bronze 8.8 g/cm3). When the mold fills, hydrostatic head pressure pushes upward against the cope sand with hundreds of kilograms of force.

lessons.title: Crucible Furnace Operation & Non-Ferrous Casting
lessons.titleSw: Uendeshaji wa Tanuri ya Crucible na Uyahushaji wa Vyuma (Alumini na Shaba)
lessons.briefing: Pouring liquid metal at 700°C to 1,150°C is an industrial operation where a single drop of sweat or moisture can cause a catastrophic steam explosion. Non-ferrous alloys—aluminium (melting point 660°C) and bronze/brass (melting point 950°C–1,050°C)—are the lifeblood of remote machine repair, producing corrosion-resistant pump impellers, bushings, valves, and electrical fittings. This capstone lesson covers refractory crucible furnace construction, clay-graphite crucible handling, fluxing and degassing (removing dissolved hydrogen gas), dross skimming, pouring mechanics, safety PPE, and comprehensive inspection rubrics.
lessons.outline: Crucible furnace design: tangential burner inlet, refractory lining (kaolin / castable refractory, 1,300°C rated), forced-air waste oil or charcoal burner; clay-graphite and silicon carbide crucible selection and preheating (preventing spalling fractures); melting thermodynamics of Aluminium (660°C) and Silicon-Bronze (1,000°C); hydrogen gas solubility and degassing protocols (degassing tablets or dry table salt + potassium chloride flux); dross skimming tools; pouring ergonomics: two-man lifting shank and pouring tongs; absolute moisture safety rules (preheating all charging scrap and skimmers); shake-out inspection and cleaning; PHOTO_CAPTURE assessment rubric of workshop foundry mold, crucible melt, or finished cast component.

exercises.prompt: Why is it strictly mandatory in foundry practice to preheat all cold scrap metal and steel skimming tools on the furnace lid before plunging them into a crucible of molten aluminium or bronze?
exercises.explanation:
Moisture trapped under molten metal flashes to high-pressure steam in milliseconds. The explosive 1,700× volumetric expansion acts like a blast charge, ejecting 1,000°C molten metal across the entire shop floor.

Why the other options are wrong: Scrap is added directly into the crucible to melt; hacksawing is not performed during the melt. Crucibles must stay hot; cooling is the opposite of the objective. Aluminium is non-ferrous and non-magnetic in both solid and liquid states.

options.text: To make the scrap metal easier to cut with a hacksaw
To cool down the crucible so the pot does not crack
Because cold scrap magnetizes the liquid aluminium

To eliminate invisible trace moisture and condensation; water trapped beneath molten metal instantly vaporizes into steam with a 1,700-fold volume expansion, triggering a violent molten metal steam explosion

exercises.prompt: In molten aluminium casting, dissolved ___ gas causes severe microscopic pinhole porosity in the finished casting, which is eliminated prior to pouring by bubbling ___ flux tablets through the melt.
exercises.explanation: Hydrogen dissolves in liquid aluminium and precipitates as gas bubbles during freezing. Degassing agents bubble through the bath, stripping out dissolved hydrogen.

exercises.prompt: Match each foundry operation to its critical technical purpose.
exercises.explanation: Tangential burners optimize heat transfer; skimming cleans oxides; shanks control crucibles; sand floors absorb spills safely.

right.text: Creates a swirling cyclonic vortex flame around the crucible for uniform heating
Removes light floating aluminium oxide crust before metal enters the mold
Two-man rigid steel carrier allowing smooth, controlled tilting of the crucible
Prevents catastrophic concrete spalling explosions if molten metal spills

exercises.prompt: When pouring molten aluminium into a greensand mold, why should the pouring lip of the crucible be kept as low as possible (under 25 mm) above the pouring basin?
exercises.explanation:
Pouring from a high distance creates turbulent splashing that entrains air and folds heavy oxide skins into the liquid metal, causing severe internal inclusion defects and cold shuts in the casting.

Why the other options are wrong: Flask floating is caused by hydrostatic head pressure inside the mold, not the height of the ladle. The weight of the crucible is identical regardless of pouring height. Liquid metal at 750°C will not freeze during a 30 cm fall, but the turbulence ruins the casting.

options.text: Low pouring height minimizes turbulence and prevents the metal stream from breaking into droplets that trap air and fold surface oxide dross into the mold cavity
Because high pours cause the sand flask to float
To make the crucible lighter to hold
To prevent the metal from freezing in mid-air

exercises.prompt: Photograph a metal casting, greensand mold cavity, blacksmithing forge operation, or heat-treated forged tool from your workshop practice. Ensure the image clearly displays clean parting lines, surface finish, gating details, or heat-treating oxide temper colors, and include your written processing log.
exercises.explanation: Photographic documentation of foundry molds, crucible melts, or heat-treated tools verifies practical mastery of dimensional accuracy, clean casting surfaces, and correct metallurgical phase transformations in workshop practice.

rubric.criterion: Photograph clearly shows greensand mold, crucible furnace, forged workpiece, or finished cast component
Foundry details (parting line, sprue/riser cutoff, draft angles) or blacksmithing features (temper colors, hammer finish) are distinct
Written report records alloy composition, pouring/forging temperatures, quench media, and dimensional tolerances
Image is well-lit, in sharp focus, showing clean metallurgical texture and professional workshop safety practice

lessons.title: Topographic Maps, Contours & Grid Coordinates
lessons.titleSw: Ramani za Topografia, Mistari ya Miinuko na Kuratibu za Gridi
lessons.briefing: When satellite constellations go offline or electronic devices lose power, a paper topographic map is an explorer's only reliable window into the physical landscape. Reading a map is not merely recognizing roads; it is the art of translating 2-dimensional contour lines into a living 3-dimensional mental image of ridges, valleys, cliffs, and water flow. This lesson covers scale ratios, contour interval arithmetic, relief interpretation (spurs vs valleys), slope gradient percentages, and the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) metric grid coordinate system (UTM Zone 37N / 37S in Kenya).
lessons.outline: Map scale ratios (1:50,000 standard survey sheet); representative fractions; contour lines (index contours, intermediate contours, supplementary); contour spacing vs terrain slope; the V-rule for river valleys and spurs; calculating slope gradient percentage: Slope% = (Rise / Run) * 100; Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) and Military Grid Reference System (MGRS); reading 6-figure and 8-figure grid references (Eastings before Northings); measuring curved trail distances with thread or map wheel.

exercises.prompt: On a standard 1:50,000 Survey of Kenya topographic map, two water boreholes are separated by exactly 7.4 cm as measured with a ruler. What is the true horizontal ground distance between them?
exercises.explanation:
At 1:50,000 scale, 1 cm = 50,000 cm = 500 m (0.5 km). Distance = 7.4 cm × 0.5 km/cm = 3.7 km (3,700 metres).

Why the other options are wrong: 1 cm = 1 km applies to 1:100,000 scale maps, not 1:50,000. This improperly divides 7.4 by 5 instead of multiplying by 0.5. This is off by a factor of 10.

options.text: 7.4 kilometres
1.48 kilometres
3.7 kilometres (3,700 metres)
370 metres

exercises.prompt: On a topographic map, when contour lines cross a river or stream valley, they form a sharp 'V' shape that always points ___ (toward the high water source), while spurs and protruding ridges form contours that point ___.
exercises.explanation: Water flows downhill, so valley contours V uphill toward the source. Spurs plunge downhill into valleys, so spur contours V downhill.

exercises.prompt: Match each cartographic element to its technical definition.
exercises.explanation: Index contours provide reference elevation; CI is vertical spacing; Eastings go right; 6-figure references locate within 100 m.

right.text: Heavy bold contour line printed with explicit elevation number every 5th line
Vertical elevation difference between any two adjacent contour lines
Vertical grid line measuring metric distance eastward across the UTM zone
Coordinate notation locating a position on earth to within 100-metre precision

exercises.prompt: An expedition climbs from a valley floor at 1,400 m to a ridge summit at 1,640 m. The horizontal distance traversed on the map is 1,200 metres. What is the calculated average slope gradient percentage?
exercises.explanation:
Vertical Rise = 1,640 m - 1,400 m = 240 m. Slope % = (240 m / 1,200 m) × 100 = 0.20 × 100 = 20%.

Why the other options are wrong: 12% would correspond to a rise of only 144 metres. 35% would require a rise of 420 metres. This neglects the percentage multiplier.

options.text: 20% slope (Rise = 240 m / Run = 1,200 m × 100)
12% slope
35% slope
2.4% slope

exercises.prompt: When reading UTM or military grid coordinates on a topographic sheet, the universal directional rule to follow is to read ___ (Eastings) before reading ___ (Northings).
exercises.explanation: The standard mnemonic is 'read right up'—read across the page horizontally (Eastings) first, then vertically up the page (Northings) second.

lessons.title: The Magnetic Compass & Declination Mathematics
lessons.titleSw: Dira ya Sumaku na Hisabati ya Mkengeuko wa Kijiografia (Declination)
lessons.briefing: A magnetic compass needle does not point to the North Pole of the Earth; it points to the wandering Magnetic North Pole dictated by Earth's molten liquid iron core. Failing to account for Magnetic Declination (the angular difference between True North, Grid North, and Magnetic North) causes a navigator to drift off course by hundreds of metres for every kilometre walked. Over a 10 km trek through featureless bush, a 5-degree uncorrected declination error results in missing a vital waterhole by nearly 1,000 metres. This lesson covers compass anatomy, the three norths, declination arithmetic, annual magnetic drift updates, and taking precision field bearings.
lessons.outline: The three Norths: True North (geographic rotation axis), Grid North (map UTM vertical lines), and Magnetic North (compass needle alignment); the marginal diagram declination diagram on topographic maps; Magnetic Declination and Grid Magnetic Angle (GMA); calculating annual magnetic change (drift rate in minutes of arc); the universal conversion formulas: "Grid to Mag: ADD if West / SUBTRACT if East"; lensatic and baseplate prismatic compass anatomy (sighting wire, prism optic, liquid capsule, dial damping); back-bearings formula (θ ± 180°); eliminating local magnetic attraction (rifles, steel vehicles, wristwatches, iron-rich basalt rock).

exercises.prompt: A navigator measures a bearing of 120° from a topographic map (Grid Bearing). The map margin states that the Grid Magnetic Angle (GMA) is 3° East. What magnetic bearing should be dialled into the compass to walk this route in the field?
exercises.explanation:
When Magnetic North is East of Grid North, magnetic bearings are smaller than grid bearings: Magnetic Bearing = Grid Bearing - GMA = 120° - 3° = 117°.

Why the other options are wrong: Adding is done for West declination, not East declination. Adding here would double the error to 6 degrees. 300° is the back-bearing, not the magnetic conversion. Failing to correct for 3° declination will cause approx. 52 metres of drift per kilometre walked.

options.text: 117° (Grid to Mag with East declination: Subtract East: 120° - 3°)
120° (no correction needed)

exercises.prompt: If an expedition is marching on a forward magnetic bearing of 078 degrees, the exact reverse back-bearing to verify they have not drifted off course is ___ degrees.
exercises.explanation: Because 78° is less than 180°, add 180°: 78° + 180° = 258°. Looking back along the trail to the origin must align with 258°.

exercises.prompt: Match each 'North' definition to its cartographic representation.
exercises.explanation: True north is rotation axis; grid north is map lines; magnetic north follows geomagnetic flux; local attraction is manmade or mineral magnetic interference.

right.text: Earth's geographic axis of rotation (marked by star symbol on maps)
Vertical metric grid lines printed on flat UTM map projections
Direction indicated by a free-floating magnetized compass needle
Compass needle deflection caused by nearby rifles, vehicles, or basalt

exercises.prompt: A map printed in 2010 notes that the Grid Magnetic Angle was 2° 10' East, with an annual change of 5' West. What is the updated GMA for the year 2026?
exercises.explanation:
Elapsed years = 2026 - 2010 = 16 years. Total drift = 16 × 5' West = 80' West = 1° 20' West. Updated GMA = 2° 10' East - 1° 20' West = 0° 50' East.

Why the other options are wrong: This improperly adds the western drift to an eastern angle instead of subtracting. This neglects 16 years of continuous magnetic pole migration. The angle has reduced toward zero, but has not yet crossed into West declination.

options.text: 3° 30' East
2° 10' East
0° 50' East
0° 10' West

exercises.prompt: To prevent severe local magnetic attraction (deviation error) when taking a field bearing, a navigator must hold the compass at least ___ metres away from a steel rifle barrel and at least ___ metres away from a 4x4 motor vehicle.
exercises.explanation: Rifles cause magnetic needle deflection within 1.5 metres; massive steel vehicle chassis and engine blocks distort magnetic fields out to 15 metres.

lessons.title: Field Resection, Triangulation & Position Fixing
lessons.titleSw: Kutambua Eneo Ulipo (Resection), Pembetatu na Upimaji wa Shambani
lessons.briefing: When you are lost in unfamiliar territory, the map and compass alone cannot save you unless you can answer the foundational question: 'Where on this map am I standing right now?' Through the mathematical technique of Resection (triangulation from known landmarks), an explorer can determine their exact 8-figure map coordinate within 20 metres without electronics. This lesson covers identifying prominent topographic features, sighting magnetic bearings, converting to grid back-bearings, plotting lines of position, resolving the 'Triangle of Error', and using linear features as handrails and catching features.
lessons.outline: The geometric principle of resection (sighting unknown position from known points); identifying distinct landmarks on map and terrain (peaks, radio masts, water towers, road junctions); taking precision magnetic bearings with a prismatic compass; converting to Grid Back-Bearings; plotting lines of position (LOP) with protractor; the 2-point resection vs the gold-standard 3-point resection; resolving the 'Triangle of Error' (cocked hat) using the rule of signs; using handrails, baselines, and catching features to prevent overshooting; aiming off technique.

exercises.prompt: You are lost in scrubland. You sight a prominent telecommunications mast at 090° Magnetic and an isolated volcanic crater hill at 180° Magnetic. The local Grid Magnetic Angle is 2° East. What are the grid back-bearings you must plot on the map to find your position?
exercises.explanation:
1. Convert to Grid: Mag to Grid with East declination: ADD East: Mast Grid = 090° + 2° = 092°; Crater Grid = 180° + 2° = 182°. 2. Calculate Back-Bearings: Mast = 092° + 180° = 272°; Crater = 182° - 180° = 002°. Sighting back from these map features at 272° and 002° intersects at your location.

Why the other options are wrong: This neglects both the declination correction and the 180° back-bearing reversal. This improperly subtracted the East declination instead of adding it. This simply swaps the two readings.

options.text: From the Mast plot 090°; from the Crater plot 180°
From the Mast plot 268°; from the Crater plot 358°
From the Mast plot 180°; from the Crater plot 090°
From the Mast plot 272° Grid; from the Crater plot 002° Grid

exercises.prompt: When plotting back-bearings from three distant landmarks on a map, the small imperfect triangle formed by the three lines of position is called the Triangle of ___, and the navigator's estimated position is taken at its geometric ___.
exercises.explanation: The Triangle of Error (cocked hat) arises from small sighting and drawing variances. The estimated location lies at the geometric center of the triangle.

exercises.prompt: Match each terrain navigation technique to its practical strategic function.
exercises.explanation: Resection fixes position; handrails guide travel; catching features stop overshooting; aiming off ensures you know which way to turn when reaching a linear target.

right.text: Sighting two or three known landmarks to pinpoint an unknown observer location
Linear feature (river, ridge, road) followed parallel to route of march
Prominent perpendicular barrier indicating a target destination has been overshot
Deliberately biasing a bearing to one side of a target located on a linear feature

exercises.prompt: Why should the two distant landmarks chosen for a resection fix ideally be separated by approximately 60° to 120° (near 90°) relative to the observer?
exercises.explanation:
Geometry dictates that lines intersecting at 90° have maximum position certainty. Shallow intersection angles (< 30° or > 150°) magnify minute angular sighting errors into massive longitudinal displacement errors.

Why the other options are wrong: A compass functions equally in all 360 degrees. A protractor is always required to plot bearings on a map. Declination is an atmospheric/geomagnetic constant independent of the landmark angle.

options.text: Because compasses only function accurately when pointed east and north
To avoid needing to use a protractor on the map
Because 90 degrees eliminates magnetic declination

Perpendicular lines of position produce a clean, sharp, unambiguous intersection; lines crossing at shallow angles (e.g. 15°) cause small sighting errors to slide the position fix hundreds of metres along the line

exercises.prompt: If you are lost along a distinct, known dirt road printed on your topographic map, you need to sight only ___ prominent distant landmark to fix your exact coordinate, because your location is the point where the landmark's back-bearing crosses the ___.
exercises.explanation: Standing on a linear feature provides one known line of position. Sighting a single landmark provides the intersecting cross-line, pinpointing the location.

lessons.title: Plane Table Surveying & Community Base Mapping
lessons.titleSw: Upimaji wa Jedwali la Ndege (Plane Table) na Kutengeneza Ramani za Jamii
lessons.briefing: When a settlement expands into unmapped territory, establishing legal land boundaries, irrigation canal routes, and defensive fortifications requires creating accurate custom base maps from scratch. The Plane Table Survey—the classical graphical method used to map continents before satellite photogrammetry—allows a surveyor to map terrain directly on a drawing board in the field without complex trigonometric calculations or electronic theodolites. This lesson covers plane table leveling, orientation by trough compass, telescopic/sight-rule alidades, radiation mapping, and establishing baseline triangulation networks.
lessons.outline: The Plane Table apparatus (hardwood drawing board, sturdy wooden tripod, 360° leveling head, trough compass, plumb-bob plumbing fork); the Alidade (sight rule with sighting vanes and fiducial edge); the 3 golden operations at every station: Leveling (circular spirit level), Centering (plumbing fork over ground peg), and Orientation (backsighting or magnetic trough compass); mapping methods: Method of Radiation (radial rays to nearby trees, corners, wells), Method of Intersection (triangulating distant peaks without visiting them), and Method of Traversing (walking closed polygon boundaries); closing error adjustments.

exercises.prompt: An expedition surveyor wants to map the exact location of a prominent rocky bluff on the opposite side of a deep, crocodile-infested river gorge. Which plane table surveying method maps the bluff without crossing the gorge?
exercises.explanation:
The Method of Intersection is designed for inaccessible features. Measuring a single baseline along one side of the river and sighting rays from both ends locates the intersection point graphically on the map board without crossing.

Why the other options are wrong: Radiation requires measuring physical distance to the target, which is impossible across the gorge. Leveling ensures the board is horizontal; it does not map distance. This would take days; intersection maps it in 30 minutes from the home bank.

options.text: Method of Radiation: Measure distance with a 100-metre tape across the river
Method of Leveling: Raise the plane table by 10 metres
Trough compass traversing: Walk around the river source
Method of Intersection: Measure an accessible baseline A-B along the home riverbank, then sight intersecting alidade rays toward the bluff from both Station A and Station B

exercises.prompt: At every plane table survey station, the three mandatory setup operations performed in strict sequence before drawing any rays are: ___, ___, and ___.
exercises.explanation: First make the board horizontal (Leveling), align the map pinhole over the ground peg (Centering), and rotate the board to match the real world (Orientation).

exercises.prompt: Match each plane table surveying accessory to its precise engineering function.
exercises.explanation: Alidade sights rays; plumbing fork centers the table over pegs; trough compass finds magnetic north; backsighting provides high-precision orientation.

right.text: Straightedge with vertical crosshair vanes used to sight landmarks and rule rays
Aligns a pencil pinhole on the paper directly over a physical ground survey stake
Narrow rectangular box used to orient the drawing board to Magnetic North
Aligning the table by sighting back along an existing line to a previous station

exercises.prompt: Why is 'Backsighting' preferred over using a magnetic trough compass for orienting a plane table when surveying a closed settlement boundary?
exercises.explanation:
Trough compasses can be deflected by buried iron minerals, fencing, or vehicles by 1° to 3°. Backsighting directly aligns with the surveyed baseline on the ground, delivering optical orientation accuracy of minutes of arc.

Why the other options are wrong: Backsighting requires visual optical line-of-sight to a ranging rod in daylight. Trough compasses are durable, but sensitive to magnetic distortion. Standard sight-rule alidades measure horizontal directions, not vertical contours.

options.text: Backsighting can be done in pitch darkness
Because trough compass needles break if used outdoors
Backsighting relies strictly on optical line-of-sight between surveyed pegs, making it completely immune to local magnetic anomalies, ironstone rocks, and compass reading errors
Backsighting automatically measures elevation contours

exercises.prompt: When surveying a 1:500 community base map using the Method of Radiation, a measured ground distance of 35.0 metres from the central station to a water well will be scaled off as exactly ___ cm along the alidade ray on the paper.
exercises.explanation: At 1:500 scale, 1 cm on paper = 500 cm = 5.0 metres on ground. Paper distance = 35.0 m / 5.0 m/cm = 7.0 cm.

lessons.title: Dead Reckoning, Pacing Calibration & Night Navigation
lessons.titleSw: Uelekezaji Njia Gizani (Dead Reckoning), Upimaji wa Hatua na Anga ya Usiku
lessons.briefing: In zero-visibility conditions—dense mountain fog, pitch-black night missions, or featureless arid flatlands—landmarks disappear from view, rendering triangulation impossible. Under these conditions, survival depends on Dead Reckoning (DR): advancing along strict compass headings while measuring elapsed distance through calibrated human pace counting. This capstone lesson covers pacing calibration across variable terrain, ranger pace-bead (ranger bead) construction, boxing impassable obstacles (90-degree doglegs), night compass bezel manipulation, and emergency celestial orientation using the Southern Cross and Orion.
lessons.outline: The dead reckoning navigational triangle (Position = Known Origin + Vector Heading + Distance Traversed); pacing calibration methodology (measuring 100-metre baseline for flat, uphill, and thick scrub); constructing ranger pace-counting beads (tallying 100m and 1km units); obstacle bypassing techniques (the 90° box method and the optical point-aiming method); night compass techniques (bezel ring click intervals, tritium luminous markers, dead-reckoning buddy teams); southern hemisphere celestial navigation: Southern Cross (Crux) and Pointers (Alpha & Beta Centauri) true south projection; equatorial star tracking (Orion's Belt rising true East and setting true West); PHOTO_CAPTURE assessment rubric of field cartography, triangulation sketch, or pace tracking record.

exercises.prompt: While marching on a dead reckoning heading of 020° across savannah at night, your scout hits a deep, flooded marsh. You execute a 90-degree box dogleg to the right to bypass the obstacle. What heading do you walk to clear the obstacle?
exercises.explanation:
A 90-degree right turn from heading 020° is: 020° + 90° = 110°. You walk on 110° until clear of the swamp, then turn 90° left back to 020°.

Why the other options are wrong: 290° would be a 90-degree turn to the left, not to the right. 200° is a 180-degree turnaround back to where you started. 090° is cardinal East, not a 90° offset from 020°.

exercises.prompt: A pace is defined as two natural footsteps, counted every time the ___ foot strikes the ground. If your calibrated pace count is 65 paces per 100 metres, marching 520 paces indicates you have traveled exactly ___ metres.
exercises.explanation: Paces are counted on the strike of one foot (traditionally the left). 520 paces / 65 paces per 100m = 8 units of 100m = 800 metres.

exercises.prompt: Match each night and dead reckoning navigation tool to its operational duty.
exercises.explanation: Ranger beads count distance; Southern cross finds South; Orion gives East/West; two-person buddy teams eliminate night lateral compass drift.

right.text: Mechanical bead cord tallying elapsed 100-metre units and full kilometres
Constellation whose extended 4.5x long axis projects true South onto horizon
Equatorial star cluster rising due East (090°) and setting due West (270°)
Two-person night formation where rear observer keeps front scout on heading

exercises.prompt: How does walking through dense, thorny scrub or climbing a steep 20% hillslope affect a navigator's personal pace count per 100 metres?
exercises.explanation:
Rough terrain and slopes force shorter steps. If your flat baseline is 65 paces/100m, climbing uphill will require 80-85 paces for the same 100 metres. If you don't adjust, you will believe you have reached 1 km after only 800 real metres.

Why the other options are wrong: Thorns and hills force shorter, high-stepping steps, never longer strides. Assuming pace count is static across mud, hills, and road is a primary cause of lost navigators. Steps shorten uphill due to fatigue and gravity, increasing the count per 100 m.

options.text: Pace count decreases because your legs take wider strides over bushes
Pace count remains perfectly identical regardless of terrain
Paces double in length when climbing uphill
Pace count increases by 15% to 35% because footsteps are shortened and compressed by obstacles and gravity; failing to compensate will cause you to underestimate distance and stop short of the target

exercises.prompt: Photograph a hand-drawn field map sketch, resection plotting exercise on a topographic sheet, plane table setup, or personal ranger pace-bead calibration from your navigation and cartography field practice. Ensure grid coordinates, compass bearings, or measured baseline paces are clearly documented in your notes.
exercises.explanation: Photographic documentation of cartographic plotting, alidade sightlines, or pace count calibration records verifies practical field proficiency in terrestrial navigation independent of electronic satellite navigation.

Navigation instruments (prismatic compass, protractor, alidade, or scale rule) are visible in the work frame
Written field notes record measured magnetic vs grid bearings, calculated declination, or calibrated pace count
Image is well-lit, in sharp focus, showing clean pencil work and legible coordinate notations

lessons.title: Week 5 — Drainage: combined vs separate, falls, and vents
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 5 — Drainage: mifumo, fall, na vents
lessons.briefing:
Drainage units cover above-ground waste you already did and underground systems. Combined systems carry foul and rain in one sewer (older towns). Separate systems keep foul and surface water apart — rain must not overload the septic tank. You should sketch both in plan as the curriculum asks.

Pipes: rigid plastics (PVC-U, PP) have largely replaced cast iron and glazed clay in new work, but you will still meet clay and CI on rehab. Bedding, cover, and haunching under roads matter. Fittings: rest bends, gulleys, inspection chambers, rodding eyes. Access is a legal/practical need — a run you cannot rod is a future excavation.

Falls: too steep and solids race leaving paper; too flat and the drain silts. Follow the diameter tables you were taught (e.g. 100 mm around 1:40 as a starting teaching value — use the spec). Ventilation of the underground system prevents trap siphonage and sewer gas in the house. IC covers must be to load class (driveway vs garden).

Testing: water test (fill to overflow, watch the level) or air test as permitted. Plug branches. Record. A drain that only “looks straight” is not tested. Keep soil tools off potable benches.
lessons.briefingSw: Combined dhidi ya separate. Mvua isizidishe septic. Chamber za inspection. Fall kwa jedwali. Vent. Jaribu maji. Cover ya barabara si ya bustani.

exercises.explanation: Combined is one pipe. Know which the site has before you connect a downpipe.

No vents are allowed

exercises.explanation: Place them at changes of direction and long runs as the drawing shows.

options.text: Decorate the lawn

exercises.explanation: Rain belongs in surface water or a soakaway/harvest tank, not the digester.

options.text: Improves treatment

Is required by CDACC
Replaces the vent

There is a rodding eye

lessons.title: Water systems, isolation, and hygiene
lessons.titleSw: Mifumo ya maji, isolation, na usafi
lessons.briefing:
Plumbing keeps potable water in and sewage out. Know the incoming stopcock, tank valves, and fixture isolators before you cut. Drain the section; opening a live PPR or copper line is a flood, not a shortcut.

Never connect waste to drinking water. Backflow risk is why we use air gaps and approved valves. Do not use the same wrench-dirty rag on a kitchen tap that just sat in a gully.

Hot water: unvented cylinders and solar thermosiphon systems have extra hazards (pressure, scalds). If it is outside your unit, stop and call the person who is allowed to open it.

Mark isolated valves so the next person does not open them on your open joint.
lessons.briefingSw: Funga stopcock na drain kabla ya kukata. Usichanganye taka na maji ya kunywa. Weka alama kwenye valve. Mifumo ya pressure ya hot water ina hatari za ziada.

lessons.title: Pipe materials and making joints
lessons.titleSw: Aina za mabomba na viungo
lessons.briefing:
PVC solvent weld needs a square cut, even chamfer, clean dry surfaces, the right cement for the pipe, and the full insertion with a twist. Hold until it grabs. Purple primer where specified is not graffiti — it is preparation. Too little cement leaks; too much puddles and weakens.

Compression joints: pipe square, olive the right way, do not overtighten brass to the point of crushing. PTFE on threads: in the direction of the thread, not as a random bandage, and not on compression olives.

PPR fusion: temperature and time from the manufacturer. Burnt sockets fail later inside the wall. Support pipes so joints are not in bending.

Pressure-test joints before you close the chase. A leak behind tiles is your name on a complaint.
lessons.briefingSw: PVC: kata sawa, safisha, cement sahihi. Compression: usikaze kupita kiasi. PTFE kwenye thread, si olive. PPR: fuata joto na muda. Jaribu shinikizo kabla ya kufunga ukuta.

exercises.prompt: Solvent-weld PVC fails most often because:
exercises.explanation: Cement cannot stick to mud or a pipe sitting on 3 mm of the socket.

options.text: The moon is full
Dirty, oval, unchamfered, or dry-fit joints without cement
Too many pipe clips
White pipes

exercises.prompt: PTFE tape belongs on:

lessons.title: Week 4 — Rainwater harvesting: gutters, downpipes, and test
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 4 — Kuvuna maji ya mvua
lessons.briefing:
CDACC plumbing includes install rainwater harvesting: interpret drawings, quantify goods, mount, and test. Gutters are troughs under the eaves. Materials: PVC, galvanised, aluminium, GRP. Accessories: running outlets, stop ends, unions, angles (90°/135°), hopper heads, downpipes, shoes, and brackets. Size from roof area and a rainfall intensity (teaching figure often ~0.0208 L/s/m² — use the figure your college cites from BS EN 12056-3).

Fall: gutters must fall toward the outlet (typically around 1:350 to 1:600 as taught — follow the manufacturer). Backfall ponds water and breeds mosquitoes. Brackets at specified centres; do not hang a 6 m PVC gutter on two nails. Expansion: plastics move — use union details that allow it. Isolation from sewage: rainwater is not connected into a foul stack without an approved design.

Mounting: PPE (height work), fascia sound, outlets cut, downpipes plumb, shoes to a gully or tank inlet with a leaf screen. First-flush diverters improve tank water. Tanks: opaque, covered, mosquito-proof, on a level plinth, overflow arranged so it does not undermine the foundation.

Test: water or hose test for leaks at unions, overflow operation, and that the gully/tank receives flow. Housekeeping: offcuts, sealant, and safe ladder work. Portfolio: take-off list plus a photo of a falling gutter and a test note.
lessons.briefingSw: Gutter, downpipe, outlet, stop end. Kadiria kutoka eneo la paa. Fall kuelekea outlet. PVC inapanuka. Tangi funika ili mbu wasizae. Jaribu uvujaji. Usichanganye maji ya mvua na soil stack ovyo.

lessons.title: Week 6 — Sanitary appliances: set-out, seals, and flush
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 6 — Vifaa vya usafi
lessons.briefing:
Sanitary appliances are a listed plumber core: WC pans, cisterns, basins, sinks, urinals, showers, bidets as the college workshop stocks. Set-out from finished floor and centre-lines so the pan sits square to the wall and the seat does not hit the cistern. Pan connectors (soil fitments) must be the right offset; a pan wedged with mortar is a crack waiting.

Basins: brackets or pedestals that actually carry the load, waste and overflow working, trap accessible. Do not support a basin only on the trap. Showers: tray level, waste with hair trap, and a fall that does not flood the room. Sealant is a second defence, not a substitute for a mechanical joint.

Flush: cistern fills to the marked waterline, drop valve or siphon as specified, no continuous trickle (wastes water and stains). Dual flush where specified. After install, flush several times and check the pan connector from the access if you have it.

Hygiene: potable supplies to cisterns via approved inlet valves; overflow discharging safely. PPE for used appliances on rehab jobs. Test: fill, flush, no drip at the stopcock, no rock on the pan.
lessons.briefingSw: WC iwe square, connector sahihi, si mortar kama wedge. Bonde liwe na bracket, si trap pekee. Cistern ijaa hadi alama, isichuruzike. Sealant si kiungo pekee. Flush mara kadhaa kisha kagua.
