lessons.title: Week 7 — Water storage tanks, overflow, and maintenance
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 7 — Tanki, overflow, na matengenezo
lessons.briefing:
Water storage is a plumber core: loft tanks, roof tanks, and ground tanks feeding gravity or pumps. Structure first — a full tank is heavy. Support as the manufacturer and the builder specify. A tank on two skinny timber across a span is how ceilings collapse. Inlet via a float/ball valve set so the waterline leaves air gap and overflow capacity.

Overflow (warning pipe) must discharge where someone will notice — not silently into a void. Covers keep out light, insects, and debris; screened vents. Potable tanks are cleaned on a schedule; biofilm and drowned rodents are public-health failures. Do not use a waste-water drum as a drinking tank.

Isolation: every tank should have valves so you can work without draining the whole site. Maintenance: replace perished ball-valve washers, check overflow, inspect for UV-brittle plastic, and chlorinate after cleaning as instructed. Pumps: isolate electrically as well as hydraulically — you already know that from isolation week.

Test: fill, confirm shut-off, overflow trial, no weep at unions, and the cover back on. Record the clean date. That is storage competence, not “fit and forget”.
lessons.briefingSw: Tanki ni nzito — msaada wa muundo. Ball valve, overflow inayoonekana, kifuniko dhidi ya mbu. Usitumie drum ya taka kwa maji ya kunywa. Valve za isolation. Safisha na rekodi. Pampu: zima umeme pia.

lessons.title: Traps, waste, and leak diagnosis
lessons.titleSw: Traps, waste, na uvujaji
lessons.briefing:
A P-trap holds a water seal that blocks sewer gas. A dry trap in a guest bathroom smells like a blocked sewer even when the line is fine. Prime it, then fix evaporation, leaks, or missing venting.

Waste runs need fall (often around 1:40 as a teaching starting point — follow the spec). Backfall holds water and solids. Boss connections into stacks must use the right fittings, not a hole and hope.

Diagnosis: dry the area, use tissue or a dye, pressurise or run water in one fixture at a time. Condensation on a cold pipe is not always a leak. Repair the source, not the ceiling stain.

PPE for sewage: gloves, wash, and keep tools for soil work separate from potable work.

lessons.title: Vapour-compression cycle and components
lessons.titleSw: Mzunguko wa vapour-compression
lessons.briefing:
Almost every fridge and split AC you service uses the vapour-compression cycle. The compressor raises pressure and temperature of the vapour. The condenser rejects heat so the refrigerant becomes liquid. The expansion device (capillary or TXV) drops pressure. The evaporator absorbs heat as liquid boils at low pressure. If you cannot point to those four on a domestic fridge, you are not diagnosing — you are guessing.

High-side vs low-side: gauges, pipe temperatures, and frost patterns tell a story. Ice on the evaporator with a warm cabinet can be airflow, defrost, or charge — not “always add gas”. The thermostat stops the compressor; it does not fix a leak.

Electrical isolation still applies: unplug, discharge capacitors as trained, and do not short a thermostat with a nail to “test cooling”.
lessons.briefingSw: Compressor inainua shinikizo. Condenser inatoa joto. Expansion inashusha shinikizo. Evaporator inachukua joto. Usiweke gesi bila kuelewa mzunguko. Zima umeme kabla ya kufungua unit.

exercises.explanation: The compressor compresses vapour; the condenser then rejects heat.

options.text: Evaporator

exercises.explanation: Capacitors store charge. Isolation is not optional.

Isolate power and prove dead as for any appliance

lessons.title: Refrigerant law, recovery, and nitrogen
lessons.titleSw: Sheria ya gesi, recovery, na nitrogen
lessons.briefing:
Venting refrigerant to air is environmentally harmful and may be illegal. Recover into a proper cylinder with recovery equipment. Label cylinders. Mixing refrigerants in one bottle is a later technician’s nightmare.

Pressure tests use dry nitrogen, never oxygen or compressed air from an oily workshop compressor. Oxygen plus oil in a system is an explosion risk. Use a regulator and know the test pressure from the manufacturer — do not “pump until it feels hard”.

Goggles and gloves when opening systems. Liquid refrigerant on skin is a freeze burn. Evacuate to the required vacuum before charging; moisture plus refrigerant plus oil makes acids and sludge.

SDS and cylinder colours: know what is in your hand. R600a (isobutane) in many domestic fridges is flammable — no smoking, no sparks, follow hydrocarbon procedures.
lessons.briefingSw: Usitoe gesi hewani — fanya recovery. Jaribu shinikizo kwa nitrogen, si oxygen. Vacuum kabla ya charge. R600a ni kuwaka; fuata taratibu za hydrocarbon.

exercises.explanation: Recovery is competent RAC practice, not optional kindness.

options.text: It is slower

NITA requires open vents for luck

exercises.explanation: Oxygen + oil is dangerous. Moisture in air is also unwelcome.

options.text: Oxygen

Workshop air from an oily compressor

exercises.explanation: Treat HC systems as flammable. Charge masses are small but ignition is real.

options.text: Always non-flammable
A hydrocarbon — flammable; needs spark-aware procedure
The same as water
Only used in cars

exercises.prompt: A deep vacuum before charging is mainly to:
exercises.explanation: Air raises head pressure; moisture damages the system chemically.

options.text: Paint the pipes
Remove air and moisture
Increase oil acidity on purpose

lessons.title: Leak, charge, and performance checks
lessons.titleSw: Uvujaji, charge, na utendaji
lessons.briefing:
Charge is a measured quantity, often by mass (weigh-in) on a capillary system, or by superheat/subcooling on TXV systems as you are taught. “Until the pipe ices” is not a method. Find and repair leaks, replace driers when the system has been open, evacuate, then charge.

Airflow is half of refrigeration. A blocked condenser (dust, cow hair, butcher-shop grease) raises head pressure and trips overloads. A blocked evaporator ices. Clean, straighten fins, check fans, then talk about gas.

After service: cabinet temperature vs spec, no abnormal noise, no ice where it should not be, electrical covers back, and a record of refrigerant type and mass. That record is professional, and it protects the next person.
lessons.briefingSw: Charge ni uzito au superheat/subcooling, si “hadi barafu”. Rekodi uvujaji. Safisha condenser na evaporator. Weka kumbukumbu ya aina na kiasi cha gesi.

Use oxygen to push liquid

Serial plate
Owner’s manual only

lessons.title: Seams, pressing, and assembly order
lessons.titleSw: Mishono, pressing, na mpangilio wa kushona
lessons.briefing:
Construction is a sequence, not a pile of random seams. A typical shirt or uniform blouse: shoulder seams, attach collar or neck facing, set sleeves (or join side seams then sleeves, depending on the method), then cuffs, then hem. If you hem first you often cannot set a sleeve. Write the order on your job card the way the assessor expects.

Plain seams are sewn, pressed open, then neatened with zigzag, overlocker, or a turned edge as specified. Underpress every seam before you cross it with another. “Sew it all then iron at the end” is how collars twist and seam allowances get trapped. Use the ham and sleeve board for curves; do not crush a puff sleeve flat on the big board.

Clip inward curves and notch outward curves so they lie. Grade bulky seams (collar, waistband) so layers form a stair, not a ridge. For zips, a centred zip needs a basted opening, the zip face-down, and stitching an even distance from the teeth. Test on a scrap if the fabric is slippery.

Quality at this stage: even seam width, matching notches, no puckers, and thread ends finished. Assessors put a ruler on your 1.5 cm — they are not guessing.
lessons.briefingSw: Fuata mpangilio: mabega, shingo, mikono, kisha hem. Press kila mshono kabla ya kuuvuka. Neatisha kwa zigzag au overlocker. Clip curves. Zip inahitaji basting. Upana wa mshono lazima uwe sawa — wakaguzi hupima.

exercises.prompt: Why underpress a seam before crossing it with another seam?
exercises.hint: Bulk in a junction cannot be pressed out later.
exercises.explanation: Each seam is a foundation for the next. This is a scored finishing behaviour.

options.text: To use electricity
So allowances lie flat and the next seam is accurate
Pressing is only for the shop window
It shortens the grainline

exercises.prompt: Notching an outward curve (e.g. a collar point area or convex seam) is done to:
exercises.hint: Extra fabric in a curve has nowhere to go.
exercises.explanation: Clips on concave, notches on convex — both help the seam allowance sit after turning.

options.text: Remove bulk so the curve turns without a ridge
Decorate the inside
Weaken the stitch on purpose
Mark the grainline

exercises.prompt: A professional open (plain) seam is usually:
exercises.hint: Open and neatened is the default woven method.
exercises.explanation: Unless the spec says French or overlocked-together, press open and neaten both edges.

options.text: Sewn, pressed to one side untrimmed always
Sewn at the planned allowance, pressed open, then neatened
Glued
Only 2 mm wide on uniforms

exercises.prompt: Why is assembly order written on a job card?
exercises.hint: Some operations are impossible after a hem or a closed side seam.
exercises.explanation: Planning is part of competence, not extra theory.

options.text: To fill paper
So sleeves, collars, and closures are attached while the garment can still be opened flat
Assessors ignore order
It replaces the pattern

exercises.prompt: Trimming layered seam allowances to different widths so they stack without a ridge is called seam ___.
exercises.explanation: Grading reduces bulk in collars, cuffs, and waistbands.

exercises.prompt: You set a sleeve and the ease forms one big pleat at the cap. The spec is a smooth head. What do you do?
exercises.hint: Ease is tiny fullness, not a tuck.
exercises.explanation: Two rows of ease stitching, steam, and even distribution are the textbook fix. A pleat is a construction fault on a plain sleeve.

options.text: Leave it; ease always looks like a pleat
Unpick, redistribute ease with two rows of gather stitches, shrink with the iron if the cloth allows, and restitch
Cut a dart out of the cap
Glue the cap to the dummy

lessons.title: Fitting, hems, and quality control
lessons.titleSw: Fitting, hem, na udhibiti wa ubora
lessons.briefing:
Fitting is a measured process. Put the garment on the client or dummy, pin on the right side, and mark with chalk. Do not cut until you have recorded the change on the pattern or a fitting sheet. A skirt that is 4 cm too long is not “trimmed at the floor”. Unpick the hem, measure from the waist with a stick or metre, mark a level hem, then rebuild the planned hem allowance (often 3–4 cm double-fold on uniforms).

Closures must work: buttons align with holes, zippers open fully, hook-and-bar takes strain off a waist zip. Buttonholes are cut after stitching, not before, unless you use a bound method that requires a window. Secure buttons with a shank on coats so the fabric can sit.

Final press is directional: seams the way they were sewn, collars rolled at the edge, hems without a second shine-line from a dirty iron. Hang the garment and walk around it: unmatched side seams, twisted legs, and hanging threads fail assessment even if the design is pretty.

Before you submit, use a QC list: measurements vs spec, symmetry, inside neatness, labels if required, and safety (no pins left in). That list is how industry and CDACC both think.
lessons.briefingSw: Fitting ni kipimo, si kukata ovyo. Rekodi mabadiliko. Hem ndefu inarekebishwa kwa kufungua na kupima kutoka kiunoni. Angalia zip, vifungo, na symmetry. Fanya orodha ya QC kabla ya kuwasilisha.

exercises.prompt: A double-fold hem is 4 cm too long. The professional fix is:
exercises.explanation: Length comes from a measured mark. Guess-cutting destroys the finish and the allowance for next term.

options.text: Cut the hem off at floor level with scissors
Unpick, re-measure from a fixed point (waist/dummy), and resew the planned hem allowance
Glue the extra fabric inside
Tell the client to grow

exercises.hint: Thickness needs space under the button.
exercises.explanation: A tight-sewn button on a coat pulls and the hole never meets.

options.text: Fashion only
So the button sits above the cloth thickness and the hole can close without strain
NITA bans shanks
It replaces the facing

exercises.prompt: Which item belongs on a final QC list?
exercises.explanation: Quality is evidence against a spec, not a feeling.

options.text: Whether the trainee likes the colour
Measurements against the spec, symmetry, threads, and no pins left in
The Wi-Fi password
The iron brand only

exercises.prompt: Fitting pins should be placed:
exercises.hint: The dummy is not the pattern.
exercises.explanation: Transfer marks. Cutting on the person is unsafe and inaccurate.

options.text: On the wrong side only so the client cannot see errors
On the body, marking the correction, then transferred to cloth/pattern before cutting
Through the machine needle
In the assessor’s file

exercises.prompt: The extra length of cloth turned up at the bottom of a skirt or trouser is the ___ allowance.
exercises.explanation: Hem allowance is planned in the pattern. It is not leftover waste.

exercises.prompt: An assessor finds three pins still in a finished uniform and a hanging bobbin thread at the zip. Result?

Those are finishing faults; remove pins, tidy threads, and only then present
They add XP in industry
Cut the zip out

lessons.title: Week 9 — Gents wear: shirt, trouser, and fly
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 9 — Nguo za wanaume
lessons.briefing:
Gents wear is a distinct core in fashion L5 (shirts, trousers, sometimes a jacket). A man’s shirt: yoke, collar and stand, placket, cuff with placket, and extra length at the back. Collar points must match; the stand sits so the collar rolls, not flaps. Interfacing in collar and stand is not optional if the spec is a uniform shirt.

Trousers: front crease on the grain, fly with zip guard, waistband with a curtain or facing, and pockets that do not gape. Rise (body rise) is measured seated as well as standing or the crotch will cut. A ladies’ block is not a gents’ block — different balance and fly construction.

Topstitching on a shirt is a quality mark: even width, matching thread, no tunnels. Buttons: men’s shirts traditionally button left over right (as worn). Confirm the college spec. Sleeve pitch: the sleeve cap notch matches the shoulder; twisting sleeves are a setting error from construction week, still assessed here.

Assessed sample: a school/office shirt or a pair of trousers with a working fly. Attach the spec sheet. Industrial attachment later will expect you to hit minutes-per-operation; here you hit quality first.
lessons.briefingSw: Shati: yoke, collar na stand, placket, cuff. Suruali: crease, fly, waistband, rise. Block ya wanawake si ya wanaume. Topstitch sawa. Interfacing kwenye collar.

exercises.prompt: A shirt collar that will not sit is often missing:
exercises.explanation: The stand is the engineered piece. Skipping it on a formal shirt is a fail.

options.text: A longer hem
A correctly interfaced stand and balanced collar points
A bust dart

lessons.title: Week 7 — Pattern grading and size sets
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 7 — Grading ya pattern na saizi
lessons.briefing:
Construction of a master pattern (size 12 or the college block) is not the end. Grading produces the size set (e.g. 8–16) using grade rules: how much the bust, waist, hip, and length change per size. You do not photocopy at 110% — that enlarges buttons, seam allowances, and dart intake wrongly. Shift cardinal points: bust point, waist, hip, shoulder, scye, hem.

Manual grading uses a grade table and tracks (move X and Y). Computer grading does the same with CAD. Nested patterns should look like a family: even gaps at side seams, not a fan that explodes at the hem only. Check that dart tips still aim at the bust point after grade.

Kenyan school uniforms often have a size chart in centimetres. Measure a sample of learners; do not import a European chart blindly. Ease must remain after grading — a size 16 that lost wearing ease is unwearable.

This week: grade a skirt block one size up and one down, nest them, and measure hip circumference against the chart. That is the CDACC grading outcome.
lessons.briefingSw: Grading si photocopy 110%. Tumia grade rules: bust, waist, hip, urefu. Cardinal points. Nested patterns ziwe familia. Ease ibaki. Pima chati ya Kenya, si ya Ulaya tu.

lessons.title: Week 8 — Ladies wear: dart, ease, and closures
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 8 — Nguo za wanawake
lessons.briefing:
Ladies wear units in Kenyan fashion L5 typically produce a blouse, dress, or skirt that proves dart manipulation, closures, and fit on a female form. Bust darts point toward the bust point and stop short (about 1.5–2.5 cm) so they do not sit as cones on the apex. Waist darts shape the torso. If the client is between sizes, you alter the pattern — you do not guess on the cloth.

Closures: centred zip, lapped zip, invisible zip, or buttons and placket. Invisible zips need the right foot and to be stitched close to the coils. A gaping back neck is a pattern/shoulder issue, not a bigger zip. Facings and bias bindings neat on the inside are marked hard.

Ease: a woven blouse needs wearing ease at bust (often ~5–8 cm depending on style). A “body-con” woven without stretch and without ease will not button. Knit ladies wear follows the textile week: stretch stitches, stay tape at the shoulder.

Assessed sample: a school or office blouse with collar or neck finish, set-in sleeve, buttoned front or zip, and a finished hem. QC against the spec from sketching week.

lessons.title: Lockstitch machine and workshop safety
lessons.titleSw: Mashine ya lockstitch na usalama
lessons.briefing:
Fashion practicals start at the table, not at the pattern. Unplug the iron when you leave the board. Cover the needle, and never sew with the presser foot up. A lockstitch machine forms a stitch when the needle thread loops around the bobbin thread. If the machine is threaded wrong — especially missing the take-up lever — you get bird’s nests, skipped stitches, or a jammed hook.

Needle size must match fabric: 70/10 or 80/12 for shirting, 90/14 or 100/16 for denim and canvas. A blunt or bent needle on heavy cloth is the usual cause of skipped stitches, not “the machine is old”. Stitch length is typically 2.0–2.5 mm for construction seams and longer for basting. Tension discs must be closed when you thread; the thread sits between them, not on top.

Bobbin winding should be even. Drop the bobbin so it rotates the way the machine manual shows, pull the thread through the slot, and hold both threads to the back before the first stitch. At the end of a seam, reverse two or three stitches, then cut threads with the thread cutter or snips — not by yanking the garment.

CDACC/NITA assessors watch whether you can thread independently, sew a straight seam on calico, and leave the station safe. That is the first unit, before any fashion drawing.
lessons.briefingSw: Anza na usalama: zima pasi, funika sindano. Lockstitch inahitaji uzi wa needle na bobbin kukutana. Chagua sindano kulingana na kitambaa: 80/12 kwa shirting, 90/14 au 100/16 kwa denim. Tension na take-up lever ni muhimu. Kadiria stitch 2.0–2.5 mm. Wakaguzi wanatazama kama unaweza kushona mshono sawa na kuacha meza salama.

lessons.title: Pattern, grain, and cutting
lessons.titleSw: Pattern, grain, na kukata
lessons.briefing:
A garment is decided on the table before a single stitch. Patterns carry grainlines, notches, drill holes, size, and cutting instructions. The grainline must sit parallel to the selvedge (or to the warp on a folded length). Off-grain collars twist; off-grain trousers twist around the leg.

Standard woven seam allowance in many TVET practicals is 1.5 cm (sometimes 1 cm on necklines after staystitching — follow the pattern). Hem allowances are larger and must be planned, not guessed at the floor. Fold fabric right sides together unless the lay plan says otherwise. Pin inside the allowance, not on the stitch line, and cut with the shears resting on the table — don’t lift the cloth and chew it in the air.

Notches match pieces: one notch often means a front, two a back, or they mark ease. Transfer markings with tailor’s tacks, chalk, or a tracing wheel as taught. Staystitch curved necks and armholes 5 mm from the edge, in the direction that stops stretch, before you handle the piece a lot.

Assessors look at a clean lay: little waste, all pieces facing the planned nap/print direction, and no missing facings. Count pieces against the pattern chart before you move the waste.
lessons.briefingSw: Grainline inafaa kuwa sambamba na selvedge. Seam allowance ya kawaida ni 1.5 cm. Kata kitambaa mezani, si hewani. Notches zinalinganisha vipande. Staystitch shingo kabla ya kushughulikia. Hesabu vipande kulingana na chart kabla ya kutupa waste.

lessons.title: Week 6 — Fashion sketching and specifications
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 6 — Mchoro wa fashion na spec
lessons.briefing:
CDACC fashion includes sketching figures and producing working drawings. A croquis is a proportioned template (often 8–9 heads for fashion, more realistic for school uniforms). Design sketches show silhouette, style lines, and fabric suggestion. They are not the same as a technical flat: flats are 2D, garment as if laid on a table, seams and topstitching visible, left and right consistent.

A spec sheet / working drawing carries measurements (bust, waist, hip, length, sleeve, hem depth, seam allowance), stitch types, notions (zip length, button size), and fabric. Without it the machinist invents, and the assessor cannot mark against a standard. Callouts: “lockstitch 2.4 mm, 1.5 cm SA, 20 cm invisible zip”.

Shade for drape, but do not hide construction. Front and back views. If there is a lining, show it. Kenyan polytechnic practicals often ask for a school skirt or shirt — draw the actual garment, not a Paris gown, unless the brief says otherwise.

Portfolio this week: one croquis illustration plus one flat plus a measurement table for a ladies’ blouse. That is how industry hands work to the sewing line.
lessons.briefingSw: Croquis ni kielelezo cha mwili. Flat ni mchoro wa kiufundi wa nguo. Spec sheet ina vipimo, stitch, zip, na kitambaa. Chora mbele na nyuma. Sare ya shule ni mradi halali.

exercises.prompt: A technical flat is best described as:
exercises.explanation: Illustration sells; flats instruct. You need both in the unit.

options.text: A painted fashion pose only
A 2D working drawing of the garment with seams, topstitch, and callouts

lessons.title: Week 5 — Textile science and fabric choice
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 5 — Sayansi ya nguo na chaguo la kitambaa
lessons.briefing:
Fashion Level 5 occupational standards start with textile principles, not only the machine. Fibres are natural (cotton, linen, wool, silk) or manufactured (polyester, nylon, viscose, blends). Cotton breathes and sews easily; it wrinkles and shrinks if not pre-shrunk. Wool felts with heat and moisture. Polyester is strong and crease-resistant but melts under a too-hot iron — that is why you test the iron on a scrap.

Yarn becomes fabric by weaving (plain, twill, satin) or knitting. Woven fabrics have warp (along the grain, little stretch) and weft. Knit fabrics stretch and need ball-point needles, stretch stitches, and a walking foot or careful feed. Cutting a woven shirt on the bias (45°) gives drape; cutting off-grain makes a hem twist after washing — a classic assessor fail.

Grainline on the pattern must follow the warp unless the designer marked bias. Selvage is the factory edge parallel to warp. Nap (velvet, corduroy) must all lie the same way or light hits as two colours. Pre-wash or steam-shrink as the fabric requires before you cut a uniform that must survive the hostel laundry.

Identify: fibre burn tests are taught with care (tiny sample, ventilation, never in a sewing classroom full of cloth). Care labels: wash temperature, tumble, iron dots. Portfolio: a fabric swatch card with fibre, weave, suitable garment, needle size, and stitch length.
lessons.briefingSw: Nyuzi asilia dhidi ya synthetic. Cotton inapumua na kuwa wrinkles; polyester inayeyuka kwa pasi moto. Weave ina warp na weft; knit inanyooshwa. Grainline ifuate warp. Pre-shrink sare. Nap ya velvet iwe upande mmoja.

exercises.prompt: Warp yarns in a woven fabric generally:
exercises.explanation: Weft is across. Grainline of most shirts follows warp.

options.text: Run across the fabric and stretch a lot
Run parallel to the selvage and have little stretch
Are always wool
Replace the grainline

exercises.prompt: A polyester school blouse should be pressed:
exercises.explanation: Shine and holes are heat damage. Use a press cloth.

options.text: On linen heat with steam forever
On a cooler setting, tested on a scrap — synthetics melt
With a welding torch
Never, because polyester cannot crease

exercises.prompt: Knit jersey for a T-shirt needs:
exercises.explanation: Sharp needles cut knits and cause holes that run.

options.text: A leather needle and 4 mm straight stitch only
Ball-point or stretch needle and a stretch stitch or overlocker
No needle
A size 110 jeans needle always

exercises.prompt: Nap fabrics such as corduroy must be cut:
exercises.explanation: One panel will look a different shade if the pile is reversed.

options.text: With pile running in mixed directions to save cloth
With all pieces in the same pile direction
On the weft only
Without grainlines

exercises.prompt: The factory-finished edge of woven cloth parallel to the warp is the ___.
exercises.explanation: Grainline is usually parallel to the selvage.

exercises.prompt: You cut a cotton uniform without pre-washing. After hostel laundry it is two sizes smaller. Cause?
exercises.explanation: CDACC textile principles exist so the garment still fits after wet treatment.

options.text: The machine stitch length

Too much interfacing
Wrong zip colour

lessons.title: Soil Composition & Foundation Sizing
lessons.titleSw: Muundo wa Udongo na Upimaji wa Msingi
lessons.briefing:
All structural durability begins with the ground. In East Africa, building failures
routinely stem from building on expansive black cotton soil (montmorillonite clay)
without proper moisture isolation or foundation depth. Before manufacturing blocks
or digging trenches, a builder must classify the subsoil: the sand-to-clay ratio
determines whether soil can support load or will heave and crack masonry. This day
teaches field soil classification tests (ribbon test, drop ball test, 24-hour glass
jar sedimentation) and foundation engineering (rubble trench with French drains).
lessons.briefingSw:
Uimara wote wa jengo huanzia ardhini. Katika Afrika Mashariki, majengo mengi huanguka
au kupasuka kwa sababu ya kujengwa kwenye udongo wa 'black cotton' unaovimba na
kupasuka wakati wa mvua. Siku hii inafundisha jinsi ya kupima udongo kwa kutumia chupa
ya kioo (jar sedimentation) na kujenga misingi imara ya mawe ya rubble trench.
lessons.outline:
1. Soil mineral fractions: gravel, coarse/fine sand, silt, and cohesive clay
2. The black cotton soil hazard: expansive montmorillonite clay in Kenya
3. Rapid field test 1: The ribbon test (extruding moist soil between thumb and finger)
4. Rapid field test 2: The drop ball test from 1.0 meter height
5. Definitive volumetric test: The 24-hour glass jar sedimentation test
6. Soil bearing capacities: bedrock vs gravel vs firm clay vs loose sand (kN/m²)
7. The Rubble Trench foundation: porous rock bed with perforated drain pipe
8. Stem wall (plinth) construction: elevating earthen walls at least 30 cm above ground grade

exercises.prompt: You perform a 24-hour jar test on a Kenyan subsoil sample. The total settled depth is 10 cm: the bottom sand layer is 7 cm, the middle silt layer is 1 cm, and the top clay layer is 2 cm. What is your engineering assessment of this soil for compressed earth blocks?
exercises.explanation:
Correct! 70% sand provides the load-bearing aggregate skeleton, and 20% clay provides natural cohesion. With 5-8% cement or lime stabilization, this soil will yield high compressive strength blocks.

Why the other options are wrong: 2 cm out of 10 cm is 20% clay, which is well within the safe 15–25% binder range. Soil with 50% clay shrinks massively during drying, causing extensive structural fissures. Organic matter decays and decomposes, leaving voids that compromise compressive strength. Structural earth must be entirely mineral subsoil.

options.text: Unusable — the soil contains far too much clay and will crack
Too sandy — the block will crumble because clay must be at least 50%
The soil requires addition of organic matter like manure
Excellent — 70% sand and 20% clay is near the ideal structural ratio for stabilized compressed earth blocks

exercises.prompt: A stone or concrete stem wall (plinth) must elevate earthen walls at least ___ cm above ground grade to protect against rainwater splash and surface erosion.
exercises.explanation: Water bouncing off hard soil during torrential rains causes severe splash erosion on earthen wall bases. Elevating the base 30 cm (12 inches) on a stone or concrete stem wall prevents wall undermining.

exercises.prompt: Match each soil test to its diagnostic purpose.

right.text: Precise volumetric percentage of sand, silt, and clay fractions
Rapid qualitative assessment of soil cohesion and clay plasticity
Cohesion test where a moist 4 cm ball is dropped from 1m to observe shattering
Free-draining stone footing that prevents frost heave and water pooling

lessons.title: Compressed Earth Blocks & Stabilization
lessons.titleSw: Matofali ya Udongo Yaliyoshindiliwa na Uimarishaji
lessons.briefing:
Fired clay bricks consume massive quantities of firewood, driving deforestation across
Kenya's water towers. Compressed Earth Blocks (CEB), made with manual toggle presses
(such as the Cinva-Ram or Auram press), provide structural masonry units with a fraction
of the carbon footprint and zero fuel cost. When stabilized with 5–8% cement or lime,
CEBs resist rain erosion and achieve compressive strengths exceeding Kenya Standard
KS 02-1070 (≥ 2.5 MPa). This day covers mechanical pressing, chemical stabilization,
optimum moisture testing, damp curing protocols, and earth mortar formulation.
lessons.briefingSw:
Kutengeneza matofali ya kuchoma kwa kuni huharibu misitu ya Kenya. Matofali ya udongo
yaliyoshindiliwa kwa mashine ya mkono (CEB) kama Cinva-Ram yanatoa uimara mkubwa bila
kuhitaji kuni hata kidogo. Yakichanganywa na asilimia 5–8 ya saruji au chokaa, matofali
haya yanadumu kwa miongo mingi. Siku hii inafundisha jinsi ya kupima unyevu, kushindilia,
na kuponya matofali chini ya plastiki.
lessons.outline:
1. Environmental and economic comparison: Fired bricks vs quarry stone vs CEB
2. The mechanics of stabilization: Cement (for sandy soils) vs Lime (for clay soils)
3. Determining Optimum Moisture Content (OMC): The hand-squeeze ball test
4. Manual block pressing: Operation of the toggle lever press (Cinva-Ram mechanism)
5. The curing imperative: 14 to 28-day hydration under black polythene sheeting
6. Compressive strength standards: KS 02-1070 requirements (dry vs wet strength)
7. Mortar compatibility: Soil-cement slurry vs destructive rigid Portland mortars
8. Interlocking CEB (ISSB) designs: Mortarless tongue-and-groove construction

exercises.prompt: A builder leaves freshly pressed cement-stabilized earth blocks directly under the hot midday sun to 'dry quickly'. What will happen to the blocks?
exercises.explanation:
Correct! Cement requires moisture to hydrate and form calcium silicate hydrate crystals. Without damp curing under plastic tarpaulins for at least 14 days, the blocks will fail under minimal load.

Why the other options are wrong: While warm temperatures help, solar heat evaporates the internal water required for cement hydration, halting crystal growth and causing severe friability. Firing ceramic bricks requires kiln temperatures above 900 °C, not ambient solar heat. Quartz sand does not melt or vitrify under sunlight.

options.text: They will achieve maximum strength faster because heat accelerates cement curing
They will turn into fired ceramic bricks
Sunlight reacts with the sand to produce glass crystals
They will dry out prematurely, stopping cement hydration and resulting in weak, crumbling blocks full of shrinkage cracks

exercises.prompt: For sandy soils, the recommended percentage of Ordinary Portland Cement by weight for stabilizing compressed earth blocks is ___% to 8%.
exercises.explanation: A stabilization ratio of 5% to 8% cement by weight provides the ideal balance between weather resistance, compressive strength (≥ 2.5 MPa), and material cost efficiency.

exercises.prompt: Match each earthen masonry term to its correct definition.

right.text: Soil moisture level where mechanical compaction achieves maximum dry density
Traps humidity for 14-28 days so cement crystals hydrate fully without evaporating
Blocks with tongue-and-groove profiles that interlock with little to no mortar
Best stabilizer for high-clay soils through long-term pozzolanic reactions

lessons.title: Earthbag & Superadobe Dome Mechanics
lessons.titleSw: Mifuko ya Udongo na Miundo ya Dome
lessons.briefing:
Earthbag construction (pioneered by architect Nader Khalili / Cal-Earth as "Superadobe")
is one of the most disaster-resilient building technologies on Earth. By filling woven
polypropylene sacks with damp subsoil, tamping them into stone-hard compressive layers,
and running 4-point barbed wire between courses for tensile resistance, builders can
construct earthquake-, hurricane-, and bullet-resistant monolithic domes using zero
roof timber, steel rebar, or fired bricks. This day covers bag filling, continuous tamping,
the compass trammel guide, corbelled dome geometry, and natural weatherproofing plasters.
lessons.briefingSw:
Ujenzi wa mifuko ya udongo (Earthbag / Superadobe) ni moja ya njia imara zaidi duniani
dhidi ya matetemeko ya ardhi na vimbunga. Kwa kujaza mifuko ya plastiki na udongo wenye unyevu,
kuipiga kwa chuma (tamping), na kuweka nyaya za miiba (barbed wire) kati ya tabaka,
unaweza kujenga kuba (dome) imara bila kuhitaji mbao za paa wala bati.
lessons.outline:
1. Superadobe fundamentals: Woven polypropylene tubular bags + damp mineral subsoil
2. The tensile key: 4-point, 2-strand 12.5 gauge barbed wire between every course
3. Continuous tamping mechanics: Converting loose soil into dense rammed monoliths
4. The Compass Trammel: Using central pivot chains to control circular radius and corbelling
5. Catenary arch vs hemispherical dome: Directing all structural loads into pure compression
6. Opening mechanics: Constructing rigid wooden arch forms for doors and windows
7. Buttresses and shear walls: Stabilizing straight wall segments with intersecting curves
8. Exterior plaster coats: Scratch coat, brown coat, and lime/Opuntia cactus water-shedding finish

exercises.prompt: Why must two parallel strands of 4-point barbed wire be laid between every course of tamped earthbags in a Superadobe structure?
exercises.explanation:
Correct! Soil has massive compressive strength but virtually zero tensile strength. Barbed wire bites into the upper and lower polypropylene fabric, locking the courses together against seismic shear and outward dome thrust.

Why the other options are wrong: While wire does deter rodents, that is not its primary structural role. Lightning protection requires heavy dedicated copper conductors, not interrupted fence wire. The wire is sandwiched entirely inside the horizontal course joints and is not exposed on the exterior.

options.text: To keep rats and rodents from chewing into the wall
To conduct lightning safely to the earth grounding rod
To hold the plaster onto the exterior bags
The wire acts as horizontal tensile reinforcement and shear keys, preventing bags from sliding under lateral and seismic forces

exercises.prompt: An inverted hanging chain represents a ___ arch curve, which channels all structural self-weight into pure compression with zero tensile stress.
exercises.explanation: A catenary curve represents the exact mathematical inversion of tension into compression. Using a catenary profile for earthbag domes prevents outward tensile buckling, making roofs self-supporting without wood or steel beams.

exercises.prompt: Match each earthbag dome component to its construction function.

right.text: Central pivoting guide to ensure precise circular radius and inward corbelling
Two lowest bag courses filled with stone to break capillary moisture wicking
Compresses loose damp soil into solid, high-density monolithic layers
Natural waterproofing additive boiled from cactus pads for lime plaster finish

lessons.title: Timber Trusses & Thermal Insulation
lessons.titleSw: Paa za Mbao na Kuzuia Joto
lessons.briefing:
In East Africa, the ubiquitous uninsulated corrugated iron (mabati) roof turns homes
into ovens by day and refrigerators by night, with roof sheets reaching 60–70 °C under
equatorial sun. Furthermore, weak roof-to-wall connections cause entire roofs to tear
away during annual thunderstorm microbursts. This day teaches the structural mechanics
of timber trusses (King Post and Howe configurations), timber preservative treatments
against termites and borers, hurricane tie strapping, and passive thermal control
strategies (generous overhang eaves, radiant barrier foil, and convective ridge vents).
lessons.briefingSw:
Nchini Kenya, mabati yasiyo na insulation hufanya nyumba kuwa kama tanuru wakati wa
mchana na baridi kali usiku. Upepo mkali wa dhoruba pia hung'oa mapaa yasiyofungwa
kwa hurricane ties. Siku hii inafundisha uhandisi wa nguzo za mbao za paa (King post
truss), matibabu ya mbao dhidi ya mchwa, na mbinu za kupunguza joto ndani ya nyumba.
lessons.outline:
1. Truss triangulation principles: Converting bending moments into pure axial tension/compression
2. The King Post Truss anatomy: Top rafters, horizontal tie beam, central king post, and diagonal struts
3. Timber species in Kenya: Cypress (Cupressus lusitanica), Blue Gum (Eucalyptus saligna), and Pine
4. Wood preservation: Boron salt diffusion (anti-termite/borer) vs copper naphthenate
5. Connection engineering: Through-bolts, 2 mm steel gusset plates, and galvanized hurricane ties
6. Wind uplift calculations: Why roofs blow OFF rather than collapse IN
7. The 60 cm overhang rule: Shading mud/CEB walls from torrential vertical rains
8. Passive convective cooling: Continuous ridge vents and ventilated double roofs

exercises.prompt: During a severe thunderstorm, a metal roof is ripped off a house. Structural forensic analysis shows the trusses lifted vertically off the wall plate while the walls remained intact. What caused this failure?
exercises.explanation:
Correct! High wind generates powerful Bernoulli suction lift. Plain wire nails possess minimal pull-out resistance under upward tension. Trusses must be anchored to ring beams with heavy galvanized hurricane ties or bolted straps.

Why the other options are wrong: Excessive weight causes downward bending collapse, not upward detachment. Steep pitches improve rainwater shedding and do not cause uplift failures on their own. Termites digest cellulose in wood, not galvanized steel sheets.

options.text: Wind passing over the roof slope created aerodynamic negative pressure (suction), which overwhelmed plain nailed connections lacking hurricane tie strapping
The roof was too heavy for the supporting timber trusses
The pitch of the roof was too steep for rainwater runoff
Termites consumed the corrugated iron metal sheets

exercises.prompt: In a traditional King Post roof truss, the central vertical King Post member is under pure ___ (tension/compression) as it suspends the horizontal tie beam.
exercises.explanation: The central king post acts as a suspension hanger. It is under axial tension, holding up the center of the bottom chord (tie beam) so it cannot sag under its own weight or ceiling loads.

exercises.prompt: Match each passive roof design element to its cooling or structural benefit.

right.text: Shades windows from midday sun and protects earthen walls from driving rain
Allows buoyant hot ceiling air to exhaust out the roof apex continuously
Reflects 95% of solar infrared radiation back toward the sky
Resists aerodynamic wind uplift forces during severe thunderstorm gusts

lessons.title: Ferro-Cement Engineering & Stormproofing
lessons.titleSw: Uhandisi wa Ferro-Cement na Kukabili Dhoruba
lessons.briefing:
Ferro-cement is a specialized form of reinforced concrete utilizing closely spaced
layers of flexible galvanized wire mesh and light skeletal steel impregnated with a rich
cement-sand mortar. With wall thicknesses of just 20 to 35 mm, ferro-cement exhibits
unmatched tensile ductility, high impact resistance, and crack control. In East Africa,
it is the premier technology for constructing low-cost, 10,000-to-50,000-litre rainwater
harvesting cisterns (at one-third the cost of plastic rotomolded tanks), curved cyclone
storm shelters, and hygienic biogas digesters. This final day covers armature framing,
mesh layering, mortar formulation (1:2 ratio, low w/c), plaster penetration, damp curing,
and a practical structural building assessment.
lessons.briefingSw:
Ferro-cement ni teknolojia ya saruji nyembamba (milimita 20-35) iliyoimarishwa kwa tabaka
nyingi za waya wa kuku (chicken wire) na mesh ya chuma. Nchini Kenya, ndiyo teknolojia
bora zaidi ya kujenga matanki makubwa ya maji ya mvua ya lita 10,000 hadi 50,000 kwa
gharama ya theluthi moja ya matanki ya plastiki, na vyumba thabiti vya dhoruba.
lessons.outline:
1. The ferro-cement principle: High specific surface area of reinforcement vs conventional RCC
2. Materials: 6 mm mild steel skeletal rebar + 4 layers of 12 mm hexagonal galvanized chicken wire
3. Mortar formulation: 1:2 to 1:2.5 Portland cement to clean quartz sand (water/cement ratio ≤ 0.40)
4. Workability without water excess: Using superplasticizers or liquid dish soap as field surfactant
5. The plastering sequence: Forcing mortar from both sides to eliminate internal voids
6. The 21-day underwater curing rule for zero-leakage water cisterns
7. Storm-resistant design: Aerodynamic rounded profiles that deflect 150 km/h wind shear
8. PHOTO_CAPTURE practical: Construct and document a ferro-cement or stabilized earth structural specimen

exercises.prompt: Why must the water-cement ratio in a ferro-cement water storage tank mortar strictly be kept at or below 0.42?
exercises.explanation:
Correct! Only about 0.25–0.28 water-cement ratio is chemically needed to hydrate cement. Any excess water beyond 0.40 occupies physical volume that evaporates, leaving porous capillary networks that leak stored water and allow air to rust the inner mesh.

Why the other options are wrong: Higher water content delays setting time, not accelerates it. Small amounts of hydrogen form initially with zinc, but keeping water low does not eliminate chemical reaction. Cement is a hydraulic binder and cannot harden without water.

options.text: Excess mixing water evaporates after setting, leaving microscopic capillary channels that cause porosity, water leaks, and rusting of wire mesh
Higher water content makes the mortar set too quickly before it can be applied
Water reacts chemically with the galvanized zinc wire coating to produce explosive gas
Cement requires zero water to bond with wire mesh

exercises.prompt: A ferro-cement armature typically consists of light skeletal steel rebar sandwiched between ___ layers of galvanized hexagonal wire netting.
exercises.explanation: Two layers of galvanized hexagonal mesh on each face (4 layers total) sandwiching the central rebar frame provides the optimal high specific surface area required for crack arrest and high tensile ductility.

exercises.prompt: Practical Assessment: Document your construction test sample (Ferro-Cement specimen or Stabilized Earth Block/Soil Jar Test).

rubric.criterion: Specimen prepared according to technical instructions (Jar test with marked layers, compressed test block, or wired mesh test panel)
Photo clearly shows material details (sedimentation levels marked on glass, smooth tamped block surfaces, or wire encapsulation)
Measurement tool (ruler, tape measure, or caliper) visible alongside specimen for scale
Handwritten note with student ID, date, and local material origin visible in frame
Brief written caption explaining the observed soil ratio, block moisture behavior, or mesh layering count

lessons.title: PV Fundamentals & Panel Selection
lessons.titleSw: Misingi ya PV na Uchaguzi wa Paneli
lessons.briefing:
A 100 W solar panel costs KSh 7 000–10 000 in Nairobi (2025). Understanding what
that number actually buys — and what it does not — is the difference between a system
that runs a household for 15 years and one that fails in 18 months. This day decodes
the photovoltaic effect, reads a panel datasheet correctly, and calculates the right
tilt angle for any location in Kenya or East Africa.
lessons.briefingSw:
Paneli ya jua ya wati 100 inagharimu KSh 7,000–10,000 Nairobi (2025). Kuelewa
kinachonunuliwa kwa pesa hiyo — na kinachokosekana — ni tofauti kati ya mfumo
unaoendesha nyumba kwa miaka 15 na unaoshindwa ndani ya miezi 18.
lessons.outline:
1. The photovoltaic effect: how a silicon p-n junction converts photons to current
2. The I-V curve: Isc, Voc, Vmp, Imp, and maximum power point (MPP)
3. Reading a panel datasheet: STC vs NOCT conditions, temperature coefficients
4. Monocrystalline vs polycrystalline vs thin-film: which to choose in Kenya
5. Panel ratings in practice: 100 W STC does not mean 100 W on your roof
6. Tilt angle calculation for Kenya latitudes (equator to 4°S)
7. Shade analysis: the one-module-in-shade problem and bypass diodes
8. Series vs parallel stringing: when and why

exercises.prompt: A 200 W monocrystalline panel has a temperature coefficient of −0.38 %/°C. On a Mombasa rooftop the cell temperature reaches 60 °C. What is the expected output?
exercises.explanation:
Correct. (60 − 25) = 35 °C above STC. 35 × 0.38 % = 13.3 % loss. 200 × (1 − 0.133) = 173 W. At 165–175 W depending on exact conditions — this is the real-world operating range.

Why the other options are wrong: Panel ratings are at STC (25 °C cell temperature). Real-world cell temperatures in Kenya routinely reach 50–65 °C, causing significant derating. Higher temperature increases thermal noise in the semiconductor, reducing the built-in junction voltage. Output decreases with temperature for crystalline silicon. (Thin-film panels also derate, though slightly less.) There is no fixed 10 % rule. Loss is calculated from the actual temperature coefficient and the temperature difference from STC. Always use the datasheet coefficient.

options.text: 200 W — the rating is the rating regardless of temperature
Approximately 165 W — temperature derate of (60−25) × 0.38 % = 13.3 % applied
Approximately 220 W — hot panels produce more energy
About 180 W — there is a fixed 10 % loss for Kenyan conditions

exercises.prompt: The maximum power point voltage (___) is always lower than the open-circuit voltage (Voc) on an I-V curve.
exercises.explanation: Vmp is typically 70–80 % of Voc. For a 12 V nominal panel: Voc ≈ 22 V, Vmp ≈ 18 V. A charge controller must track Vmp (MPPT) or be set below Voc (PWM) to extract useful power.

exercises.prompt: Match each panel datasheet term to its correct definition.

right.text: Maximum current at zero voltage (shorted terminals)
Maximum voltage at zero current (open terminals)
Rated power = Vmp × Imp at STC
Squareness of I-V curve = (Vmp × Imp) / (Voc × Isc)

lessons.title: Battery Systems & Bank Sizing
lessons.titleSw: Mifumo ya Betri na Upimaji wa Benki
lessons.briefing:
The battery bank is the most expensive, most failure-prone, and most misunderstood
component of any off-grid solar system. A 200 Ah lead-acid bank costs KSh 25 000–40 000
and should last 3–5 years with correct use — or 12 months with common mistakes. This day
covers chemistry, depth of discharge, C-rating, state of charge monitoring, and the
arithmetic of sizing a bank for a real Kenyan household.
lessons.briefingSw:
Benki ya betri ndicho kipande cha gharama zaidi, chenye kushindwa zaidi, na
kisichoelewa zaidi katika mfumo wowote wa jua nje ya gridi. Benki ya lead-acid
ya 200 Ah inagharimu KSh 25,000–40,000 na inapaswa kudumu miaka 3–5 kwa matumizi
sahihi — au miezi 12 na makosa ya kawaida.
lessons.outline:
1. Battery chemistry overview: lead-acid (FLA, AGM, Gel) vs lithium (LiFePO4)
2. Key parameters: capacity (Ah), voltage, depth of discharge (DoD), cycle life
3. The C-rating: why a 100 Ah battery is not always 100 Ah
4. State of Charge (SoC): voltage tables, hydrometer readings, coulomb counting
5. Sizing a battery bank: autonomy days, DoD, efficiency losses
6. Worked example: sizing for a typical Kenyan household (lights, phone, radio, TV)
7. Battery wiring: series, parallel, series-parallel; cable sizing to battery terminals
8. Maintenance: equalisation, watering, temperature compensation

exercises.prompt: A household has a 200 Ah (C20) FLA battery bank at 12 V. The inverter is running a 500 W load. What is the discharge current and roughly how long before reaching 50% DoD?
exercises.explanation:
500 W ÷ 12 V = 41.7 A. At C5 rate (~41 A for a 200 Ah bank), effective capacity drops to ~80% = 160 Ah. 50% DoD = 80 Ah. Time = 80 ÷ 41.7 ≈ 1.9–2.4 hours depending on actual derating.

Why the other options are wrong: This calculation ignores C-rate derating. At 41.7 A discharge from a 200 Ah bank (C4.8 rate), actual available capacity is only 75–80% of rated, not 100%. Ohm's law and power: P = V × I, so I = P ÷ V = 500 ÷ 12 = 41.7 A — not 500 A. The 500 W is the power, not the current. The C20 rate for a 200 Ah bank is 10 A (200 ÷ 20), not 20 A. At the actual discharge rate of 41.7 A (C4.8), the C20 capacity figure does not apply directly.

options.text: Current = 41.7 A; usable time = 4.8 hours (half of 200 Ah ÷ 41.7 A)
Current = 500 A; the battery would be damaged immediately
Current = 41.7 A; time = 10 hours because 200 Ah ÷ 20 A = 10 hours
Current = 41.7 A; usable time ≈ 2.4 hours (using 80% of rated Ah at this high discharge rate)

exercises.prompt: A technician measures 12.05 V on a 12 V FLA battery that has been resting for 3 hours. This indicates the battery is at approximately ___% state of charge.
exercises.explanation: From the OCV table: 12.00 V = 25% SoC, 12.20 V = 50% SoC. 12.05 V falls just above the 25% mark — battery is nearly empty and should be recharged immediately to prevent sulfation damage.

exercises.prompt: Match each battery term to its correct definition or value.

right.text: Recommended maximum discharge — preserves 500 cycle life
Capacity when discharged fully over 20 hours
Critically discharged FLA cell — charge immediately
Controlled overcharge at 15.5 V to dissolve sulfation (FLA only)

lessons.title: Charge Controllers & System Sizing
lessons.titleSw: Vidhibiti vya Chaji na Upimaji wa Mfumo
lessons.briefing:
The charge controller is the brain of the solar system. It protects the battery from
overcharge and over-discharge, tracks the panel's maximum power point, and provides
load control outputs. Choosing the wrong controller — or sizing it incorrectly — wastes
10–30% of your available solar energy or destroys your battery bank. This day covers
PWM vs MPPT operation, controller rating arithmetic, and a complete system sizing
worksheet from load survey to component selection.
lessons.briefingSw:
Kidhibiti cha chaji ni ubongo wa mfumo wa jua. Inalinda betri dhidi ya kuchajwa
kupita kiasi na kutochajwa kupita kiasi, inafuatilia hatua ya nguvu ya juu ya paneli,
na kutoa matokeo ya udhibiti wa mzigo. Kuchagua kidhibiti kibaya — au kukipima vibaya —
inapoteza asilimia 10–30 ya nishati ya jua inayopatikana.
lessons.outline:
1. PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) controllers: operation, losses, when to use
2. MPPT (Maximum Power Point Tracking) controllers: operation, 10-30% energy gain
3. Controller current rating: panel Isc × 1.25 safety factor
4. MPPT voltage window: Voc array must not exceed controller Voc input rating
5. Load survey: auditing household loads accurately
6. Panel array sizing: peak sun hours for Kenya, derating factors
7. Complete worked example: 12 V 150 W system for a rural household
8. System wiring order and common mistakes that destroy controllers

exercises.prompt: A customer has two 200 W, 24 V nominal panels (Vmp 36 V, Voc 44 V, Isc 5.8 A) wired in series connected to a 24 V AGM battery bank. Which controller is correct?
exercises.explanation:
Two 44 V panels in series = 88 V Voc (plus cold temperature correction ≈ 91 V). A 100 V Voc rated MPPT is correct. Output current: (400 W × 0.95) ÷ 24 V = 15.8 A → 20 A MPPT is the correct minimum rating.

Why the other options are wrong: Two 24 V panels in series gives an array Voc of 88 V. A 30 A PWM controller rated 12/24 V typically has a maximum input of 55 V — it would be instantly destroyed by 88 V. Also, PWM would force the 36 V Vmp panels to charge at 28 V, wasting 22 % of power. The output current calculation is correct (16.7 A) but a 10 A controller is undersized. Always select the next standard size above calculated minimum: 20 A. A 10 A controller would overheat and fail. Solar panels do not self-regulate. Without a charge controller, panels will overcharge the battery to Voc (88 V for this series string), destroying it within hours.

options.text: A 20 A MPPT controller with Voc input rating ≥ 100 V and output current ≥ 16 A
A 30 A PWM controller rated 12/24 V
A 10 A MPPT controller — two 200 W panels = 400 W which at 24 V is only 16.7 A
No controller needed — two panels in series automatically regulate voltage to 24 V

exercises.prompt: When installing a solar system, the correct first connection is: battery to controller. The second connection is: ___ to controller.
exercises.explanation: The battery must be connected first so the MPPT controller can detect the system voltage and initialise correctly. Connecting panels first to an MPPT without a battery can expose the controller to full Voc with no load — potentially damaging the input stage.

exercises.prompt: Match each system sizing parameter to its correct description or formula.

right.text: Hours per day of 1 000 W/m² equivalent irradiance at a location
Combined loss multiplier for temperature, dust, and cable losses (~0.78)
(Total panel watts × 0.95) ÷ Battery bank voltage
Total array Isc × 1.25 safety factor

lessons.title: DC Wiring, Fusing & Safety
lessons.titleSw: Uwiring wa DC, Fyuzi na Usalama
lessons.briefing:
DC wiring is where most solar systems fail — not the panels, not the batteries, but
undersized cables, loose connections, and missing fuses. A DC arc at 48 V carries
far more energy than an AC arc at the same voltage; DC does not have a zero-crossing
to extinguish the arc. This day teaches the voltage-drop formula, cable sizing tables,
fuse selection, earthing, and the professional wiring standards that prevent fires and
system failures in Kenyan solar installations.
lessons.briefingSw:
Uwiring wa DC ndipo mifumo mingi ya jua inashindwa — si paneli, si betri, bali waya
ndogo, miunganisho huru, na fyuzi zilizokosekana. Arc ya DC kwa 48 V hubeba nishati
zaidi sana kuliko arc ya AC kwa voltage ile ile; DC haina sifuri ya kuvuka kuzima arc.
lessons.outline:
1. DC circuit fundamentals: Ohm's law, power, and why DC wiring differs from AC
2. Voltage drop: the 3% rule and the voltage-drop formula
3. Cable sizing: cross-section selection tables for DC solar systems
4. Fuse and circuit breaker selection: where to fuse, what rating to use
5. Connector types: MC4, Anderson, ring terminals — crimping vs soldering
6. Earthing and bonding: why and how to earth a DC solar system
7. DC distribution boards and bus bars for larger systems
8. Common wiring faults and how to identify them before energising

exercises.prompt: A 12 V solar system has a 600 W inverter drawing 50 A maximum. The cable run from battery to inverter is 4 m one-way. Maximum allowed voltage drop is 3%. What minimum cable area should be used?
exercises.explanation:
Correct. ΔV_max = 3% of 12 V = 0.36 V. A = (2 × 4 × 50 × 0.0175) ÷ 0.36 = 7.0 ÷ 0.36 = 19.4 mm². Next standard cable size above 19.4 mm² is 25 mm², though 16 mm² is the minimum many installers use with derating safety margin at shorter runs. Strictly 25 mm² is safest.

Why the other options are wrong: 2.5 mm² at 50 A over 4 m gives ΔV = (2 × 4 × 50 × 0.0175) ÷ 2.5 = 7.0 V — nearly 58% voltage drop. This would cause the inverter to shut down immediately on low-voltage protection. There is no universal standard cable size. Sizing depends on current and cable length. 6 mm² at 50 A over 4 m: ΔV = (2 × 4 × 50 × 0.0175) ÷ 6 = 11.7% drop — far above the 3% limit. The voltage drop formula applies at all cable lengths. At 50 A and 10 mm²: ΔV = (2 × 4 × 50 × 0.0175) ÷ 10 = 0.70 V = 5.8% — still above the 3% limit for a 12 V system.

options.text: 2.5 mm² — sufficient for 50 A in short runs
6 mm² — this is the standard cable for all solar installations
10 mm² — the voltage drop formula is unnecessary for runs under 5 m
16 mm² — calculated as A = (2 × 4 × 50 × 0.0175) ÷ 0.36 = 19.4 mm², use next size up

exercises.prompt: Every fuse on a DC solar system must be placed within ___ mm of the positive battery terminal to protect the cable from the battery's full fault current.
exercises.explanation: The 300 mm (12 inch) maximum rule ensures the unprotected cable section is too short to ignite before the fuse blows. Closer is always better — 150 mm is ideal. Fuses placed at the load end only protect the load, not the cable run from the battery.

exercises.prompt: Match each DC wiring component to its correct specification or use.

right.text: IP67, 30 A / 1 000 V DC; weatherproof panel-to-cable connection
High-current bolt-in DC fuse for battery-to-inverter protection (50–400 A)
Low-cost automotive fuse for circuits up to 30 A
Resettable overcurrent protection; must specify DC voltage rating explicitly

lessons.title: Commissioning & Fault-Finding with a Multimeter
lessons.titleSw: Uanzishaji na Utambuzi wa Hitilafu kwa Multimeter
lessons.briefing:
A KSh 600 digital multimeter in the hands of someone who knows how to use it can
diagnose 90% of solar system faults in 20 minutes. A KSh 80 000 system left to a
guesser will fail and not be repaired. This final day of the solar unit teaches the
complete commissioning sequence for a new installation and a systematic fault-finding
methodology for diagnosing every common failure mode: no charge, low voltage, dead
loads, and battery that won't hold charge.
lessons.briefingSw:
Multimeter ya digital ya KSh 600 mikononi mwa mtu anayejua kuitumiaa inaweza
kutambua asilimia 90 ya hitilafu za mfumo wa jua katika dakika 20. Mfumo wa
KSh 80,000 ulioacha kwa mkisia utashindwa na hautarekebishwa.
lessons.outline:
1. Multimeter functions: DC voltage, AC voltage, current (DC clamp), resistance, continuity
2. Safe multimeter practice: lead placement, range selection, avoiding common injuries
3. Commissioning sequence: the 8-step process for a new solar installation
4. Verifying panel output: Voc test, Isc test (with clamp meter)
5. Verifying charge controller operation: bulk, absorption, float stage indicators
6. Fault tree: battery not charging — step-by-step differential diagnosis
7. Fault tree: loads not working — isolating controller, fuse, cable, or load fault
8. PHOTO_CAPTURE practical: document your multimeter measurements on a real or simulated system

exercises.prompt: During commissioning, you measure Voc at the panel output terminals (covered): 43.2 V (expected: 44 V). You then measure at the controller PV input terminals (same cable, covered): 0 V. What is the fault?
exercises.explanation:
Correct. Voltage is present at the panel but not at the controller PV terminals — the break is in the cable run between them. Inspect every MC4 connector for a full engagement click, check any string combiner fuse, and test continuity along the cable.

Why the other options are wrong: 43.2 V is 98% of the 44 V rated Voc — well within the ±5% acceptable tolerance. Panel Voc varies with temperature and manufacturing tolerance. The panel is fine. If the open circuit is between the panel and the controller, the controller PV input terminals will show 0 V regardless of the controller's health. Isolate the cable run first before concluding the controller is faulty. Panel Voc is an intrinsic property of the panel — it appears across the panel output terminals regardless of what is connected downstream, as long as the circuit is open. 0 V at the controller means the cable is broken or disconnected.

options.text: The panels are faulty — Voc should be exactly 44 V
There is an open circuit between the panel junction box and the controller PV input — check the MC4 connectors and any in-line fuse in that run
The controller is faulty — it should show panel voltage at its PV terminals
Normal — Voc only appears at the PV input when the controller is connected to the battery

exercises.prompt: When using a multimeter to measure DC current through an ammeter input, connecting the leads to the wrong terminals (V/Ω instead of A) causes a ___ which can blow the meter fuse or damage the circuit.
exercises.explanation: The V/Ω input has very high internal impedance (> 1 MΩ) — safe for voltage measurement. The A (ammeter) input has near-zero impedance to shunt maximum current through the measuring shunt resistor. Connecting the A terminals across a voltage source creates a near-short circuit, typically blowing the meter's internal fuse instantly.

exercises.prompt: Commissioning practical: document multimeter measurements on your solar system.

rubric.criterion: Photo 1 — Battery resting voltage: multimeter in DC V mode, leads on battery terminals, reading clearly visible
Photo 2 — Panel Voc test: multimeter on panel output (or controller PV input), reading clearly visible
Photo 3 — Charge current: clamp meter around positive charge cable, reading visible (or screenshot of controller display showing charge amps)
All readings labelled with handwritten or typed labels in the photo or submitted notes
Readings are within expected ranges (battery 11.8–14.6 V; Voc within 5% of datasheet; charge current > 0 in daylight)

lessons.title: Week 2 — DC safety, batteries, commissioning, and maintenance
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 2 — Usalama wa DC, betri, commissioning
lessons.briefing:
Solar DC arcs do not pass through zero like AC and can persist. Cover modules or isolate strings using rated devices before working. Use DC-rated isolators, fuses, connectors, and cable. Never mix incompatible “MC4-style” brands unless the manufacturer approves them. Crimp with the correct tool and pull-test.

Batteries store dangerous energy. Match chemistry and BMS settings; fuse close to the positive terminal; ventilate lead-acid banks; keep lithium batteries within manufacturer temperature limits. Torque lugs to specification and record it. Commission in the manufacturer’s order: polarity, insulation where required, open-circuit voltage, battery voltage, inverter settings, controlled load test, and monitoring.

Handover includes shutdown/startup, expected daily limits, cleaning without standing on panels, and an emergency contact. Maintenance compares current output with baseline, checks hot/loose terminals, cleans safely, and records battery health.
lessons.briefingSw: Wiki 2 — Usalama wa DC, betri, commissioning: usalama, utaratibu sahihi, ukaguzi wa ubora, na huduma kwa jamii.

exercises.prompt: Which action is the safest professional starting point for solar commissioning?
exercises.explanation: A competent craft worker assesses risk, scope, people, tools, and standards before starting.

options.text: Start immediately without inspecting the site or client
Assess hazards and needs, select PPE/tools, explain the plan, then begin
Copy a social-media clip without checking local conditions
Let an untrained bystander make every technical decision

exercises.prompt: What is the strongest evidence that solar commissioning was completed well?
exercises.explanation: Quality is demonstrated with a repeatable inspection, measurement, or functional test.

options.text: The worker says it is fine
A documented inspection or functional test against the job specification
The cheapest material was used
The work was hidden before testing

exercises.prompt: The documented check used to prove this work meets its requirements is a quality ___.
exercises.hint: A planned check, not an opinion.
exercises.explanation: A quality test provides evidence for the client, trainer, and next technician.

exercises.prompt: During commissioning, a string polarity is reversed and the isolator crackles. What is the correct response?
exercises.explanation: Community trades carry public consequences. Defects are corrected and tested, never concealed.

options.text: Continue and conceal the problem
Stop, make the area safe, explain the defect, correct it, then test and document
Ask the client to sign before seeing the work
Remove the safety device so the job appears complete

lessons.title: Week 1 — Site survey, demand, and solar resource
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 1 — Survey, matumizi, na jua
lessons.briefing:
A solar system starts with a load audit, not a panel catalogue. List every appliance, its watts, hours per day, and surge current. Daily energy is watts × hours. Separate essential loads (clinic fridge, lights, router) from optional loads. Inspect the roof for orientation, shading from trees and water tanks, corrosion, wind exposure, access, and structural condition.

Use a sun-path app or repeated observation, but verify on site. One shaded cell can reduce a whole string. Decide whether the project is off-grid, grid-tied, or hybrid; each has different protection and legal requirements. Record cable routes and distances because voltage drop determines conductor size.

The survey report includes client needs, load table, photos, risks, proposed equipment location, and an initial single-line diagram. Do not promise “24-hour power” before calculating worst-month generation and storage.
