lessons.title: Soil Science — Texture, Structure, pH & Field Testing
lessons.titleSw: Sayansi ya Udongo — Muundo, pH na Majaribio ya Shambani
lessons.briefing: Healthy soil is the foundation of food security. Before a farmer adds any amendment or plants any crop, they must understand what their soil actually is: its texture class, its structure, its organic matter content, and its pH. These four parameters determine water-holding capacity, nutrient availability, and biological activity — the three pillars of soil fertility. All four can be assessed accurately with no laboratory equipment.
lessons.outline: Soil mineral fractions (sand, silt, clay) and texture triangle; field ribbon test and jar sedimentation test; soil structure types (granular, blocky, platy, massive) and their fertility implications; soil organic matter (SOM) and its role in CEC and water retention; pH scale and nutrient availability window; field pH testing with indicator strips; liming (CaCO3) and acidification correction; soil colour and Munsell chart interpretation.

exercises.prompt: A farmer squeezes moistened soil and produces a ribbon of 6 cm before it breaks. The ribbon feels sticky and slightly gritty. What texture class is most likely, and what is the primary farming challenge?
exercises.explanation:
A ribbon > 5 cm indicates high clay content. Sticky feel confirms clay dominance. Clay soils have high CEC (fertility) but compact easily, drain slowly, and crack when dry. Organic matter additions improve structure and drainage.

Why the other options are wrong: Sandy soils produce ribbons < 2.5 cm and feel gritty. A 6 cm sticky ribbon indicates clay, not sand. Loam ribbons are 2.5-5.0 cm and feel neither particularly gritty nor particularly sticky. 6 cm places this firmly in the clay range. Silt feels silky and smooth, not sticky. A 6 cm ribbon that is sticky indicates clay dominance, not silt.

options.text: Sandy loam — poor water retention; needs frequent irrigation
Loam — ideal balanced soil requiring no amendment
Clay or clay loam — good fertility but prone to compaction and waterlogging; add organic matter to improve structure
Silt loam — silky feel indicates high silt with no drainage concerns

exercises.prompt: In the 24-hour jar sedimentation test, sand settles within ___ minutes, silt within ___ hours, and clay within ___ hours. The optimal soil pH range for most food crops is ___ to ___.
exercises.explanation: Settling time reflects particle size and density: sand (largest) settles fastest, clay (smallest) slowest. pH 6.0-7.0 is optimal because most macro and micronutrients are simultaneously available in this range; outside it, either aluminium toxicity (< 5.5) or iron/zinc lockout (> 7.5) reduces yields.

exercises.prompt: Match each soil structure type to its fertility implication.
exercises.explanation: Granular structure is the goal of all soil management. Platy structure is often caused by livestock trampling, heavy machinery, or tillage when soil is too wet. Massive structure indicates severe compaction or destruction of all aggregates.

right.text: Excellent — crumbly aggregates with good pore space for roots and drainage
Poor — horizontal layers restrict drainage and root penetration
Very poor — compacted with no visible structure; needs deep tillage
Moderate — common in clay; improves with organic matter additions

exercises.prompt: A field pH test returns 5.2 on clay loam soil destined for maize. What action and approximate lime rate are appropriate?
exercises.explanation:
pH 5.2 is in the 5.0-5.5 range. For clay loam, the Kenya MOH/KALRO guidance recommends 2-4 t/ha CaCO3 to raise to 6.5. Incorporation 3-6 months ahead allows full chemical reaction with the soil before crop establishment.

Why the other options are wrong: Maize optimal pH is 6.0-6.8. Below 5.5, aluminium toxicity reduces root development and phosphorus availability. Sulfur would worsen the problem. pH 5.2 is strongly acid. Aluminium (Al3+) becomes toxic below 5.5, and phosphorus is locked by aluminium ions, significantly reducing maize yields. The correct rate for pH 5.0-5.5 is 2-4 t/ha, not 6-8 t/ha. Over-liming can raise pH above 7.5 causing micronutrient deficiencies. Also, lime must be incorporated 3-6 months before planting to react fully.

options.text: Apply sulfur to lower the pH further — maize prefers acid soils
No action needed — pH 5.2 is adequate for all crops
Apply 2-4 t/ha of agricultural lime, incorporate 3-6 months before planting — this raises pH from 5.0 toward the optimal 6.5
Apply 6-8 t/ha lime immediately before planting for fastest response

exercises.prompt: Each 1% increase in soil organic matter retains approximately ___ litres of additional water per square metre per 30 cm depth. A typical Kenyan smallholder soil depleted by burning and tillage has SOM below ___%.
exercises.explanation: SOM's water retention: 1% SOM holds 20 L/m2/30cm — equivalent to 2 mm of additional rain stored in the root zone. This can extend the effective growing season by days to weeks during dry spells. Kenyan smallholder soils often measure 0.5-0.8% SOM due to residue burning and continuous tillage — rebuilding to 2-3% is achievable with compost additions over 3-5 seasons.

lessons.title: Composting & Organic Soil Amendments
lessons.titleSw: Kutengeneza Mboji na Marekebisho ya Udongo wa Kikaboni
lessons.briefing: Compost is the single most powerful and cheapest soil amendment available to African smallholders. A well-managed 1 m3 compost pile converts crop residues, kitchen waste, and animal manure into finished compost in 6-8 weeks — providing organic matter, balanced nutrients, and billions of beneficial microorganisms per gram. This lesson covers the four parameters that control composting speed, the full construction sequence, and three alternative systems for water-scarce or space-limited situations.
lessons.outline: The four composting control parameters (C:N ratio, moisture, aeration, particle size); hot aerobic composting — pile construction and turning schedule; temperature monitoring and thermophilic pathogen kill; finished compost quality indicators; compost tea production and application; bokashi fermentation for kitchen waste; vermicompost integration; biochar — production and soil amendment properties; liquid manure (slurry) from cattle dung.

exercises.prompt: A compost pile on Day 6 measures only 32°C at the centre and smells of ammonia. What is the most likely cause and the correct fix?
exercises.explanation:
Ammonia smell indicates excess nitrogen being lost as NH3 gas — classic sign of a C:N ratio below 20:1. Low temperature means decomposition is not generating sufficient heat. Adding brown carbon-rich material (straw, 80:1 C:N) and turning corrects both issues.

Why the other options are wrong: A dry pile would show low temperature and an earthy or dusty smell, not ammonia. Ammonia specifically indicates nitrogen excess from too much green material. Ammonia loss = too much N already. Adding more green material would make the ammonia problem worse, not better. By Day 4-7, a well-managed compost pile should reach 55-70°C. 32°C indicates the pile is not thermophilic — the imbalanced C:N is preventing the microbial bloom needed for heat generation.

options.text: Pile is too dry — add water to reach correct moisture
Pile needs more green material — the C:N is too high
C:N ratio is too low (too much green/N material) — turn pile and add dry straw or dry leaves to raise C:N
Temperature is correct — 32°C is normal for Day 6

exercises.prompt: The minimum pile volume for thermophilic (hot) composting is ___ cubic metre.
exercises.explanation: Minimum 1 m3 is required to generate and retain sufficient heat for the thermophilic microbial community. Smaller piles lose heat faster than they generate it. The 200-400 billion CFU/g figure explains why compost is a microbial inoculant as much as a nutrient source — reseeding degraded soils with soil life is as important as adding N, P, and K.

exercises.prompt: Match each composting system to its best use case.
exercises.explanation: Each system targets a different situation. Hot composting is the workhorse for bulk farm waste. Bokashi solves the kitchen-waste problem. Compost tea provides a fast-acting liquid amendment between solid compost applications. Biochar is a 100-1000 year carbon investment that changes soil structure.

right.text: Large volumes of farm waste; pathogen kill needed; 18-day turnaround
Kitchen waste including meat and dairy; airtight bucket; no smell
Quick foliar or soil drench; delivers soluble nutrients and microbes
Long-term carbon sequestration and CEC improvement in sandy soils

exercises.prompt: Why must biochar be charged with compost or manure before soil application?
exercises.explanation:
Fresh biochar is a highly adsorptive carbon sponge. If applied uncharged, it will strip plant-available N, P, and K from the soil solution, causing temporary nutrient deficiency (sometimes called the 'biochar hunger'). Charging fills the pores with nutrients before application.

Why the other options are wrong: Biochar is not toxic to soil microbes. In fact, its porous structure provides ideal habitat for bacteria and fungi after charging. The concern is nutrient adsorption, not toxicity. Biochar pH is typically 7-10 depending on production temperature, but at field application rates (1-5 t/ha) the pH effect on soil is minimal. The buffering concern is not the primary reason for charging. Activated carbon is a different product made at higher temperatures with steam activation. Composting-based charging fills biochar pores with nutrients and microbes — it does not change the physical structure.

options.text: Biochar itself contains no nutrients — its porous structure initially adsorbs existing soil nutrients, temporarily reducing plant-available fertility until charged
Biochar is toxic to soil microbes and must be neutralised with compost
Biochar raises soil pH above 9.0 and must be buffered before application
Charging converts biochar into activated carbon for better filtration

exercises.prompt: Compost tea should be applied within ___ hours of finishing aeration. Bokashi pre-compost has a pH of approximately ___ and must be buried at least ___ cm deep to avoid burning plant roots.
exercises.explanation: Compost tea microbes die within 4 hours once the aerator is removed — the high microbial count is only maintained while oxygen is supplied. Bokashi pH of 4 is highly acidic — direct root contact would burn. Burying 20 cm deep protects roots while the acid pre-compost is rapidly neutralised and broken down by soil microbes over 2-4 weeks.

lessons.title: Water-Wise Farming — Zai Pits, Swales & Drip Irrigation
lessons.titleSw: Kilimo cha Kuokoa Maji — Mashimo ya Zai, Mifereji na Umwagiliaji
lessons.briefing: In semi-arid Kenya, where rainfall is bimodal, erratic, and declining, the difference between food security and food crisis is often 50 mm of rain that runs off bare, compacted soil rather than soaking in. Water-wise farming techniques — zai pits, half-moon catchments, contour swales, and low-cost drip irrigation — capture, store, and deliver every raindrop to the root zone of the crop, multiplying the effective rainfall by 2-4 times.
lessons.outline: Rainfall-runoff relationship and infiltration rate; zai pit design and spacing (0.9 m apart, 30x30x15 cm); half-moon catchment bunds; contour swale design using A-frame level; keyline cultivation principle; low-cost drip irrigation from jerrycan or gravity tank; bucket drip kit design (0.5 mm emitter holes, dripper spacing); mulching and its effect on evaporation; FOFIFA tied ridges for moisture conservation.

exercises.prompt: A farmer has a 0.25 ha plot on a 5% slope in a semi-arid area receiving 500 mm of annual rain. During a 30 mm rainstorm, the compacted crusted soil absorbs only 3 mm/hour. Approximately what percentage of this storm's rain is lost to runoff?
exercises.explanation:
If the storm delivers 30 mm in 30 min = 60 mm/hour rain rate. Infiltration is only 3 mm/hour. In 30 min, 1.5 mm infiltrates while 28.5 mm runs off = 95% loss. This is why crusted, bare soil is catastrophic in semi-arid areas — virtually all rain is lost.

Why the other options are wrong: 50% absorption assumes around 30 mm/hour infiltration rate. Compacted crusted soil only achieves 2-5 mm/hour. At 3 mm/hour in a 30-minute storm, only ~5% infiltrates. Semi-arid rainfall is often intense and convective. High-intensity short-duration storms are the norm, and they overwhelm the infiltration capacity of bare compacted soils, producing flash runoff. Evaporation occurs over hours to days, not during the storm itself. During the storm, the primary loss mechanism is runoff. 30% runoff would require an infiltration rate of ~42 mm/hour — not possible on compacted crust.

options.text: Approximately 50% runs off — most soils absorb at least half of incoming rain
No runoff occurs — rain in semi-arid areas is always light and absorbed fully
About 30% runs off — the remainder is lost to evaporation
The storm delivers 30 mm in roughly 30 minutes; at 3 mm/hour absorption rate only about 1.5 mm infiltrates — approximately 95% runs off

exercises.prompt: Standard zai pits are ___ cm wide x ___ cm long x ___ cm deep, spaced ___ m apart in all directions. At this spacing there are approximately ___ pits per hectare.
exercises.explanation: 30x30x15 cm pits at 0.9 m x 0.9 m spacing gives 1/0.81 = 1.235 pits per m2, so 12,350 pits per hectare (commonly rounded to 12,300). Each pit receives a handful of manure before planting, creating a microhabitat of concentrated fertility and water at every seed point.

exercises.prompt: Match each water-wise technique to its primary mechanism of action.
exercises.explanation: These techniques act at different scales: zai pits at the individual plant, tied ridges at the row, swales at the field/catchment. They can be combined — swales intercept hillslope runoff that is then distributed to zai-pit fields below.

right.text: Concentrate runoff and organic matter at individual plant points on degraded crusted soil
Intercept hillslope runoff along the contour and allow slow infiltration to recharge groundwater
Convert inter-row furrows into a series of small water-retention basins between tie dams
Reduce surface evaporation by 50-75% while adding organic matter as it decomposes

exercises.prompt: A household sets up a jerrycan gravity drip system with 0.5 mm holes in the lateral pipe, elevated 1 m. Each hole delivers approximately 30 mL/hour. If the system runs for 6 hours, how much water does one emitter deliver, and is this sufficient for a mature tomato plant?
exercises.explanation:
30 mL/hour x 6 hours = 180 mL. A fruiting tomato needs 1,000-2,000 mL/day. Multiple emitters per plant or longer run time is needed. Jerrycan drip is best for seedlings or drought-stressed crops receiving supplemental irrigation, not sole-source irrigation for heavy feeders.

Why the other options are wrong: 180 mL is far below the 1,000-2,000 mL/day mature tomatoes require. Jerrycan drip provides supplemental irrigation — it must be paired with rain-fed or higher-volume supply for fruiting crops. Volume delivered = flow rate x time. 30 mL/hour x 6 hours = 180 mL. The accumulative volume over time is what reaches the plant. 180 mL = 0.18 L, not 1.8 L. 1.8 L would require 300 mL/hour flow rate, which is much larger than a 0.5 mm hole at 1 m head delivers.

options.text: 180 mL per emitter per 6-hour session — mature tomatoes need 1-2 L/day so 2-3 sessions per day or longer run time is needed
180 mL — this fully meets mature tomato water needs
30 mL — the system only delivers at the flow rate, not accumulative
1.8 L — units must be converted from mL to L

exercises.prompt: The A-frame level is used to mark the ___ (gradient = zero) line on a hillslope for swale construction. A swale berm must always include an ___ spillway section ___ cm lower than the main berm to prevent catastrophic failure during heavy rain.
exercises.explanation: A contour is a line of equal elevation — water placed on a true contour swale spreads evenly left and right with no tendency to flow. An overflow spillway 20 cm lower than the berm crest ensures that when the swale fills in a major storm, water exits in a controlled location rather than overtopping and eroding the berm catastrophically.

lessons.title: Agroforestry & Nitrogen-Fixing Trees
lessons.titleSw: Kilimo Msitu na Miti ya Kukuza Naitrojeni
lessons.briefing: Agroforestry — integrating trees with crops and livestock — is the most documented path to long-term soil fertility restoration in East Africa. Nitrogen-fixing trees deliver 50-200 kg of biologically fixed nitrogen per hectare per year through their root nodules, replacing expensive synthetic fertiliser. Properly designed agroforestry systems also provide fuelwood, fodder, shade, windbreaks, and improved water infiltration — all from trees already growing on the farm.
lessons.outline: Biological nitrogen fixation mechanism (Rhizobium nodules, nitrogenase enzyme); key N-fixing species for East Africa (Calliandra calothyrsus, Leucaena leucocephala, Tithonia diversifolia, Sesbania sesban, Gliricidia sepium); improved fallow with Sesbania; fertiliser trees as green manure; Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR); alley cropping design (tree rows 6m apart, pollarding height 0.5-1.0m); windbreak design; multi-purpose tree selection; legume intercropping.

exercises.prompt: A farmer cuts open a root nodule from a Leucaena tree and finds the interior is white/grey in colour. What does this indicate and what action should be taken?
exercises.explanation:
Active nodules contain leghaemoglobin which gives a pink/red colour. White or grey interior indicates the Rhizobium are absent, dead, or inactive. Causes include: wrong Rhizobium strain, soil pH < 5.5 (kills Rhizobium), waterlogging, or high soil nitrogen (N inhibits fixation when fertiliser N is abundant).

Why the other options are wrong: This is incorrect. Pink/red colour from leghaemoglobin is the indicator of active fixation. White or grey indicates inactive nodules. Active nodules are pink/red from early establishment. White nodules in mature trees indicate a problem, not a developmental stage. Size does not predict activity. Colour is the key indicator: pink/red = active, white/grey = inactive, regardless of size.

options.text: White nodules indicate maximum nitrogen fixation — the colour shows pure NH3 production
White nodules are normal in young trees — they turn pink after 6 months
Only nodule size matters — small white nodules will fix more N than large pink ones
White/grey nodules are inactive — no nitrogen fixation occurring; check soil pH (Leucaena requires pH > 5.5), consider Rhizobium inoculant on seeds of replacement plants

exercises.prompt: Tithonia diversifolia leaves contain ___ to ___% nitrogen by dry weight, similar to synthetic urea. Applying 3 t/ha of fresh Tithonia biomass provides approximately ___ kg of nitrogen equivalent per hectare.
exercises.explanation: At 4% N (midpoint) in fresh biomass (approximately 25% DM): 3 t/ha fresh x 0.25 DM fraction = 0.75 t/ha dry matter. 0.75 t DM x 40 kg N/t DM (at 4% N) = 30 kg N — but fresh weight at 3.5-4.5% N on fresh weight basis: 3,000 kg x 0.04 = 120 kg N. Range 3.5-4.5% gives 105-135 kg N equivalent per ha. A powerful free fertiliser from a plant that grows on degraded land margins.

exercises.prompt: Match each agroforestry species to its primary advantage in East Africa.
exercises.explanation: Matching species to site and farming system is critical. Leucaena fails on acid soils (pH < 5.5) where Calliandra thrives. Sesbania is for the farmer who can afford one fallow season. Desmodium is for maize-belt farmers with stem borer and Striga pressure.

right.text: Highest N fixation rate (100-500 kg/ha/year) for alley cropping on neutral soils
Tolerates acid soils and waterlogging; 35% crude protein fodder for dairy cattle
Short 1-2 year improved fallow that delivers 40-200 kg N before next maize crop
Push-pull intercrop — repels stem borers and suppresses Striga weed

exercises.prompt: In the push-pull pest management system, what role does Desmodium intercropped with maize play, and what does the Napier grass border do?
exercises.explanation:
Desmodium (silverleaf) releases isothiocyanates that push stem borer moths away from the maize stand. Napier grass at borders produces a sticky exudate that traps stem borer larvae after hatching, acting as a dead-end trap crop. This also suppresses Striga through allelopathic root exudates.

Why the other options are wrong: Desmodium does not directly kill insects — it repels them through volatile chemicals. Napier grass does not form a physical barrier; it attracts and traps larvae biochemically. Desmodium does fix some nitrogen as a legume, but the primary purpose of this system is pest and Striga management. Napier grass is a C4 grass and does not fix nitrogen. The mechanism is chemical, not physical shading. The parasitic wasp habitat aspect has some truth but is not the primary mechanism. The core is push (volatile repellent) and pull (attractive trap crop).

options.text: Desmodium kills stem borers with natural insecticide; Napier grass blocks physical entry into the field
Both Desmodium and Napier grass fix nitrogen — the system is primarily for soil fertility
Desmodium releases volatile compounds that repel stem borers away from maize (push); Napier grass attracts stem borers to the field border where they lay eggs but larvae survive poorly (pull)
Napier grass shades stem borer pupae preventing emergence; Desmodium provides habitat for parasitic wasps

exercises.prompt: In alley cropping with Leucaena rows spaced ___ to ___ metres apart, trees are pollarded to ___ to ___ metre height. FMNR costs approximately ___ per hectare since it manages trees that are already ___ on the farmland.
exercises.explanation: Alley spacing of 4-8 m allows adequate light to reach inter-row crops while providing significant N-fixing tree biomass. Pollarding at 0.5-1.0 m keeps trees as hedges rather than large shade trees. FMNR's near-zero cost arises because farmers protect and manage stumps already present in their fields — no tree nursery, no planting, no seedling cost.

lessons.title: Seed Saving, Variety Selection & Open-Pollinated Crops
lessons.titleSw: Kuhifadhi Mbegu, Uchaguzi wa Aina na Mazao ya Kuzaliana Wenyewe
lessons.briefing: Seed sovereignty — the ability of farmers to save, replant, and exchange their own seed — is the deepest form of food security. Open-pollinated varieties (OPVs) reproduce true to type from saved seed, unlike F1 hybrids which must be purchased every season. This lesson covers the science of seed selection, processing, storage, and variety trials that enable a community to build a locally adapted, high-yielding seed bank without dependency on commercial suppliers.
lessons.outline: Open-pollinated variety (OPV) vs F1 hybrid — genetics, reproduction, and seed saving rules; positive mass selection — selecting 10-15% of best plants; isolation distances for cross-pollinating crops (maize 200-500 m, brassicas 500 m); seed drying to safe moisture content (< 12% for cereals, < 8% for legumes); hermetic storage and moisture indicators; seed viability testing (germination rate test); community seed bank design; variety trial methodology (mother-baby trial); labelling and record-keeping.

exercises.prompt: A farmer saves seed from an F1 hybrid maize variety for three seasons running. What happens to the crop performance, and why?
exercises.explanation:
F1 hybrids exploit heterosis from crossing two inbred parental lines. F2 offspring (from saved F1 seed) undergo Mendelian segregation, with 75% of gene pairs becoming homozygous. Favourable dominant-dominant combinations drop from ~100% to ~56% in F2, producing dramatically lower and uneven yields.

Why the other options are wrong: Adaptation through selection takes many generations and requires genetic diversity. F1 hybrids start with limited diversity, and segregation in F2/F3 primarily produces poorly performing homozygous lines, not adapted ones. F1 yield advantage specifically comes from the first-generation heterozygosity. Saving seed destroys this advantage. Commercial seed companies rely on this biological fact to maintain annual seed purchase dependency. All traits that benefit from heterozygosity — including yield, stress tolerance, and disease resistance — decline in F2 generation. It is not selective loss of disease resistance only.

options.text: Yields improve season by season as the plants adapt to local conditions
Yields stay the same — F1 seed and saved seed from F1 perform identically
Only the disease resistance is lost; yield potential is maintained through saving
Yields decline sharply in F2 and F3 generations as heterozygosity is lost — offspring no longer have the favourable gene combinations of the original hybrid cross

exercises.prompt: Maize seed for saving must be isolated at least ___ metres from other maize varieties to prevent cross-pollination. Safe moisture content for stored maize seed is below ___%. A germination test using 50 seeds returns 38 germinated — the germination rate is ___% and the recommendation is ___.
exercises.explanation: Maize is wind-pollinated over 200-500 m. Below 12% moisture, weevils cannot complete their life cycle and mould is suppressed. Germination: 38/50 x 100 = 76% — falls in the 70-85% marginal-to-good range. Increase seeding rate by 15-20% and plan to source better seed for the next season.

exercises.prompt: Match each crop to its minimum seed-saving isolation distance.
exercises.explanation: Isolation distance depends entirely on pollination mechanism: wind and insect carriers need much larger distances than self-pollinators. Communities without large isolation distances can use time isolation (staggering planting dates) for wind-pollinated crops like maize.

right.text: 200-500 m from other maize varieties
5-10 m — almost no cross-pollination risk
500-1,000 m from other Brassica species
5-10 m adequate for most smallholder saving

exercises.prompt: After 24 hours, a jar of dried beans sealed hermetically shows condensation on the inner walls. What does this mean and what action should be taken?
exercises.explanation:
Condensation forms when moisture evaporating from beans condenses on cooler jar walls — confirming moisture content is still above the safe threshold (< 8% for legumes). Storing at this moisture in hermetic bags would lead to mould growth and loss of germination viability within months.

Why the other options are wrong: Condensation is a moisture warning, not a normal sign. In hermetic storage, high-moisture seed would create an anaerobic, humid environment that promotes mould even without oxygen — leading to mycotoxin contamination and seed death. Wood ash is added before sealing as a preventive measure, not as a cure for already-wet seed. The correct action is to break the seal, continue drying, then re-test before closing for storage. Condensation is a moisture indicator, not a temperature indicator. Cool seed does not produce condensation on inner jar walls unless moisture is being actively released.

options.text: Condensation is normal in sealed jars — proceed with hermetic storage immediately
Add wood ash immediately — ash will absorb the moisture inside the sealed jar
The beans are still too moist — continue drying in the sun for another 1-2 days, then repeat the jar test before sealing for long-term storage
The condensation indicates seed is sufficiently cool for storage — proceed

exercises.prompt: Visit a farm or market and photograph at least two different locally named crop varieties of the same species (e.g. two types of bean, two varieties of sorghum, or two local maize varieties). For each, record: local name, perceived advantages according to the farmer or seller (taste, drought tolerance, maturity time, storability), and any visible seed morphology differences (colour, size, shape).
exercises.explanation: Documenting local variety diversity is the first step in community seed banking. Farmers' knowledge of variety performance under local conditions is irreplaceable and often exceeds formal breeding station data for smallholder-relevant traits like drought escaping and taste.

rubric.criterion: Two clearly different varieties of the same crop species are photographed side by side
Local name of each variety is recorded
At least two farmer-perceived advantages per variety are documented
At least one visible morphological difference between varieties is described

lessons.title: Identify and replace core components
lessons.titleSw: Tambua na badilisha sehemu kuu

exercises.prompt: Match each component to its role.
exercises.hint: Think forget on power-off vs keep files.
exercises.explanation: RAM loses data at power-off. Storage keeps the OS and user files. The PSU feeds DC to the board; the CPU executes code.

right.text: Volatile working memory
Persistent storage
Converts AC to DC rails
Executes instructions

exercises.prompt: A PC powers fans but never beeps or shows a logo. Which check is most useful next?
exercises.hint: No POST usually means power, CPU, or memory — not applications.
exercises.explanation: If the machine never posts, start with 24-pin/8-pin power, CPU seating, and RAM. Software cannot run yet.

options.text: Reinstall Microsoft Office
Reseat RAM and confirm motherboard power connectors
Buy a new monitor immediately
Format the SSD

exercises.prompt: The firmware that initialises hardware before the operating system loads is the ___.
exercises.hint: UEFI is the modern equivalent; either name is used in many TVET papers. We accept BIOS here.
exercises.explanation: BIOS/UEFI runs power-on self-test and then hands control to the bootloader.

exercises.prompt: A college lab PC suddenly shuts down under load and smells hot. PSU rails were never tested. What should you do?
exercises.hint: Heat plus shutdown points to power or cooling.
exercises.explanation: Technicians measure 12V/5V/3.3V, clean dust, and confirm the CPU cooler is seated before gambling on random replacements.

options.text: Keep running Prime95 to confirm
Replace RAM first because it is cheapest
Stop the test, check ventilation and measure PSU voltages before swapping parts
Install a second operating system

lessons.title: Cables, IP addressing, and LAN devices
lessons.titleSw: Nyaya, anwani za IP, na vifaa vya LAN

exercises.prompt: Which device is primarily responsible for forwarding frames inside one LAN?
exercises.hint: Think MAC addresses, not internet links.
exercises.explanation: Switches learn MAC addresses and forward Ethernet frames. Routers make IP decisions between networks.

options.text: Router
Switch
Modem only
Printer

exercises.prompt: The connector used on a typical Cat6 Ethernet patch cord is ___.
exercises.explanation: RJ45 terminates twisted-pair Ethernet. Poor crimps cause intermittent lab failures.

exercises.prompt: Match the address type to what it identifies.
exercises.explanation: MAC is L2 identity, IP is L3 location, ports distinguish services such as 80/443.

right.text: A specific network interface
A host on an IP network
An application service on a host

exercises.prompt: A new office PC has IP 192.168.1.50 but cannot reach the internet. The default gateway is blank. What should you configure?
exercises.hint: No gateway means no path off the LAN.
exercises.explanation: The default gateway is the router that NAT/firewalls traffic to the WAN. DNS then resolves names such as safaricom.co.ke.

options.text: The MAC address of Google
The LAN router IP as default gateway, plus DNS
A public IP on every printer
Disable the switch

lessons.title: Operating systems for technicians
lessons.titleSw: Mifumo ya uendeshaji kwa mafundi

exercises.prompt: Why should a workshop technician avoid daily work as Administrator or root?
exercises.hint: Least privilege is a core TVET and security control.
exercises.explanation: A compromised or mistaken admin session can wipe disks, dump passwords, and disable AV. Use a standard account plus elevation when needed.

options.text: It makes the PC boot faster
Malware and mistakes then inherit full system rights
Microsoft Office will not install otherwise
RAM cannot be upgraded

exercises.prompt: On Linux, the command that prints the current directory is ___.
exercises.explanation: pwd shows where you are; ls lists files; cd changes directory.

exercises.prompt: Match the tool to the job.
exercises.hint: Slow PC vs new partition vs crash history.
exercises.explanation: Task Manager is live resource use; Disk Management is storage layout; Event Viewer is historical errors.

right.text: Inspect Windows processes and startup
Create and format volumes
Read system and application logs

exercises.prompt: A campus PC is full. Users dump downloads on the C: drive. What is the professional fix?
exercises.hint: Do not destroy the OS to free space.
exercises.explanation: Technicians relocate data, clean temp files carefully, and set policies. Deleting system folders creates a bigger outage.

options.text: Delete the Windows folder
Move user data to a data partition or shared drive and educate users
Disable the page file forever
Install a second BIOS

lessons.title: Workshop and electrical safety
lessons.titleSw: Usalama wa warsha na umeme

exercises.prompt: What should you do first before opening a desktop PSU-side cover?
exercises.explanation: Unplug mains, then hold the case power button so capacitors discharge. Only then open the chassis.

options.text: Touch the motherboard to discharge yourself
Unplug the PC and hold the power button to drain residual charge
Spray water on the PSU to cool it
Increase the room humidity with a kettle

exercises.prompt: A wrist strap that connects you to the computer chassis is used to prevent ___.
exercises.hint: It is also called static electricity damage.
exercises.explanation: Electrostatic discharge (ESD) can silently destroy RAM, NICs, and motherboard chips.

exercises.prompt: A learner smells burning plastic from a lab PC. What is the correct first action?
exercises.hint: Life and fire safety beat the exam clock.
exercises.explanation: Isolate power, do not use water on electrical fires, and escalate. CDACC workshops treat this as an incident, not a race.

options.text: Keep troubleshooting so you do not lose the practical marks
Pour water on the machine
Switch off at the wall, unplug, and report to the instructor
Cover the PC with a cloth and continue

exercises.prompt: Which fire extinguisher class is appropriate for a live electrical cabinet?
exercises.explanation: CO₂ or dry powder are used on electrical fires. Water can electrocute the technician.

options.text: Class A water
Class B foam only
CO₂ or dry powder rated for electrical fires
Wet chemical for kitchens only

lessons.title: Stop and steer: hydraulics, discs, suspension
lessons.titleSw: Simama na elekeza: hydraulics, discs, suspension
lessons.briefing:
Brakes convert motion to heat. The pedal moves a booster (vacuum or electric) then a tandem master cylinder. Fluid in two circuits (diagonal or front/rear split) goes through lines, often an ABS modulator, to calipers (disc) or wheel cylinders (drum). Pads clamp a disc; shoes expand in a drum. A leaking hose or boiling old fluid is a long pedal.

ABS does not create grip; it limits lock so you can still steer. If the ABS light is on, you still have foundation brakes — but the anatomy of the modulator and sensors is now in play.

The same corner holds the hub, bearing, disc, caliper bracket, steering arm, spring, and damper. A warped disc complaint is often a hub face or a sticking slide. A pull under braking can be a seized caliper, a collapsed hose, or alignment after a bent arm.

Steering: rack (or box), track rods, and geometry (toe, camber, caster). Suspension: spring supports the mass; damper controls the oscillation. Anatomy sites draw them together because a tyre only works when it is pointing and loaded correctly.

lessons.title: Cooling and lubrication loops
lessons.titleSw: Mizunguko ya baridi na mafuta
lessons.briefing:
Combustion heat would seize the engine without two loops. Coolant carries heat from jackets in the block and head to the radiator. Air through the core (ram air + fans) dumps that heat. The thermostat holds temperature until the engine is warm, then opens. The pump (belt or electric) moves the liquid. An expansion tank gives the system a place to grow and a place to bleed.

Pressure (cap rating) raises the boiling point. Test only to spec. Plastic tanks on aluminium cores fail at the crimp; copper/brass can be soldered. Blocked tubes make cold vertical stripes on a hot core.

Oil is a film, not just a level on the dipstick. The pump picks up from the sump, through a pickup screen, to galleries, bearings, and often a cooler or filter bypass. Low level, aeration, or a blocked pickup is a bearing death sentence. Coolant in oil or oil in coolant is a shared-wall failure: gasket, cracked head, or cracked block.

Bleed after any open repair. An air lock at the head or heater matrix looks like a “bad thermostat”. Fans and shrouds are part of the anatomy — a missing shroud is a highway overheat waiting in Nairobi traffic.
lessons.briefingSw: Coolant inachukua joto kwenda radiator. Thermostat inafungua baada ya joto. Pump inasukuma. Mafuta ni filamu kwenye bearings. Hewa kwenye mfumo inaiga thermostat mbaya.

lessons.title: Drivetrain: clutch, gears, shafts, differential
lessons.titleSw: Drivetrain: clutch, gia, shafts, diff
lessons.briefing:
The drivetrain is everything after the crank flange: flywheel or flexplate, clutch or torque converter, gearbox, then shafts to a differential that splits torque to the wheels and allows them to turn at different speeds in a corner.

FWD: transaxle in the engine bay, short driveshafts with CV joints to the front hubs. RWD: gearbox, propshaft with U-joints, rear axle/diff, then half-shafts. 4WD/AWD adds a transfer case or coupling and a second axle.

Gear ratios multiply torque. A slipping clutch smells and revs without road speed. A failed CV clicks on lock. A worn U-joint clunks on take-up. A locked diff or a broken spider gear is a corner hop or a bang.

Do not confuse drivetrain vibration with engine misfire: road-speed vs engine-speed is the anatomy test. Support the engine/gearbox on the correct mounts before you chase a “vibration at 80”.
lessons.briefingSw: Baada ya crank: flywheel, clutch au converter, gearbox, shafts, diff. FWD ina transaxle. RWD ina propshaft. Gia zinazidisha torque. CV inabofya kwenye lock.

lessons.title: Electrical nervous system: battery, alternator, loads
lessons.titleSw: Mfumo wa umeme: betri, alternator, loads
lessons.briefing:
Think of the electrical system as a nervous system on a cutaway layer: battery (stored energy), starter (cranking load), alternator (running generation), distribution (cables, fusible links, boxes), controllers (ECU, body modules), and loads (lamps, pumps, ignition, infotainment).

The battery must crank and buffer. The alternator must cover running loads plus recharge. A “dead battery” after night parking can be a parasitic draw or a charging fault — measure voltage and current; do not guess.

Earths are half the circuit. A painted earth or a chewed loom at the hatch hinge is a living anatomy lesson. Fuses protect wires, not your schedule: a repeated fuse is a short, not a market for a bigger fuse.

Starting path: ignition/enable → starter relay → solenoid → pinion to ring gear. Charging path: belt → alternator → output cable → battery positive, with the ECU sometimes commanding the field.

Never work live on an SRS airbag circuit. Disconnect and wait as the data says. Anatomy includes what you must not probe.
lessons.briefingSw: Betri inahifadhi. Starter inazungusha. Alternator inazalisha injini ikiwaka. Earth ni nusu ya mzunguko. Fuse inalinda waya, si kazi yako.

lessons.title: Engine cutaway: air, fuel, spark, bottom end
lessons.titleSw: Cutaway ya injini
lessons.briefing:
The engine is a pump that burns a mixture and turns heat into crank rotation. Vocational maps split: top end (head, valves, cam, intake, exhaust, ignition or injectors) and bottom end (block, pistons, rods, crank, sump).

Four-stroke order: intake, compression, power, exhaust. Spark-ignition (petrol) lights a compressed mix. Compression-ignition (diesel) injects into hot air. Wrong fuel, wrong glow/spark, or no air (blocked filter / collapsed hose) all look like “no power”.

Air path: filter → meter/MAF if fitted → throttle or diesel intake → manifold → valve → cylinder. Exhaust: valve → manifold → turbo if fitted → after-treatment → silencer. A boost leak after a turbo is a power complaint with a black or clean tailpipe depending on fueling.

Bottom-end noises and oil pressure are not “add thicker oil and release”. Low pressure, mayonnaise, coolant in oil, or white smoke send you to the cooling and sealing lesson next — the systems share the head gasket and jackets.

Always isolate: fuel delivery, spark/glow, compression, timing, air. Anatomy prevents swapping a coil when the timing chain has jumped.
lessons.briefingSw: Injini ni pampu ya moto. Top end: kichwa, valves, intake, exhaust. Bottom end: block, pistoni, crank. Four-stroke: intake, compression, power, exhaust. Tenganisha hewa, mafuta, cheche, compression.

lessons.title: Whole-car map: body, cabin, chassis
lessons.titleSw: Ramani ya gari: body, cabin, chasi
lessons.briefing:
Car-anatomy sites start with a map, not a single bolt. A vehicle is a carrying structure plus systems hung on it. The chassis (or subframe + body-in-white on a unibody car) is the skeleton: rails, cross-members, and mounting points that locate the engine, suspension, steering, and fuel tank. The body/cabin is the occupant cell and crash structure. Doors, glass, and trim are not the frame.

Unibody cars combine body and structure. Body-on-frame pickups still have a ladder frame you can point to. Either way, loads travel: engine torque into mounts, braking into knuckles and subframe, pothole loads into springs and then the body. If a mount or rail is rusted, “just replace the part” is not a diagnosis.

Walk a car the way a cutaway is layered: engine bay (power + cooling + charging), cabin (controls, HVAC, restraints), floor (exhaust, fuel, brake/fuel lines), corners (hub, bearing, brake, spring, damper, steering arm), rear (tank, spare, driveline).

Kenya workshop habit: look for accident pull, wet battery trays, crushed sills, and missing undertrays before you chase a noise. The map tells you which system can make that symptom.

Sources: vocational vehicle-systems units (body/frame, suspension, driveline, steering, fuel, intake/exhaust, lubrication, coolant, electrical, brakes, wheels) and standard service-technician component maps.
lessons.briefingSw: Chasi ni mifupa. Body ni seli ya abiria. Tembea gari kama cutaway: engine bay, cabin, floor, pembe, nyuma. Kutu au ajali kwenye rail si “badilisha sehemu tu.”

lessons.title: Clinical Examination, Vital Signs & Ruminant Physiology
lessons.titleSw: Uchunguzi wa Kitabibu, Viashiria vya Uhai na Fiziolojia ya Wanyama Wacheuaji
lessons.briefing: In pastoral and agrarian societies, livestock represent the community's bank, food reserve, and draft power. Diagnosing an ailing cow, sheep, or camel before an infectious disease sweeps through the herd requires disciplined clinical examination. An animal cannot speak; the community paravet must read subtle physiological indicators—rectal temperature, respiratory rate, mucous membrane coloration, rumen contraction frequency, and lymph node swelling. This lesson covers physical restraint techniques, species-specific vital sign baselines, ruminant stomach anatomy (rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum), and emergency treatment of acute frothy bloat.
lessons.outline: Large animal handling and physical restraint (cattle nose tongs, tail jack, halter, casting ropes using the Reuff method); systematic clinical examination sequence (distance appraisal, head-to-tail physical exam); normal vital sign tables (cattle, sheep/goats, camels, donkeys: temperature, pulse, respiration); mucous membrane evaluation (conjunctival and vulvar capillary refill time); superficial lymph node palpation (prescapular, precrural, submandibular); the 4-chambered ruminant stomach; rumen motility auscultation in the left paralumbar fossa (2 to 3 contractions every 2 minutes); acute bloat pathophysiology (frothy vs free-gas); emergency trocharization and administration of vegetable oil / dimethicone anti-foaming agents.

exercises.prompt: A pastoral herder presents a 3-year-old Boran cow that is breathing rapidly with an extended neck. Physical examination reveals a rectal temperature of 39.1°C, mucous membranes are pale white, and the left prescapular lymph node in front of the shoulder is swollen to the size of a tennis ball. What condition is strongly indicated?
exercises.explanation:
Theileria parva sporozoites invade lymphocytes, causing massive lymphadenopathy (dramatic swelling of prescapular and precrural nodes). The parasite then destroys red blood cells, causing severe pallor and pulmonary oedema.

Why the other options are wrong: Bloat presents with left flank abdominal distension, not lymph node enlargement. Hardware disease presents with arched back, grunting, and low-grade fever, without massive prescapular lymph node swelling. Estrus does not cause lymphadenopathy, pale membranes, or respiratory distress.

options.text: East Coast Fever (ECF / Theileriosis) — massive enlargement of the prescapular lymph nodes combined with severe hemolytic anaemia and respiratory distress is the hallmark presentation
Acute bloat from eating wet clover
Hardware disease caused by a swallowed nail
Normal physiological estrus (heat)

exercises.prompt: In a healthy adult cow, auscultation of the left paralumbar fossa should reveal a deep rolling muscular contraction of the rumen at a normal frequency of ___ to 3 contractions every ___ minutes.
exercises.explanation: A healthy rumen contracts 2 to 3 times every 2 minutes. Complete absence of sounds indicates rumen stasis, toxemia, or severe metabolic disease.

exercises.prompt: Match each compartment of the ruminant stomach to its primary physiological role.
exercises.explanation: Rumen ferments; reticulum filters hardware; omasum absorbs water; abomasum secretes acid.

right.text: Giant 150L microbial fermentation vat converting cellulose into volatile fatty acids
Honeycomb chamber that traps heavy foreign metal debris (hardware disease)
Muscular book-page leaves that compress cud and absorb water and electrolytes
The true acid-glandular stomach secreting hydrochloric acid and digestive enzymes

exercises.prompt: A dairy cow grazing on lush morning alfalfa pasture collapses with extreme distension of the left flank. A passed stomach tube fails to release gas because it clogs with thick green lather. What immediate emergency treatment will collapse the foam?
exercises.explanation:
Pasture bloat produces stable micro-bubbles that trap gas in viscous foam. Non-polar oils (vegetable oil or mineral oil) break surface tension, coalescing the foam into free gas that the cow belches out.

Why the other options are wrong: Penicillin has zero immediate effect on mechanical foam surface tension. Adding more water increases ruminal volume, accelerating suffocation. Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) releases more CO2 gas when mixed with acid, worsening the bloat.

options.text: Administer 500 mL of cooking vegetable oil or dimethicone/poloxalene directly into the rumen to break the foam bubble surface tension
Inject antibiotic penicillin into the left flank
Force the cow to drink 20 litres of cold water
Administer large doses of baking soda

exercises.prompt: To safely restrain a standing cow and prevent it from kicking backward during a clinical examination, an assistant can perform the tail ___, grasping the tail base and pushing it vertically upward over the spine.
exercises.explanation: The 'tail jack' flexes the sacrococcygeal joint, immobilizing the pelvic hindquarters and preventing kicking without causing pain or injury.

lessons.title: Vector-Borne Livestock Diseases — ECF & Trypanosomiasis
lessons.titleSw: Magonjwa ya Mifugo Yanayoenezwa na Wadudu — Ndigana (ECF) na Nagana
lessons.briefing: Across sub-Saharan Africa, vector-borne hemoparasites inflict devastating losses on pastoral herds. East Coast Fever (ECF / Theileriosis)—transmitted by the brown ear tick—kills up to 90% of unvaccinated exotic and crossbred cattle within 3 weeks of infection. Nagana (Animal African Trypanosomiasis)—transmitted by the tsetse fly—causes chronic wasting, severe anaemia, and reproductive failure across 10 million square kilometres of fertile grazing land. This lesson covers vector biology, field blood/lymph smear microscopy, clinical staging, life-saving chemotherapeutic protocols (Buparvaquone, Diminazene Aceturate, Isometamidium), and non-chemical vector control traps.
lessons.outline: East Coast Fever (Theileria parva): vector Rhipicephalus appendiculatus (brown ear tick); pathogenesis (lymphoproliferation, Koch's Blue Bodies in lymph node aspirate smears, pulmonary oedema death); treatment: Buparvaquone (2.5 mg/kg IM) + long-acting oxytetracycline; ITM (Infection and Treatment Method) live vaccine protocol; Trypanosomiasis (T. congolense, T. vivax, T. brucei): vector Glossina spp. (tsetse fly); clinical picture (intermittent fever, progressive cachexia, 'razor-back', jugular pulse); diagnosis: wet blood mount, buffy coat microhaematocrit centrifuge technique; curative vs prophylactic drugs: Diminazene aceturate (Berenil) vs Isometamidium chloride; tsetse fly biconical / Nzi blue fabric traps with attractant odor lures.

exercises.prompt: A dairy heifer in an area endemic with brown ear ticks develops an acute 41.5°C fever, swollen prescapular lymph nodes, and cloudy white eyes. A lymph aspirate reveals Koch's blue bodies inside lymphocytes. What is the specific life-saving chemotherapeutic drug?
exercises.explanation:
Buparvaquone is the specific antiprotozoal drug that kills Theileria parva schizonts and piroplasms. Administered at 2.5 mg/kg IM, it stops the disease if given before irreversible pulmonary edema sets in.

Why the other options are wrong: Diminazene treats Trypanosomiasis and Babesiosis; it has zero efficacy against Theileria parva (ECF). Penicillin is an antibacterial that does not kill protozoan parasites. Ivermectin treats external parasites and nematodes, not hemoprotozoa.

options.text: Buparvaquone (2.5 mg/kg deep intramuscularly)
Diminazene aceturate (Berenil)
Penicillin G
Ivermectin injection

exercises.prompt: The brown ear tick that transmits East Coast Fever (*Theileria parva*) in East Africa is scientifically named ___ appendiculatus, while the tsetse fly vector that transmits Trypanosomiasis belongs to the genus ___.
exercises.explanation: Rhipicephalus appendiculatus vectors ECF; Glossina species (morsitans, pallidipes) vector Trypanosomiasis (Nagana).

exercises.prompt: Match each veterinary drug to its specific clinical application.
exercises.explanation: Buparvaquone cures ECF; Berenil cures active Tryps; Samorin prevents Tryps for months; oxytetracycline treats secondary respiratory bacteria.

right.text: First-line curative antiprotozoal against East Coast Fever (Theileriosis)
Fast-acting curative therapeutic injection against active Trypanosomiasis
Depot prophylactic injection protecting cattle against tsetse for 3-4 months
Broad-spectrum antibiotic controlling secondary bacterial lung infections

exercises.prompt: Why are Nzi and biconical tsetse fly traps constructed specifically from royal blue and black fabrics?
exercises.explanation:
Extensive behavioral research confirms that tsetse flies are visually lured by royal blue (which mimics large host silhouettes) and instinctively land on black surfaces before flying up into transparent light traps.

Why the other options are wrong: Tsetse flies are attracted visually, not by heat generated by fabric. The purpose is specifically attracting and killing tsetse flies. The color is chosen strictly for insect optical physiology.

options.text: Tsetse flies possess specialized photoreceptors attracted from long distances to royal blue wavelengths, while matte black stimulates landing and upward entry into the collection cage
Blue fabric absorbs heat, warming the trap to 37°C
Because blue fabric repels mosquitoes
To make the traps easy for pastoralists to find in the bush

exercises.prompt: In a pastoral cow with chronic Trypanosomiasis (Nagana), the hallmark physical indicators include progressive emaciation with a 'razor-back' spine, chalk-white mucous membranes, and a visible pulsing of the ___ vein in the lower neck.
exercises.explanation: Severe hemolytic anemia thins the blood, causing turbulent venous regurgitation that produces a visible bounding jugular pulse in the neck furrow.

lessons.title: Pastoral Vaccine Management & Biosecurity Protocols
lessons.titleSw: Usimamizi wa Chanjo za Mifugo na Mipango ya Kuzuia Magonjwa (Biosecurity)
lessons.briefing: In pastoral ecosystems, acute epidemic diseases—Anthrax, Blackquarter (Blackleg), Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia (CBPP), and Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR)—can decimate 50% of a district's livestock population within weeks. Prevention via mass immunization is infinitely cheaper than treatment. However, veterinary vaccines consist of delicate live-attenuated organisms or fragile protein toxoids that instantly denature if exposed to direct sunlight or ambient desert heat above 8°C. This lesson covers high-consequence pastoral epizootics, the solar-direct drive vaccine cold chain, reconstitution protocols, needle hygiene, and carcass disposal biosecurity (never opening an Anthrax carcass).
lessons.outline: High-consequence pastoral epizootics: Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis), Blackquarter (Clostridium chauvoei), CBPP (Mycoplasma mycoides), Foot-and-Mouth Disease (FMD), and PPR (goat plague); the veterinary cold chain (+2°C to +8°C requirements, conditioned icepacks in vaccine carriers); live lyophilized vaccines vs killed bacterin toxoids; reconstitution rules (sterile diluents, 2-hour field viability window); injection site anatomy: Subcutaneous (SC) loose neck tenting vs Intramuscular (IM) triangular neck zone; syringe calibration and automatic multi-dose drenchers; the fatal Anthrax biosecurity rule: sudden death with dark unclotted blood from orifices, strict prohibition of necropsy/slaughter, and 2-metre deep pit burial with quicklime.

exercises.prompt: A pastoralist finds an adult cow dead in the pasture with no prior illness. Dark, tarry blood is slowly oozing from the nose and rectum, and the blood shows no signs of clotting. What action must the paravet enforce immediately?
exercises.explanation:
Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) produces indestructible spores only upon exposure to atmospheric oxygen. Opening or butchering the carcass contaminates the soil for decades and exposes humans to lethal cutaneous, gastrointestinal, or pulmonary anthrax.

Why the other options are wrong: Performing a necropsy is the single most dangerous mistake; it spreads anthrax spores across the entire pasture. Consuming anthrax meat causes severe intestinal anthrax with near 100% human mortality. This poisons the entire downstream water supply for hundreds of people and livestock.

options.text: Perform an immediate post-mortem necropsy to examine the liver
Butcher the meat quickly and boil it for human consumption
Drag the carcass into the nearest river to wash it away

Strictly forbid butchering, opening, or skinning the carcass; bury the whole unopened carcass at least 2 metres deep covered in quicklime, as opening it exposes Bacillus anthracis to oxygen, triggering deadly soil-contaminating spores

exercises.prompt: Once a live lyophilized veterinary vaccine (such as CBPP or PPR) is reconstituted with sterile diluent in the field, it must be administered to the livestock within a maximum window of ___ hours, after which remaining vaccine must be discarded.
exercises.explanation: Live attenuated vaccine organisms lose viability rapidly once rehydrated at field temperatures. Potency drops below protective thresholds beyond 2 hours.

exercises.prompt: Match each pastoral livestock disease to its characteristic clinical indicator.
exercises.explanation: Anthrax oozes dark unclotted blood; Blackquarter crackles with gas; CBPP produces marbled lung pneumonia; FMD causes mouth drooling and foot blisters.

right.text: Sudden death with dark unclotted tar-like blood oozing from all body orifices
Hot painful thigh/shoulder swelling that becomes cold and crackles with gas (crepitation)
Severe painful coughing with outstretched neck; marbled lungs on post-mortem
Excessive ropy salivation (drooling) and painful blisters on dental pad and hooves

exercises.prompt: When administering an intramuscular (IM) injection of an antibiotic or curative drug to cattle, where is the anatomically correct and safe location on the animal?
exercises.explanation:
The neck triangle avoids major nerves (sciatic nerve in rump) and preserves expensive prime rump/hindquarter meat cuts from injection abscesses.

Why the other options are wrong: Rump injections risk damaging the sciatic nerve (causing permanent leg paralysis) and devalue prime beef cuts. This risks puncturing intestines or causing peritonitis. The tail has insufficient muscle mass and causes intense pain.

options.text: Directly into the center of the rump muscle
The muscular triangle of the neck (bounded above by the nuchal ligament, below by cervical vertebrae, and behind by the shoulder joint)
Directly into the abdominal wall near the navel
Into the tail muscle

exercises.prompt: Veterinary vaccines containing aluminum hydroxide adjuvants (such as Blackquarter bacterins) must be kept between +2°C and +8°C and must NEVER be allowed to ___, because low temperatures precipitate the adjuvant into irreversible crystals that destroy vaccine potency.
exercises.explanation: Freezing ruins killed adjuvanted vaccines. Conditioned icepacks (at 0°C with free water droplets) must be used instead of deep-frozen sub-zero icepacks.

lessons.title: Livestock Obstetrics, Dystocia & Emergency Wound Care
lessons.titleSw: Uzazi wa Mifugo, Kufungua Uzazi Uliokwama (Dystocia) na Matibabu ya Vidonda
lessons.briefing: Calving, lambing, and kidding season is the most critical period in the pastoral calendar. A calf or lamb lost to dystocia (difficult, obstructed birth) is a lost year of milk and herd reproduction; an untreated uterine prolapse or infected hyena bite kills a productive dam. A competent paravet must master internal vaginal exploration, correcting abnormal fetal presentations (head deviations, leg flexions, breech deliveries), applying obstetric calving chains, administering epidural anesthesia, and cleaning and suturing deep traumatic lacerations.
lessons.outline: The three normal stages of ruminant parturition (cervical dilation, fetal expulsion, placental expulsion); normal anterior presentation (two front hooves pointing downward, head resting on knees); defining Dystocia causes (maternal-fetal disproportion, uterine inertia, fetal malpresentation); internal examination hygiene (chlorhexidine/soap, copious methylcellulose lubricant); correcting leg flexions (carpal/shoulder) and head back deviations; calving ropes/chains placement (double half-hitch above and below fetlock); traction timing with maternal labor contractions; caudal epidural anesthesia (lignocaine into Co1-Co2 space); post-partum uterine prolapse replacement; traumatic wound management (debridement, povidone-iodine flushing, interrupted mattress sutures, fly strike/myiasis treatment).

exercises.prompt: A paravet conducts an internal vaginal examination on a cow in prolonged labor. Two legs are felt in the birth canal, but the pads of the hooves are pointing UPWARD toward the cow's tail head, and the second joint above the fetlock bends in the OPPOSITE direction to the fetlock. What presentation is this?
exercises.explanation:
In anterior (front) legs, hooves point downward and knee and fetlock bend in the same direction. In posterior (rear) legs, hooves point upward and the hock bends opposite to the fetlock. The calf is positioned backward.

Why the other options are wrong: Front legs have soles pointing downward, not upward. The anatomy of the two joints confirms these are the two hind legs of a single calf. Uterine torsion presents with a corkscrew vaginal spiral that blocks entry of the hand, not clearly palpated rear limbs.

options.text: Posterior presentation (the back legs are presenting, meaning the calf is coming backwards / breech orientation)
Normal anterior presentation (front legs)
Twins delivering simultaneously
Uterine torsion (twisted uterus)

exercises.prompt: When applying obstetric calving ropes to an extended calf leg, a ___ half-hitch must be used, placing one loop above the fetlock joint and the second loop below the fetlock, to prevent concentrated force from ___ the calf's leg bones.
exercises.explanation: A single loop acts like a garrote and snaps fragile cannon bones under pull. A double half-hitch distributes tension across two separate joints.

exercises.prompt: Match each veterinary obstetric and surgical procedure to its clinical rule.
exercises.explanation: Repulsion creates working room; cupping protects the uterus; hanging drop verifies epidurals; mattress stitches hold tension on thick cattle hide.

right.text: Pushing fetus back into wide abdomen before correcting a folded head or leg
Covering sharp fetal claws with your palm to prevent tearing uterine walls
Confirms correct needle placement in the negative-pressure epidural space
Tension-relieving stitch pattern that everts thick livestock skin edges

exercises.prompt: Why is it strictly forbidden in veterinary obstetrics to use a 4x4 motor vehicle, tractor, or mechanical winch to pull a stuck calf during dystocia?
exercises.explanation:
Mechanical pulling generates thousands of pounds of force. If the fetus is locked by wide hips, winches will snap the maternal pelvis, tear the birth canal open, and cause immediate fatal internal hemorrhage. Traction must never exceed two adult men.

Why the other options are wrong: While fumes are unpleasant, the immediate catastrophic danger is mechanical trauma and structural tearing. The ropes hold, but the cow's body tears apart. This is a myth; the danger is maternal and fetal death from physical trauma.

options.text: Because vehicles emit exhaust fumes that poison the calf
Because ropes break under mechanical tension
It causes the milk to sour immediately
Mechanical traction exerts uncontrolled tons of pulling force, crushing the calf's ribcage, rupturing the maternal pelvis, and causing fatal uterine artery avulsion

exercises.prompt: To stop violent maternal abdominal straining while manipulating a difficult calving or replacing a prolapsed uterus, a caudal epidural injection of 5 mL of 2% ___ is injected into the first inter-coccygeal space at the base of the tail head.
exercises.explanation: Lignocaine (Lidocaine) 2% blocks sensory and motor nerves to the reproductive tract, stopping straining while allowing the cow to maintain motor function in her legs.

lessons.title: Acaricide Plunge Dips & Parasite Resistance Management
lessons.titleSw: Mabwawa ya Kuoshea Ng'ombe (Plunge Dips) na Kuzuia Usugu wa Wadudu
lessons.briefing: Controlling tick vectors—the carriers of East Coast Fever, Babesiosis, Anaplasmosis, and Heartwater—requires disciplined community infrastructure. The communal plunge dip (a 15,000-litre concrete vat through which hundreds of cattle swim weekly) is the most cost-effective tick control tool in Africa. However, poor dip management—allowing rainwater dilution, failing to test chemical wash strength, or using the wrong acaricide class—triggers rapid tick resistance, rendering million-shilling facilities useless. This capstone lesson covers plunge dip civil engineering, chemical classes (amidines, synthetic pyrethroids, organophosphates), the dip vat titration test kit, replenishing depleted vats, hand spray-race calibration, and rotational strategies to break tick resistance.
lessons.outline: Communal plunge dip architecture: collection crush, footbath silt traps, 15,000L deep swim tank, splash curtains, draining race with sump return; acaricide chemical classes: Amidines (Amitraz 0.025%), Synthetic Pyrethroids (Deltamethrin / Cypermethrin), Organophosphates (Chlorfenvinphos); the 'Stripping' phenomenon (ticks and hair removing chemical faster than water); dip wash titration testing protocols (testing chemical active ingredient strength); topping-up and reinforcement arithmetic; operating mechanical spray races; managing acaricide resistance (chemical class rotation every 2-3 years, refugia maintenance); PHOTO_CAPTURE assessment rubric of livestock examination, dip facility, or veterinary equipment.

exercises.prompt: A communal cattle dip tank filled with an Amitraz (Amidine) acaricide wash is tested with a field titration kit and found to be under-strength after 1,000 cattle have swum through it. Why does the chemical concentration drop faster than water volume?
exercises.explanation:
As cattle pass through, the lipophilic chemical adheres to grease on the hair, removing active molecules faster than water is lost. Topping up requires a richer 'replenishment rate' (e.g., 1:600 instead of 1:1,000) to maintain lethal concentration.

Why the other options are wrong: Amitraz is non-volatile in water and does not evaporate rapidly. Cattle dislike the taste and do not drink significant volumes; water loss is mechanical carryout on coats. Stripping is a physical surface-absorption phenomenon, not bacterial degradation.

options.text: The chemical evaporates into the air within 2 hours
Cattle drink the dip wash in large quantities

The 'Stripping' phenomenon: Cattle hair and hide absorb the chemical active ingredient molecules preferentially faster than water, leaving the remaining bath progressively diluted and requiring higher-rate reinforcement concentrate when topping up
Bacteria in the cattle dung destroy the chlorine atoms

exercises.prompt: When using Amitraz (an Amidine class acaricide) in an open concrete plunge dip, the wash is chemically unstable at neutral or acidic pH and must be stabilized by adding hydrated ___ (calcium hydroxide) to maintain a high alkaline pH of greater than ___.
exercises.explanation: Amitraz hydrolyzes and degrades in acidic or neutral wash water. Adding 10 kg of hydrated lime per 1,000 L maintains pH > 10, keeping the active ingredient stable for months.

exercises.prompt: Match each plunge dip structural element to its functional design purpose.
exercises.explanation: Footbaths stop mud; 2.2 m forces swimming; forks dunk ears and horns; draining races conserve expensive chemical.

right.text: Washes caked mud off hooves so soil does not bind and deactivate tank chemicals
Forces adult cattle to swim, completely submerging the body and perineum
Used by operator on gantry to gently dunk cow heads underwater twice
Sloped holding pens where cattle stand to allow excess wash to drain to sumps

exercises.prompt: To manage and prevent chemical acaricide resistance among tick populations in a pastoral grazing zone, how should communal dipping programs rotate acaricides?
exercises.explanation:
Resistance develops to a specific biochemical mechanism of action. Rotating chemical classes breaks the evolutionary cycle by killing ticks that survived the previous class. Switching brand names within the same class is useless.

Why the other options are wrong: Brand names have no biological relevance; switching brands of the same class maintains continuous selection pressure for resistance. Sub-lethal under-dosing is the primary cause of rapid resistance evolution. Cocktail mixing triggers multi-class cross-resistance and causes severe chemical toxicities.

options.text: Switch brand names every week while keeping the same active chemical
Rotate between completely different chemical classes (e.g., switch from an Amidine like Amitraz to a Synthetic Pyrethroid like Deltamethrin) every 2 to 3 years
Dilute the chemical to 10% of normal strength during the dry season
Mix organophosphates, amidines, and pyrethroids together in the same tank

exercises.prompt: Photograph a livestock clinical examination, cattle plunge dip or spray-race facility, veterinary medicine kit, or cold-chain vaccine carrier from your pastoral animal health practice. Ensure the image clearly displays animal restraint, dosage syringes, dip water testing, or clinical diagnostic instruments, and include your written clinical inspection report.
exercises.explanation: Photographic documentation of veterinary facilities, cattle handling races, or clinical examination equipment verifies practical competency in pastoral animal health management and biosecurity protocols.

rubric.criterion: Photograph clearly shows livestock examination, plunge dip facility, spray race, or veterinary clinical equipment
Handling safety (crushes, halters, head gates) or medical instruments (syringes, thermometers, testing kit) are distinctly visible
Written report records animal vital signs, diagnostic findings, drug dosages/routes, or dip vat chemical concentration
Image is sharp, well-lit, showing professional animal welfare and biosecurity standards

lessons.title: Week 2 — Compost, material recovery, and circular enterprise
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 2 — Compost, recovery, na biashara
lessons.briefing:
Compost needs carbon-rich browns, nitrogen-rich greens, moisture like a wrung sponge, oxygen, and time. Exclude batteries, glass, plastics, treated timber, meat where the system cannot manage it, and human waste unless a specialised process exists. Turn or aerate; record temperature where pathogen control is claimed.

Material recovery: sort by buyer specification, remove contamination, bale or bundle safely, and store dry. Glass by colour where demanded; metals separated; e-waste sent to licensed handlers. Never heat wires to burn off insulation—the fumes poison workers and neighbours.

Business records include input weight, recovery rate, labour, transport, buyer price, rejects, and PPE costs. Community benefit is real only if the enterprise is safe, lawful, and solvent.
lessons.briefingSw: Wiki 2 — Compost, recovery, na biashara: usalama, utaratibu sahihi, ukaguzi wa ubora, na huduma kwa jamii.

exercises.prompt: Which action is the safest professional starting point for material recovery?
exercises.explanation: A competent craft worker assesses risk, scope, people, tools, and standards before starting.

options.text: Start immediately without inspecting the site or client
Assess hazards and needs, select PPE/tools, explain the plan, then begin
Copy a social-media clip without checking local conditions
Let an untrained bystander make every technical decision

exercises.prompt: What is the strongest evidence that material recovery was completed well?
exercises.explanation: Quality is demonstrated with a repeatable inspection, measurement, or functional test.

options.text: The worker says it is fine
A documented inspection or functional test against the job specification
The cheapest material was used
The work was hidden before testing

exercises.prompt: The documented check used to prove this work meets its requirements is a quality ___.
exercises.hint: A planned check, not an opinion.
exercises.explanation: A quality check provides evidence for the client, trainer, and next technician.

exercises.prompt: A buyer offers more money if workers burn cable insulation to recover copper quickly. What should the supervisor do?
exercises.explanation: Community trades carry public consequences. Defects are corrected and tested, never concealed.

options.text: Continue and conceal the problem
Stop, make the area safe, explain the defect, correct it, then test and document
Ask the client to sign before seeing the work
Remove the safety device so the job appears complete

lessons.title: Week 1 — Waste audit, segregation, and collection safety
lessons.titleSw: Wiki 1 — Ukaguzi na kutenganisha taka
lessons.briefing:
Start with a waste audit: source, type, mass or volume, contamination, collection frequency, and destination. Segregate at source because a clean PET bottle has value and a PET bottle mixed with food and sharps is a hazard. Use locally understood labels and colours; train users and inspect bins.

PPE depends on risk: gloves resistant to puncture, boots, high-visibility clothing, and respiratory protection where dust requires it. Never hand-sort closed bags that may contain needles. Medical waste, batteries, chemicals, oil, and e-waste need authorised routes; do not burn them in an open pit. Collection routes protect workers from traffic and overfilled containers.

Record weights and rejected loads. Data proves diversion from landfill and whether the enterprise is profitable.

lessons.title: Day 1: Slow Sand Gravity Filter Sizing & Stratification
lessons.titleSw: Siku ya 1: Upimaji na Utengenezaji wa Chujio la Mchanga
lessons.briefing:
Slow sand filtration is the primary bio-mechanical technology for drinking water in decentralized or reconstructed societies. Unlike pressurized rapid sand filters which require backwash pumps and chemical dosing, slow sand operates strictly under gravity and biological predation.

CRITICAL SPECIFICATIONS & STRATIFICATION:
1. Under-drainage layer: 10-15 cm of clean, washed coarse gravel (12 to 25 mm diameter) surrounding the perforated exit manifold.
2. Intermediate pea-gravel layer: 5 cm of washed pea gravel (2 to 6 mm diameter) placed above the coarse stones to prevent fine filter sand from migrating downward into the underdrain.
3. Active filter sand bed: 60 to 90 cm of clean quartz river sand. Effective grain size D10 must be between 0.15 mm and 0.35 mm with a Uniformity Coefficient (U = D60/D10) of less than 3.0.
4. Supernatant raw water head: 0.7 to 1.0 meter depth maintained continuously over the sand surface to provide positive hydrostatic head and prevent disturbance to the top layer.
5. Filtration velocity: 0.1 to 0.2 meters per hour (100 to 200 liters per hour per square meter of filter surface area).

OPERATIONAL WARNING:
Never allow the sand bed to drain dry. If the biological hyponeuston layer loses hydration, the microbial predators perish and the bed requires a full 14 to 21-day ripening cycle to regain pathogen removal efficacy.

exercises.prompt: Match each stratification stratum of the slow sand filter to its exact engineering requirement.
exercises.hint: The sand layer is the deepest filtering stratum; gravel protects the outlet.
exercises.explanation: Graded stratification ensures hydraulic conductivity without sand loss into the treated effluent cistern.

right.text: 60-90 cm depth, D10 grain size 0.15-0.35 mm
5 cm depth, 2-6 mm pea gravel
10-15 cm depth, 12-25 mm coarse stones
0.7-1.0 m continuous gravity water depth

exercises.prompt: The standard filtration rate of a slow sand filter operates between 100 and ___ liters per hour per square meter.
exercises.hint: Normal range is 0.1 to 0.2 meters per hour (100 to 200 L/m²/hr).
exercises.explanation: Velocities above 200 L/m²/hr shear the biological layer and force pathogens through the sand bed without sufficient detention time.

exercises.prompt: During filter assembly, an apprentice suggests using unwashed ocean beach sand because it is already fine and plentiful. Why is this catastrophic for a drinking water system?
exercises.hint: Marine sand carries soluble salts and shell fragments that cement under water.
exercises.explanation: River quartz sand is inert. Marine sand leaches high salt and dissolved shell lime, altering pH, hardening water, and cementing the bed into impermeable sandstone.

exercises.hint: Think about particle migration between disparate grain sizes.
exercises.explanation: Without a transition size, fine sand immediately sifts downward into coarse stone gaps, causing subsidence, channeling, and sand discharge into the outlet.

options.text: To chemically kill enteric viruses

To add mineral flavour to the water
